teile.einleitung: OSIRIS-REx was a NASA space probe that brought samples from the asteroid Bennu to Earth. The capsule landed in 2023 and contained the largest sample from an asteroid so far. After that, the probe flew on to another target under a new name.
wichtigste: Bennu is a dark, carbon-rich asteroid.
OSIRIS-REx was launched in 2016 and reached Bennu at the end of 2018.
It took its sample in 2020 with a short burst of nitrogen.
In September 2023 the capsule landed with about 121.6 grams of material.
Bennu is a loose rubble pile asteroid.
As OSIRIS-APEX, the probe is flying on to the asteroid Apophis.

abschnitte.text: **Bennu** is a dark **B-type asteroid** with a lot of **carbon**, about half a kilometre across. Such bodies are considered almost unchanged material from the early days of the **solar system**. That is why researchers hope to find in them traces of the first building blocks of planets. The name **REx** stands for **Regolith Explorer**. Regolith is the loose rubble on the surface.

The probe was launched in **2016** and reached Bennu at the **end of 2018**. For two years it measured the asteroid precisely. In October **2020** came the sampling, the **Touch-And-Go**. The sampling arm **TAGSAM** touched the surface for only a few seconds. A **burst of nitrogen** swirled dust and pebbles into the sampling head. The arm sank in with almost no resistance. So Bennu is as loose as a **ball pit**, a **rubble pile** of loosely held-together lumps.

In **September 2023**, the probe dropped a capsule, which landed on a parachute in the desert of Utah in the USA. Inside was about **121.6 grams** of material, the largest asteroid sample ever brought back. The goal had been at least 60 grams. The samples contain **clay minerals**, **phosphates** and **salts** that form when salt water evaporates. They show that liquid **salt water** once existed on Bennu's parent body.

Bennu is considered a **potentially hazardous asteroid**. Orbit calculations give a probability of impact of about **1 in 2,700** for the time around the year **2182**. That is very small. Thanks to the measurements by OSIRIS-REx, Bennu's orbit is now known very precisely.

After dropping the capsule, the probe flew on and is now called **OSIRIS-APEX**. Its new target is the asteroid **Apophis**. It will fly very close past the Earth in April 2029. Shortly afterwards, the probe is to explore it.

gewusst: When the sample container was opened, so much dust lay outside the actual chamber that the researchers studied this material first.
Amino acids were also found in the Bennu samples, important building blocks found in living things.

teile.einleitung: Light is the fastest thing in the universe. In a single second it travels almost 300,000 kilometres. Even so, the universe is so huge that even light can take a very long time to get somewhere.
wichtigste: Nothing in the universe is faster than **light**.
Light travels almost 300,000 kilometres per second.
In one second, light could whizz around the Earth about 7.5 times.
A radio signal from the Earth takes a few minutes to reach Mars.
Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.
The distance light travels in a year is called a **light year**.

abschnitte.text: The **speed of light** is almost **300,000 kilometres per second**. Nothing can be faster, no spaceship and no particle. The radio waves we use to control space probes are also exactly as fast as light. In one second, light could whizz around the whole Earth **about 7.5 times**. For the distance from **Geneva to St Gallen**, it needs only **about a thousandth of a second**.

Light takes just over a second to travel from the Moon to the Earth. Sunlight has already been travelling for a good **8 minutes** when it reaches us. To the distant planet **Neptune** it takes **about 4 hours**. A radio signal from the Earth to **Mars** needs **a few minutes**, depending on where the two planets are at the time. That is why you cannot steer a Mars rover directly like a toy car.

The distance light travels in a year is called a **light year**. That is almost **10 trillion kilometres**. Despite the word “year”, a light year is not a time but a **distance**. Astronomers need this unit because kilometres are far too small for the distances between the stars. The nearest star after the Sun is just over four light years away.

When we look at a distant star, we do not see it as it is today. Its **light was travelling for a long time** before it reached our eyes. So we see the star as it was **in the past**. With very distant galaxies, the light has even travelled for billions of years. That is why, with large telescopes, researchers look far back into the past of the universe.

For a long time many people thought light was infinitely fast. In the 17th century, the Danish astronomer **Ole Rømer** noticed that the eclipses of one of Jupiter's moons sometimes came late. He explained this by saying that light takes different lengths of time depending on the distance to Jupiter. Today the speed of light is fixed exactly, and the **metre** is even defined with its help.

gewusst: If the Sun suddenly went out, we would only notice after a good 8 minutes.
The speed of light is fixed at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.

teile.einleitung: The Hubble Space Telescope has been orbiting the Earth since 1990 and has taken some of the most famous pictures of the universe. It shows stars, nebulae and distant galaxies more sharply than is hardly possible from the Earth.
wichtigste: The space shuttle Discovery took Hubble into space in April 1990.
The main mirror has a diameter of 2.4 metres.
Hubble orbits just over 500 kilometres above the Earth.
Astronauts visited Hubble five times to service and repair it.
Hubble is a joint project of NASA and ESA.
The James Webb Telescope was launched in 2021 as its successor.

abschnitte.text: On 24 April 1990, the space shuttle **Discovery** was launched on mission STS-31, and the next day it released Hubble into its orbit. The telescope bears the name of the US astronomer **Edwin Hubble**. He showed that there are many other galaxies besides the Milky Way and that the universe is expanding. Hubble is a project of the American **NASA** and the European **ESA**. Europe supplied solar panels and a camera, among other things.

At its heart is a **main mirror** 2.4 metres across, which collects the light of distant objects. Hubble flies just over 500 kilometres above the Earth, above the **atmosphere**. The air shimmers and swallows some of the light, which is why telescopes on the ground see less sharply. In space, Hubble has a calm, clear view. It observes visible light, but also some ultraviolet and infrared.

Shortly after the launch, it was noticed that the mirror had a small **grinding error** and the pictures were blurred. In 1993, on the first **servicing mission**, astronauts installed corrective optics, and after that the pictures were pin-sharp. Up to 2009 there were five visits in all by space shuttles. Instruments were swapped, batteries renewed and faults repaired. Because Hubble flies so low, the space shuttles were able to reach it.

In 1995, Hubble looked for ten days at a tiny, apparently empty patch of sky. In the picture, the **Hubble Deep Field**, about 3,000 distant galaxies could be seen. Hubble also helped to work out the **age of the universe** more precisely. People all over the world know its pictures of gas nebulae such as the “Pillars of Creation”.

On 25 December 2021, the **James Webb Space Telescope** was launched. It has a bigger mirror and observes mainly in **infrared light**. This lets it look even further back into the past of the universe. Hubble is still working, and the two telescopes complement each other.

gewusst: Hubble goes around the Earth in about 95 minutes.
The Hubble Deep Field showed that even a tiny piece of sky is full of galaxies.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's orbit is the path along which the Earth circles the Sun. It takes about 365.25 days for one lap, which is a year. As it does so, it races through space at about 30 kilometres per second without us feeling anything.
wichtigste: The Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once.
On average it is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun.
The Earth's orbit is an almost circular ellipse.
The Earth moves along its orbit at about 30 kilometres per second.
The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January.
The seasons are caused mainly by the tilt of the Earth's axis, not by the distance from the Sun.
Because of the quarter day, there is a leap year every four years.

abschnitte.text: The Earth's orbit is the path the Earth takes around the Sun. The Sun's **gravity** keeps the Earth on this path; otherwise it would fly off straight into space. One whole lap takes about 365.25 days; that is a **year**. The orbit is about 940 million kilometres long.

The Earth's orbit is an **ellipse**, but it looks almost like a circle. The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January, at about 147 million kilometres; this point is called the **perihelion**. It is furthest away at the beginning of July, at about 152 million kilometres; this is the **aphelion**. On average the distance is about 150 million kilometres, which is called an astronomical unit.

The Earth flies around the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second, which is over 100,000 kilometres per hour. Near the Sun, in January, it is a bit faster than in July. We feel nothing of this, because everything on Earth moves along evenly with it. It is like being on a smoothly running train, where you only notice it is moving by looking at the landscape.

Many people believe it is warm in summer because the Earth is closer to the Sun then. That is not true, because in our part of the world it is winter in January, even though the Earth is closest to the Sun then. The main reason for the seasons is the **tilt of the Earth's axis** of about 23.4 degrees. Because one orbit takes about a quarter of a day longer than 365 days, a 29 February is added every four years; this is the **leap year**.

For a long time people believed the Earth was at the centre and the Sun circled around it. In 1543, **Nicolaus Copernicus** published his work in which the Earth circles the Sun. At the beginning of the 17th century, Johannes Kepler realised that planetary orbits are ellipses. Later, Isaac Newton used gravitation to explain why the planets move around the Sun like this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A slightly stretched, oval circle shape.
The point of the orbit where the Earth is closest to the Sun.
The point of the orbit where the Earth is furthest from the Sun.
The average distance between the Earth and the Sun, about 150 million kilometres.

gewusst: In the minute you spend reading, you travel about 1,800 kilometres around the Sun with the Earth.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach the Earth.
On your birthday, the Earth is almost exactly at the same spot in its orbit as when you were born.

teile.einleitung: Neutrino astronomy explores the universe with neutrinos, tiny and almost invisible particles. They pass through almost everything and bring news from the inside of stars and from distant galaxies. This needs huge detectors deep underground, in ice or in the sea.
wichtigste: Neutrinos are electrically neutral and only react through the weak interaction and gravity.
That is why they pass through almost everything and are very hard to detect.
Magnetic fields do not deflect them, so they point back to their source.
About two dozen neutrinos from supernova 1987A were detected.
Masatoshi Koshiba received part of the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 2002.
Super-Kamiokande in Japan contains about 50,000 tonnes of pure water.

abschnitte.text: **Neutrinos** are electrically neutral and do not feel the strong nuclear force. Apart from gravity, they only react with matter through the **weak interaction**, and extremely rarely. They fly almost unhindered through planets, stars and through us too. Every second, many billions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through every square centimetre of our bodies without us noticing anything.

Charged particles from space, the **cosmic rays**, are deflected by magnetic fields. When they arrive here, you can no longer tell where they came from. Neutrinos, on the other hand, fly in a **straight line**. So their direction points straight back to their **source**. They also come from places that no light can escape from, for example from the core of an exploding star.

In 1987, a star exploded in a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way. The detectors **Kamiokande II**, **IMB** and **Baksan** recorded about **24 neutrinos** between them. They were the first neutrinos from a source outside the solar system. They arrived a few hours **before the light**. The neutrinos left the collapsing core of the star at once, while the light was only released when the shock wave reached the surface. For the detection of cosmic neutrinos, **Masatoshi Koshiba** received the Nobel Prize in 2002, together with Raymond Davis and Riccardo Giacconi.

Because neutrinos react so rarely, you need a great deal of material. **Super-Kamiokande** in Japan is a tank with about **50,000 tonnes** of pure water, about 1,000 metres deep in a mine. Over 11,000 light sensors, so-called **photomultipliers**, watch for tiny flashes of light. The rock above shields off disturbing radiation. The **IceCube** experiment at the South Pole uses a cubic kilometre of ice as its detector.

The European project **KM3NeT** anchors long strings of light sensors several thousand metres deep on the floor of the **Mediterranean**, off Sicily and off southern France. The seawater shields off disturbances and serves as the medium for the light. In 2023, KM3NeT recorded a neutrino with an estimated energy of about **220 peta-electronvolts**. This event, published in 2025, was far above all the neutrino energies measured before.

gewusst: A neutrino could fly through a wall of lead many light years thick and would have a good chance of not hitting anything.
The neutrinos from the Sun show what is happening in its core right now, while its light takes a very long time to get out.

teile.einleitung: Enceladus is a small, icy moon of the planet Saturn. It is famous because fountains of water shoot out into space from its south pole. Beneath its icy crust lies an ocean, which is why researchers are very interested in it.
wichtigste: Enceladus is a moon of Saturn about 500 kilometres across.
William Herschel discovered it in 1789.
It is named after Enceladus, a giant from Greek legend.
Its fresh icy surface reflects almost all sunlight.
Fountains of water rise from the “tiger stripes” at the south pole.
Beneath the icy crust lies an ocean of salt water that surrounds the whole moon.
The ice grains from the fountains feed Saturn's E ring.

abschnitte.text: The astronomer **William Herschel** discovered Enceladus in 1789 with his large reflecting telescope. In the same year he also found Saturn's moon Mimas. Herschel was already famous because he had discovered the planet Uranus. The name comes from Greek legend: **Enceladus** was a giant who fought against the gods of Olympus. According to the legend, he was buried under the island of Sicily.

Enceladus is small: its diameter is only about **500 kilometres**. Our Moon is almost seven times wider. The surface is made of clean, fresh **ice**. This ice reflects almost all the sunlight. That is why Enceladus is one of the brightest bodies in the whole solar system.

At the south pole of Enceladus there are four long, parallel cracks. Because they look like the stripes of a tiger in pictures, they are called **tiger stripes**. Fountains of water vapour and tiny ice grains shoot out of these cracks into space. They were discovered by the space probe **Cassini**, which studied Saturn for many years. Some of the ice grains do not fall back but spread out along the moon's orbit. This is how Saturn's wide, thin **E ring** is formed and renewed.

According to current knowledge, beneath the icy crust lies a **global ocean** of salt water. This is shown by a slight wobble of the moon in its orbit: the icy crust is not firmly attached to the core, there is water in between. The fountains bring water from this ocean to the surface. This makes it possible to study the ocean without drilling through the ice.

In Cassini's measurements, researchers found salts and various carbon compounds. In 2023, **phosphates** were also detected in the ice grains. **Phosphorus** is an important building block of genetic material and cells. That is why Enceladus is considered one of the most exciting places to search for conditions for life. Nobody knows whether living things really exist there.

gewusst: Enceladus is so bright that it reflects more light than fresh snow on Earth.
Without Enceladus, Saturn's E ring would not exist in its present form.
The space probe Cassini even flew right through the water fountains and took samples.

teile.einleitung: Countless tiny grains float in space: cosmic dust. Every day some of it trickles down onto the Earth, and stars and planets even formed from such dust long ago.
wichtigste: Cosmic dust is also called space dust.
Many tonnes of it fall onto the Earth every day.
Particles from space smaller than a millimetre are called micrometeorites.
Such grains have even been found on rooftops.
A lot of the dust in the solar system comes from comets and asteroids.
In 2006, the Stardust probe brought comet dust to Earth.

abschnitte.text: Many tiny grains of rock, carbon or ice float in space. They are called **space dust** or **cosmic dust**. Many of them are smaller than the thickness of a hair. A large part of the dust in the solar system comes from **comets**, which lose dust when they come close to the Sun. Collisions between **asteroids** also create dust.

Every day, many tonnes of tiny dust grains trickle down from space onto the Earth. But we do not notice them because they are so small. Particles smaller than a millimetre that reach the ground are called **micrometeorites**. Researchers have even found such grains in the dirt in **gutters** and on **rooftops**. To see them, you need a **microscope**.

abschnitte.titel: Building material for stars and planets
abschnitte.text: In space there are huge clouds of **gas and dust**. When such a cloud contracts under gravity, new stars form. **Planets** form from the rest. Our Sun and the Earth also formed like this about 4.6 billion years ago. So some of the atoms in our bodies were once stardust.

NASA's **Stardust** probe flew to a comet and collected its dust. For this it used **aerogel**, an extremely light foam. The fast dust grains got stuck in it without breaking. In 2006, a capsule with the dust landed on Earth. Researchers all over the world were then able to study it.

gewusst: Aerogel is so light that it consists almost entirely of air.
Sometimes you can see dust in the solar system as a faint glow in the sky, the zodiacal light.

teile.einleitung: In space there is no air to breathe and no water from the tap. A life support system makes sure that astronauts can still breathe, drink and stay healthy. On the International Space Station ISS, it works almost like a small cycle.
wichtigste: The ISS gets most of its oxygen through the **electrolysis** of water.
In the **Sabatier reactor**, carbon dioxide and hydrogen are turned into methane and water.
In 2023, the ISS was able to recover about 98 per cent of its water.
The cabin of the ISS has an air pressure of about 1 bar, as at sea level.
During the flight, the Apollo capsule contained pure oxygen at about a third of normal pressure.
The ESA project **MELiSSA** is researching a closed cycle with microorganisms and plants.

abschnitte.text: On the ISS, most of the oxygen for breathing comes from **water**. Using electricity from the solar panels, water is split into **oxygen** and **hydrogen**. This process is called **electrolysis**. The carbon dioxide the astronauts breathe out is filtered from the air. In the **Sabatier reactor**, it reacts with the hydrogen to form **methane** and **water**. The water can be used again.

Water is precious in space, because every litre has to be taken up by rocket. That is why the ISS collects almost everything: moisture from the air, sweat and even urine. The water is cleaned until it is cleaner than much drinking water on Earth. In **2023**, the system reached a recovery rate of **about 98 per cent**.

The cabin of the ISS has an air pressure of **about 1 bar**, as at sea level. The air is mixed in a similar way to the Earth's, with a lot of **nitrogen** and some oxygen. On the **Apollo flights** it was different: during the flight, the astronauts breathed **pure oxygen** at about a third of normal pressure. This saved weight but brought a higher risk of fire.

A spacesuit has a lower pressure than the cabin. If an astronaut simply went outside, **nitrogen** dissolved in the blood could form bubbles, as with divers who come up too fast. This is called **decompression sickness**. That is why astronauts breathe **pure oxygen** for a long time before a spacewalk. This removes the nitrogen from the body.

On **Apollo 13** in 1970, an oxygen tank was damaged, and the crew had to move into the lunar module. There the **lithium hydroxide canisters** that bind carbon dioxide from the air were not enough. The astronauts adapted canisters from the command module using tape and other things they had on board. For long journeys, ESA is researching a closed cycle with **MELiSSA**, in which **microorganisms and plants** recycle waste, air and water.

gewusst: On Apollo 13, the capsule's canisters were square and the lunar module's fittings round, so they had to improvise.
On the ISS, drinking water is recovered from urine.

teile.einleitung: Europa Clipper is a NASA space probe. It is on its way to Jupiter to study its icy moon Europa closely. The main question is: does Europa offer conditions in which life would be possible?
wichtigste: Europa Clipper was launched on 14 October 2024 on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy.
The probe is due to arrive at Jupiter in April 2030.
On the way, it picks up speed from Mars and the Earth.
It orbits Jupiter and flies past Europa 49 times.
This keeps the dangerous radiation small on each flyby.
The solar arrays measure about 30 metres from tip to tip.
The REASON radar measures the thickness of the icy crust.

abschnitte.text: Europa Clipper was launched on **14 October 2024** from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The rocket was a **Falcon Heavy** from the company SpaceX. Originally, NASA's Space Launch System was planned for this. Europa Clipper is the largest probe NASA has ever built for a planetary mission. Its **solar arrays** measure about **30.5 metres** from tip to tip.

The journey to Jupiter is very long. That is why the probe uses so-called **swing-bys**: it flies close past planets and picks up speed as it does so. In March 2025, Europa Clipper flew past **Mars**. In December 2026, the probe is due to fly past the **Earth**. Then in **April 2030**, it is due to arrive at Jupiter.

Europa lies deep in Jupiter's **radiation belt**. This radiation damages the probe's electronics. That is why Europa Clipper does not orbit the moon itself, but **Jupiter**. In doing so, the probe flies past Europa **49 times**. After each short flyby, it recovers far out, where the radiation is weaker. The lowest flyby brings it to about 25 kilometres from the surface.

Scientists suspect a **global saltwater ocean** beneath Europa's icy crust. The probe studies the **thickness of the ice**, the ocean, the composition and the geology of the moon. The instrument **REASON** is a **radar** that can see through ice. It sends radar waves into the crust and receives the echoes from layers inside. But Europa Clipper does not search directly for living things. It is meant to find out whether Europa offers **conditions friendly to life**.

gewusst: The scientific flybys of Europa are due to begin in 2031.
With its solar arrays unfolded, Europa Clipper is wider than a basketball court is long.

teile.einleitung: At half moon, exactly half of the Moon's disc is bright. There is a waxing and a waning half moon. You can see them in the sky at different times of day.
wichtigste: At half moon, half of the Moon's disc is bright.
About 7 days after new moon you see the first half moon.
With the waxing half moon, the right side is bright in Switzerland.
The waxing half moon is also called the first quarter, and after it comes the full moon.
You can see the waxing half moon in the afternoon and evening.
You can see the waning half moon well in the early morning.

abschnitte.text: The Moon does not shine by itself. It is lit up by the **Sun**, and we see the reflected light. Depending on how the Sun, Earth and Moon are placed in relation to each other, we see more or less of the bright side. At **half moon**, exactly **half** of the disc is bright. Then, seen from the Earth, the Sun and Moon are roughly at right angles to each other.

After **new moon**, a thin crescent appears first. It gets wider every day; the Moon is **waxing**. About **7 days** after new moon, the first half moon is there. Here in Switzerland, the **right side** is bright then. It is also called the **first quarter**, because a quarter of the lunar month is over. You can see it well in the **afternoon and evening**, and it sets at midnight.

After the waxing half moon, the Moon gets rounder and rounder. About a week later it is **full moon**, and the whole disc shines. After that the Moon **wanes** again. This means you see **less of it** every day. A whole lunar cycle from new moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days.

About a week after full moon comes the **waning half moon**. Now the left side is bright. It is also called the **last quarter**. It only rises at midnight. That is why you can see it well in the **early morning**, often even in daylight in the morning. After that it becomes a thin crescent again until it is new moon.

gewusst: In the southern hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is the other way round: there the left side is bright at the waxing half moon.
You do not only see the Moon at night. The half moon can often be seen in the sky in broad daylight too.

teile.einleitung: A model of the solar system shows the Sun and the planets made smaller. This makes it easier to imagine their sizes and distances. You quickly notice how huge and empty the solar system is.
wichtigste: If the Sun is the size of a football, the Earth is only the size of a **pinhead**.
With a Sun of 22 cm, the Earth is about 24 metres away.
If everything is made a billion times smaller, the Sun is about 1.4 metres across.
A **tellurion** shows how the Earth and Moon circle the Sun.
In the **planetarium** of the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne, the starry sky is projected onto the dome.
About 500 years ago, **Nicolaus Copernicus** wrote that the Earth circles the Sun.

abschnitte.text: Imagine the Sun is a **football** 22 cm across. Then the Earth is only the size of a **pinhead**. It is **about 24 metres** from the football. Jupiter would be a marble more than 120 metres away. Neptune would already be over 700 metres away. That is why a model at the right scale **hardly fits into a classroom**: **the distances are huge**.

If everything is made **a billion times smaller**, the **Sun is about 1.4 metres** across. The Earth would be about the size of a grape and 150 metres away. Neptune would be about 4.5 kilometres away. In Switzerland there are several **planet trails** where you can walk through such a model. At each planet there is a board with information.

A **tellurion** is a model with a small mechanism. It shows how **the Earth and Moon circle the Sun**. Often the Sun is a lamp, so you can also see day and night or the phases of the Moon. In the **Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne** there is a **planetarium**. In this domed hall, the starry sky is projected onto the ceiling, and you can look at the stars as on a clear night.

abschnitte.titel: Earth or Sun in the middle
abschnitte.text: In the past, many people thought that **the Earth** was at the centre of the universe. The Sun, Moon and stars were thought to turn around it. About 500 years ago, **Nicolaus Copernicus** wrote that the Earth and the other planets **circle the Sun**. This is called the **heliocentric view of the world**. Later, scientists such as Galileo Galilei and Johannes Kepler confirmed this idea with their observations and calculations.

gewusst: The Sun is so big that over a million Earths would fit inside it.
In the football model, the nearest star after the Sun would be thousands of kilometres away.

teile.einleitung: A refracting telescope is a telescope that uses glass lenses to make distant things look closer. It was the very first kind of telescope. With it, researchers discovered moons, craters and countless stars over 400 years ago.
wichtigste: In 1608, the spectacle maker **Hans Lipperhey** in the Netherlands applied for a patent for a telescope.
The large lens at the front is called the **objective**, and the small lens by the eye the **eyepiece**.
The magnification is the focal length of the objective divided by the focal length of the eyepiece.
Simple lenses produce coloured fringes: **chromatic aberration**.
An **achromat** made of two types of glass greatly reduces this colour error.
The largest refracting telescope used successfully is at the Yerkes Observatory in the USA.

abschnitte.text: In **1608**, the spectacle maker **Hans Lipperhey** in the Netherlands submitted a **patent application** for a telescope. Soon the Italian scientist **Galileo Galilei** heard about it too. He built telescopes himself and pointed them at the sky. In this way he discovered, among other things, the four large moons of Jupiter and mountains on the Moon.

A refracting telescope has two important parts. At the front sits a large lens, the **objective**. It collects the light and forms an image. At the back you look through a small lens, the **eyepiece**, which magnifies this image like a magnifying glass. The **magnification** is calculated like this: focal length of the objective divided by focal length of the eyepiece. With 1,000 mm and 25 mm, that gives a magnification of **40 times**.

In the **Galilean telescope**, the eyepiece is a **diverging lens**. So it shows an **upright** image. This design is still found today in opera glasses. In the **Keplerian telescope**, the eyepiece is a converging lens. The image is then upside down, but you can see a larger field of view. In astronomy, an upside-down image does not matter.

A simple glass lens bends the colours of light by different amounts. Blue light is bent more strongly than red. That is why bright stars get **coloured fringes**. This image error is called **chromatic aberration**. In the 18th century a solution was found: an objective made of **two different types of glass**, the **achromat**, greatly reduces the error.

The largest refracting telescope ever used successfully for research is at the **Yerkes Observatory** in the USA. Its objective is **102 cm** across. Even larger lenses are not built, because a lens can only be held at its edge. **Large lenses sag under their own weight**, and the image becomes blurred. That is why large telescopes today use mirrors.

gewusst: With a simple refracting telescope, Galileo discovered the four large moons of Jupiter, which are still called the “Galilean moons” today.
Binoculars are basically two small refracting telescopes side by side.

teile.einleitung: If you throw a ball upwards, you always see it fall back down. But if you throw fast enough, you can get away from the Earth. The minimum speed needed is called the escape velocity.
wichtigste: The escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to escape from a celestial body without any further propulsion.
At the Earth's surface it is about 11.2 km/s.
It is also called the second cosmic velocity.
On the Moon, about 2.4 km/s is enough.
At about 60 km/s, Jupiter has the highest escape velocity of the planets.
It does not depend on the mass of the rocket.
For black holes it is greater than the speed of light.

abschnitte.text: The **escape velocity** is the minimum speed a body needs to escape from a celestial body **without any further propulsion**. At this speed it has enough **kinetic energy** to overcome the pull completely. After that it does not come back. If it is slower, it is pulled back again. In the calculation, **air resistance** is left out.

At the Earth's surface, the escape velocity is about **11.2 kilometres per second**. That is about 40,000 kilometres per hour. It is also called the **second cosmic velocity**. The **first cosmic velocity** is lower, about 7.9 km/s. It is enough for an orbit around the Earth, but not to fly away completely.

If you want to leave the whole **solar system**, you also have to escape the Sun's pull. The speed needed is called the **third cosmic velocity**. From the Earth it is about **16.7 km/s**. This makes use of the Earth's movement around the Sun, so the rocket already starts with a lot of momentum. Space probes such as the Voyager probes have left the solar system in this way.

The escape velocity depends only on the **mass** and the **radius** of the celestial body. The **Moon** has much less mass than the Earth. So about **2.4 km/s** is enough there. The most massive planet, **Jupiter**, has an escape velocity of about **60 km/s**. The mass of the rocket makes no difference. A heavy rocket needs more energy, but the same speed as a light one.

In a **black hole**, the mass is squeezed into a very small space. That is why the escape velocity there is **greater than the speed of light**. So you would have to be faster than light to escape. That is not possible. That is why not even **light** can leave a black hole, and it looks black.

gewusst: At 11.2 km/s, you would get from Geneva to Bern in just over 10 seconds.
On very small asteroids, the escape velocity is so low that you could fly away with a powerful jump.

teile.einleitung: Nuclear fusion is the energy source of the Sun and the other stars. Light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones, and an enormous amount of energy is released.
wichtigste: In the Sun, mainly hydrogen fuses into helium.
Fusion takes place mainly in the Sun's core.
At the centre of the Sun it is about 15 million kelvin hot.
About 600 million tonnes of hydrogen are converted every second.
In the process, the Sun loses about 4 million tonnes of mass every second.
The tunnel effect is what makes fusion possible at these temperatures.

abschnitte.titel: The furnace in the Sun's core
abschnitte.text: Fusion only takes place in the **Sun's core**, out to about a quarter of the Sun's radius. Only there are the pressure and temperature high enough. At the centre it is about **15 million kelvin**, with a density of about 150 grams per cubic centimetre. Every second, about 600 million tonnes of **hydrogen** fuse into **helium** there. Only a small fraction of this mass is turned into energy.

A helium nucleus is a little lighter than the nuclei it is made from. The missing mass becomes energy according to Albert Einstein's formula **E = mc²**. If you convert the Sun's luminosity, it loses about 4 million tonnes of mass every second. That sounds like a lot, but it is tiny compared with the Sun's huge mass.

Atomic nuclei are positively charged and repel each other; this hurdle is called the **Coulomb barrier**. According to classical physics, even in the hot core of the Sun the particles hardly have enough energy to overcome it. But quantum physics knows the **tunnel effect**. With a small probability, two protons still get close enough together. Because there are so incredibly many particles, this happens all the time.

In the Sun, mainly the **proton-proton chain** takes place. In stars with much more mass than the Sun, the **CNO cycle** provides most of the energy. In it, **carbon**, **nitrogen** and **oxygen** act as helpers that are not used up themselves. The CNO cycle depends strongly on temperature and so only dominates in hotter stellar cores.

Gravity squeezes the Sun together, while gas and radiation pressure push outwards. In every layer the two balance each other; this is **hydrostatic equilibrium**. If the fusion rate rises, the core expands a little, cools down and slows fusion again. The energy first travels outwards as **radiation**, and from about 0.7 solar radii by **convection**. Depending on the model, it takes 10,000 to 170,000 years to reach the surface.

gewusst: The sunlight warming you today was created as energy in the core tens of thousands of years ago.
Research facilities such as ITER in France are trying to use nuclear fusion on Earth to generate electricity.

teile.einleitung: Terrestrial planets are planets made of rock and metal with a solid surface. In our solar system, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars belong to this group. Researchers are also looking for such planets around other stars, among other things with a telescope led by Switzerland.
wichtigste: Terrestrial planets are made mainly of rock and metal.
In the solar system they are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
They are made up of a core, a mantle and a crust.
The Earth has the highest average density and the strongest magnetic field of this group.
Jupiter and Saturn, on the other hand, are gas giants without a solid surface.
Seven roughly Earth-sized planets orbit the star TRAPPIST-1.
The space telescope CHEOPS, led by the University of Bern, measures planets of other stars.

abschnitte.text: Terrestrial planets are also called **rocky planets**. They are made mainly of **silicate rock** and metals such as **iron** and **nickel**. That is why they have a solid surface you could stand on. In our solar system, the four inner planets belong to this group: **Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars**. They are much smaller than the outer planets.

These planets are built in layers like an onion. When they formed, they were hot and liquid. The heavy metals sank inwards and formed the **core**. Above it lies the **mantle** of rock. Right on the outside is the thin, solid **crust**.

The four rocky planets are very different. **Mercury** is small and close to the Sun, so it can hardly hold on to any gas. It has only a wafer-thin envelope, the **exosphere**. The **Earth** has the strongest **magnetic field** of the group. It is created in the liquid outer iron core and protects us from charged particles from the Sun. The Earth also has the highest average **density** of all planets, about 5.5 grams per cubic centimetre.

Jupiter and Saturn are called **gas giants**. They are made mainly of **hydrogen** and **helium** and have no solid surface. They are much bigger than the rocky planets. Saturn has the lowest density of all planets. On average it is even lighter than water.

Other stars have planets too. In 2017, researchers announced that the small star **TRAPPIST-1** is orbited by seven roughly Earth-sized planets. **Super-Earths** are also often found: they are heavier than the Earth but lighter than Neptune. The space telescope **CHEOPS** was launched in December 2019 as an ESA mission led by the **University of Bern**. It measures how much a star dims when a planet passes in front of it.

gewusst: There are no super-Earths at all in our solar system, but they are common around other stars.
Some of the planets of TRAPPIST-1 lie in a zone where liquid water would be possible.

teile.einleitung: Our solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a huge cloud of gas and dust. Its centre became the Sun, and the planets, moons, asteroids and comets formed from the rest. Astronomers are still researching exactly how this happened.
wichtigste: The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud of gas and dust.
The cloud contracted under its own gravity and began to spin.
The Sun formed in the middle, with a protoplanetary disc around it.
Planetesimals grew from dust, and the planets grew from them.
The inner planets are rocky planets because it was too hot near the Sun for ice and light gases.
The Moon probably formed when the young Earth collided with a body the size of Mars.
Asteroids and comets are leftovers from this time.

abschnitte.text: About 4.6 billion years ago, where we are now there was a huge **molecular cloud** of hydrogen, helium and dust. Perhaps it was set off by the shock wave of a nearby exploding star. The cloud contracted under its own gravity. As it did so, it spun faster and faster, like a figure skater pulling in her arms.

In the dense centre it became hotter and hotter, and the pressure grew greater and greater. Finally **nuclear fusion** began there: hydrogen fused into helium, and the Sun began to shine. To this day the Sun contains over 99 per cent of the mass of the whole solar system. Around it, the rest of the cloud flattened into a spinning **protoplanetary disc**.

In the disc, grains of dust stuck together and became bigger and bigger clumps. Lumps a kilometre in size are called **planetesimals**. They collided and grew into planets over a few million years. This process is called accretion.

Close to the Sun it was too hot for ice and light gases, so only rock and metal were left there. That is why Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are **rocky planets**. Further out, beyond the so-called **snow line**, there was also a lot of ice. There Jupiter and Saturn were able to collect huge amounts of gas and become gas giants, while Uranus and Neptune became ice giants.

According to the most widely held theory, the young Earth collided with a body the size of Mars, called **Theia**. The Moon formed from the debris that was flung out. Not all the material became planets: asteroids in the asteroid belt and comets at the edge of the solar system are leftovers. That is why space probes are especially keen to study them, to learn more about the beginnings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flat, spinning disc of gas and dust around a young star.
A small celestial body from which planets grow.
The joining of atomic nuclei, which releases a great deal of energy.
The distance from the Sun beyond which it was cold enough for water to freeze into ice.

gewusst: The oldest known material from the solar system is found in meteorites and is about 4.57 billion years old.
Today, telescopes can directly observe protoplanetary discs around other young stars.
Some of the Earth's water probably comes from asteroids that crashed onto the young Earth.

teile.einleitung: The Hubble constant tells you how fast the universe is expanding today. It links the distance of a galaxy with the speed at which it is moving away from us.
wichtigste: The Hubble-Lemaître law is v = H0 · d.
The further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us.
The Hubble constant is usually given in kilometres per second per megaparsec.
In 1929, Edwin Hubble found a value of about 500, which was far too large.
The larger H0 is, the younger the universe is according to this estimate.
H0 is today's value; in the past the rate of expansion was greater.

abschnitte.text: The **Hubble-Lemaître law** is written as v = H0 · d. Here v is the **recession velocity** of a galaxy and d its distance. The two quantities are **proportional**: double the distance means double the speed. The factor between them is the **Hubble constant H0**. The law is named after Edwin Hubble and the Belgian scientist Georges Lemaître.

Distance is measured in **megaparsecs** (Mpc); one megaparsec is just over three million light years. With H0 equal to 70 km/s per Mpc: a galaxy moving away at 2,100 km/s is 2,100 divided by 70, so 30 Mpc away. If you cancel out the units, you are left with **1 divided by time**. If you divide the speed of light by H0, you get the **Hubble radius** of about 4,300 Mpc.

abschnitte.titel: H0 and the age of the universe
abschnitte.text: If you imagine running the expansion backwards, you can estimate the age of the universe. This age is roughly the **reciprocal** of H0. A faster expansion means that the galaxies reached their present distance more quickly. So a larger H0 means a **younger universe**. With values around 70, this gives an age of roughly 14 billion years.

In 1929, Edwin Hubble worked out a value of about **500 km/s per Mpc**. He had underestimated the distances because the calibration of the **Cepheids**, certain pulsating stars, was wrong at the time. His value was about seven times too large. Today's measurements lie between about 67 and 73 km/s per Mpc.

H0 is called a constant because today the value is the same **everywhere in space**. But the rate of expansion changes over time, so in general people speak of the **Hubble parameter**. Very nearby galaxies are not good for measuring it. Their **own movements**, caused by the gravity of their neighbours, amount to a few hundred km/s and distort the result.

gewusst: Our neighbouring galaxy Andromeda is coming towards us despite the expansion of the universe, because gravity is stronger there.
Expressed in seconds, the Hubble constant is tiny: about 2.3 times 10 to the power of minus 18 per second.

teile.einleitung: Elliptical galaxies are star systems without spiral arms that look round or oval. They consist mainly of old stars and are among the largest galaxies in the universe.
wichtigste: Elliptical galaxies have no spiral arms and look round to oval.
Their labels range from E0 (round) to E7 (strongly flattened).
They contain mainly old, reddish stars and hardly form any new ones.
The stars move in orbits in all directions.
Many form when galaxies merge.
M87 in the Virgo Cluster is a famous giant elliptical galaxy.

abschnitte.text: Elliptical galaxies look like glowing balls or eggs. In **Hubble's tuning fork diagram**, they are at the handle. They are labelled with **E** and a number from 0 to 7. The number is calculated from the visible ratio of the short axis to the long axis: 10 times (1 minus b/a). **E0** is round, **E7** is the most **flattened**. Between the elliptical and the spiral galaxies are the **lenticular galaxies (S0)**. They have a disc and a bright core, but no spiral arms.

Elliptical galaxies usually look **reddish**. Hardly any new stars form in them. The hot, blue stars only live a short time and have long since gone out. What remains is mainly **old, red stars**. There is very little **cool gas and dust** from which new stars could form. Their gas is usually very hot and glows in **X-ray light**, but it cannot collapse to form stars.

abschnitte.titel: Stars like a swarm of bees
abschnitte.text: In a spiral galaxy, the stars orbit in an orderly way in a flat disc. In an elliptical galaxy it is different: the stars move in orbits **in all directions**, a bit like bees in a swarm. These disorderly, fast movements keep the galaxy in balance against **gravity**. Experts speak of a high **velocity dispersion**.

According to current understanding, many large elliptical galaxies form when galaxies **merge**. When two spiral galaxies collide, the orderly orbits of the discs are thrown into a jumble. The gas is used up or heated. This happens especially often in the dense **centre of galaxy clusters**. There, so-called **cD galaxies** grow into the largest known galaxies.

A famous example is **M87** in the centre of the **Virgo Cluster**. It is a huge elliptical galaxy. A **jet**, a beam of matter several thousand light years long, shoots out of its core. It is powered by an enormous **black hole** in the middle of the galaxy.

gewusst: The first image of a black hole, published in 2019, shows the black hole at the centre of M87.
Our Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy will probably also merge into an elliptical galaxy in a few billion years.

teile.einleitung: IceCube is a huge detector in the ice of Antarctica. It searches for neutrinos, tiny particles from space that pass through almost everything unhindered.
wichtigste: IceCube is located at the Amundsen-Scott research station at the South Pole.
The sensors watch over about one cubic kilometre of ice.
They hang at depths between about 1,450 and 2,450 metres.
Since it was completed in 2010, there have been 5,160 sensors on 86 cable strings.
The holes were melted into the ice with hot water.
In 2022, IceCube showed that the galaxy NGC 1068 is a source of neutrinos.

abschnitte.text: **Neutrinos** are very light particles with no electric charge. They fly through planets and people without anyone noticing. Only very rarely does one collide with an atom. This creates charged particles that give off a faint **blue light** in the ice. To catch such rare events, you need a huge measuring volume.

IceCube is located at the **Amundsen-Scott** research station at the South Pole. The sensors are spread over about one **cubic kilometre** of ice. They hang at depths between about 1,450 and 2,450 metres. There the high pressure has squeezed the air bubbles in the ice together, so it is very clear. The light can travel far and be measured by the sensors.

For the sensors, a **hot water drill** melted holes up to 2.5 kilometres deep into the ice. One hole took about 30 hours. Then cables with sensors were lowered into them, and the water froze solid again. In total there are 86 cable strings with 5,160 **Digital Optical Modules**. The detector has been complete since 2010.

In 2013, IceCube presented two neutrinos with about 1,000 **tera-electronvolts**. They were named after the characters **Bert and Ernie** from Sesame Street and were the first clues to neutrinos from distant space. In 2018, a neutrino was traced back to the **blazar** TXS 0506+056. A blazar is an active galactic nucleus whose jet points towards the Earth. In 2022 came the proof that the galaxy **NGC 1068**, also called Messier 77, sends out many neutrinos.

gewusst: The Earth itself serves IceCube as a filter: neutrinos from the other side of the Earth get through, other particles do not.
The core of NGC 1068 is heavily hidden by dust in visible light, but this is no obstacle for neutrinos.

teile.einleitung: Mir was a Soviet and later Russian space station. It orbited the Earth from 1986 to 2001 and was for a long time the largest structure in space. Space travellers from many countries lived and did research on it.
wichtigste: The Russian name **Mir** means “peace” or “world”.
The station orbited the Earth from **1986 to 2001**.
It was built up from **several modules** one after the other.
**Valeri Polyakov** lived on Mir for about 437 days in a row in 1994 and 1995.
In the 1990s, American **Space Shuttles** docked with it.
In 2001, Mir came down in a controlled way into the **Pacific**.

abschnitte.text: In Russian, the name **Mir** means **“peace”** or **“world”**. The Soviet Union launched the first part of the station into space in 1986. After the end of the Soviet Union, **Russia** went on running the station. Mir orbited the Earth until **2001**, much longer than originally planned. It was inhabited almost without a break.

Mir was not made in one piece. It was built **from several modules one after the other**. First came the core module with the living quarters. Then, over the years, more modules were docked, for example for research and observation. In the end, the station looked like a large structure with many arms and solar panels. This way of building was later also used for the ISS.

The cosmonaut **Valeri Polyakov** lived on Mir for **about 437 days** in a row in 1994 and 1995. This is still the longest continuous stay of a human in space. Many guests from other countries also visited the station. The German ESA astronaut **Thomas Reiter** lived on board for **about 179 days** in 1995 and 1996. In the 1990s, the American **Space Shuttles** also docked with Mir.

In **1997**, the crew experienced two serious accidents. First a **fire** broke out on board, which the space travellers were able to put out after a while. A few months later there was a **collision** with an uncrewed supply spacecraft. A module was damaged, and air escaped. The crew was able to seal off the module and was not injured.

After 15 years, Mir had grown old, and Russia was taking part in building the new International Space Station ISS. So in **2001**, Mir was deliberately slowed down. It entered the atmosphere and mostly burned up. The remaining debris **came down in a controlled way in the Pacific**, far from inhabited areas.

gewusst: Thomas Reiter was the first German to go on a spacewalk outside the station.
Over the years, space travellers from about a dozen countries lived on Mir.

teile.einleitung: JUICE is a space probe of the European Space Agency ESA. It is flying to Jupiter, where it is to explore the large icy moons beneath whose surfaces oceans are suspected.
wichtigste: JUICE stands for “Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer”.
The probe was launched on 14 April 2023 on an Ariane 5 from Kourou.
Arrival at Jupiter is planned for July 2031.
The focus is on Ganymede and Callisto; JUICE only flies close past Europa twice.
The instrument NIM was built at the University of Bern.
About 85 square metres of solar panels provide the electricity.

abschnitte.text: The name **JUICE** stands for “Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer”. The targets are **Ganymede**, **Europa** and **Callisto**. Beneath their thick shells of ice there could be oceans of liquid water. JUICE concentrates mainly on Ganymede and Callisto. It only flies close past Europa twice; the detailed exploration of this moon is being done by the NASA probe **Europa Clipper**.

JUICE was launched on 14 April 2023 on an **Ariane 5** from the Kourou spaceport in French Guiana. For the long journey it uses several **swing-by manoeuvres**, flybys that give it momentum. In August 2024, JUICE became the first probe ever to fly past the **Moon** and the **Earth** one shortly after the other. On 31 August 2025 came **Venus**, and in September 2026 the Earth again. Another Earth flyby is planned for 2029, and arrival at Jupiter for July 2031.

Jupiter is about five times as far from the Sun as the Earth. The strength of sunlight decreases with the **square of the distance**. So at Jupiter it is about 25 times weaker than here. That is why JUICE needs about 85 square metres of **solar panels** to produce enough electricity.

There are ten scientific instruments on board. The **Neutral gas and Ion Mass spectrometer NIM** was developed and built at the **University of Bern**. It is part of the particle package PEP and studies gases and ions in the thin atmospheres of the moons. The radar **RIME** is to look about 9 kilometres deep into the ice with radar waves. This is to reveal layers and possible pockets of water.

gewusst: The double flyby of the Moon and the Earth in 2024 was a world first and saved a lot of fuel.
JUICE is to be the first probe to go into orbit around a moon other than the Earth's Moon, namely Ganymede.

teile.einleitung: The Lambda-CDM model is the standard model of cosmology. It describes what the universe is made of and how it has developed since the Big Bang. With just a few basic quantities, it explains many observations amazingly well, but it also leaves questions open.
wichtigste: The **Lambda** stands for the **cosmological constant**, a form of dark energy.
**CDM** means “cold dark matter”.
In its simplest form, the model has **six** free basic parameters.
Structures form **hierarchically**, from small to large.
If dark energy is a cosmological constant, its equation of state parameter is w = -1.
Analyses by DESI from 2024 and 2025 suggest that dark energy might change over time.

abschnitte.text: The Greek letter **Lambda** stands for the **cosmological constant**. It describes an energy contained in empty space that speeds up the expansion of the universe. This is called **dark energy**. **CDM** stands for cold **dark matter**. This matter gives off no light but acts through its gravity. According to the model, the universe consists mostly of dark energy and dark matter, while normal matter makes up only about 5 per cent.

“Cold” here does not mean a low temperature in the everyday sense. It means that the particles of dark matter were moving **slowly** at the time structures formed. That is why they were able to gather into clumps early on. Small clumps formed first, which later merged into larger ones. This **hierarchical** formation led to galaxies, galaxy clusters and the great web of threads and empty spaces.

In its simplest form, the model needs only **six** free basic parameters. With them, for example, the patterns in the **cosmic background radiation** can be described very precisely. An important tool is **baryon acoustic oscillations**. These are sound waves from the early universe that left behind a typical length of **about 150 megaparsecs**. Astronomers use this length as a “standard ruler”.

Dark energy is described by an **equation of state parameter w**. If it is a true cosmological constant, then **w = -1**, and its density stays the same everywhere and at all times. Researchers test whether this is true with large surveys of the sky. The analyses of the **DESI** project from 2024 and 2025 suggest that dark energy might change over time. This is not yet certain.

Despite many successes, the model also has weak points. In the **cusp-core problem**, the centres of galaxies are denser in computer simulations than in observations. In addition, nobody knows what particles dark matter is made of. The nature of dark energy is also a mystery. That is why the model is constantly being tested and may one day be extended.

gewusst: One megaparsec is more than 3 million light years, so the standard ruler is almost half a billion light years long.
According to the model, the normal matter that stars, planets and people are made of is only a small part of the universe.

teile.einleitung: Parallax is the apparent shift of an object when you look at it from two different places. In astronomy it is used to measure the distance of stars. It is one of the most important methods for measuring the universe.
wichtigste: Annual parallax comes about because the Earth goes around the Sun.
The radius of the Earth's orbit, about 150 million kilometres, serves as the baseline.
In 1838, Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel was the first to measure the parallax of a star.
The further away a star is, the smaller its parallax.
The distance in parsecs is the reciprocal of the parallax in arcseconds.
The Gaia satellite measured the parallaxes of over a billion stars.

abschnitte.text: Hold up your thumb in front of you with your arm stretched out. Look at it with only your left eye and then only your right eye, one after the other. The thumb seems to jump back and forth against the background. That is **parallax**. The closer the thumb is, the bigger the jump. From the shift and the distance between your eyes, you can calculate the **distance**.

abschnitte.titel: The Earth as a measuring rod
abschnitte.text: For stars you need a much bigger distance than between two eyes. Observations are compared **half a year** apart. Then the Earth is on opposite sides of the Sun. A nearby star seems to shift slightly against the distant background and over the course of a year traces a small ellipse. The **radius of the Earth's orbit**, about 150 million kilometres, serves as the **baseline**.

abschnitte.titel: A long road to the first measurement
abschnitte.text: One of the arguments **Tycho Brahe** used against the Earth moving was that he could see no stellar parallax. In fact, the stars are so far away that his instruments were far too inaccurate. Only in **1838** did **Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel** succeed in measuring it. He worked out the parallax of the star **61 Cygni** as about 0.3 arcseconds. This was direct proof that the Earth moves around the Sun.

The angles are tiny. Even the nearest star, **Proxima Centauri**, has a parallax of only about **0.77 arcseconds**. For small angles: the parallax is inversely proportional to the distance. So **double the distance** means **half the parallax**. The distance in **parsecs** is simply the reciprocal of the parallax: with 0.25 arcseconds it is 1 divided by 0.25, so 4 parsecs.

On the ground, the **turbulence** of the atmosphere gets in the way. It makes stars twinkle and smears their images; this is called **seeing**. That is why satellites measure much more precisely. After **Hipparcos**, ESA's **Gaia** satellite was launched at the end of 2013. By the beginning of 2025 it had measured the parallaxes of over a billion stars and made the largest three-dimensional map of the **Milky Way** so far.

gewusst: For bright stars, Gaia achieved accuracies of a few tens of millionths of an arcsecond.
Shortly after Bessel, measurements were also made for the stars Vega and Alpha Centauri.

teile.einleitung: Gravity, also called gravitation, is the force with which all bodies that have mass attract each other. It makes an apple fall from a tree, keeps us standing on the Earth and makes the planets circle the Sun. Isaac Newton was the first to describe it with a law, in 1687.
wichtigste: Gravity is the force of attraction between all bodies with mass.
In 1687, Isaac Newton published the law of universal gravitation.
The force of gravity depends on the masses of the bodies and the distance between them.
At the Earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity is about 9.81 m/s².
On the Moon, weight is about 6 times smaller than on Earth.
The mass of a body stays the same everywhere; only its weight changes.
The Moon's pull is the main cause of low and high tide.

abschnitte.text: Every body with mass attracts every other body; this is called **gravity**. With small things this force is tiny, which is why we do not notice two apples attracting each other. Only very large masses such as the Earth, the Sun or whole galaxies create a strong pull. Gravity keeps us on the ground and gives us our **weight**.

The Englishman **Isaac Newton** published his law of gravitation in 1687. It says: the force gets bigger the bigger the masses are, and smaller the further apart the bodies are. If the distance doubles, the force becomes four times weaker. Newton realised that the same force makes an apple fall and steers the Moon around the Earth.

At the Earth's surface, without air resistance, all bodies fall with an **acceleration due to gravity** of about 9.81 m/s². The **mass** of a body, measured in kilograms, is the same everywhere. So an astronaut with a mass of 60 kg also has 60 kg on the Moon. But her weight there is about 6 times smaller, because the Moon has much less mass than the Earth, so she can jump much higher there.

The Moon's pull tugs at the water of the oceans and is the main cause of **low and high tide**. The Sun also contributes a little. The Sun's gravity keeps all the planets in their orbits. Without it, the planets would fly off straight into space.

In 1915, **Albert Einstein** gave a new explanation of gravity with his general theory of relativity. According to him, masses bend space and time, a bit like a ball making a dent in a stretched sheet. Among other things, this theory predicts black holes and **gravitational waves**. GPS satellites also have to take Einstein's theory into account; otherwise navigation would be inaccurate.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter a body contains, measured in kilograms.
The force with which a body is pulled by a celestial body.
How quickly a falling body keeps getting faster.
The regular rising and falling of sea level, in other words low and high tide.

gewusst: You also pull on the Earth, but because the Earth is so much heavier, it hardly moves.
Galileo Galilei found out that heavy and light bodies fall at the same speed without air resistance.
On Jupiter you would be more than twice as heavy as on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Gas planets are huge planets made mainly of gases, with no solid ground. In our solar system there are four of them: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
wichtigste: Our solar system has four gas planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Gas planets have no solid ground; a probe cannot land there.
Jupiter and Saturn consist mainly of hydrogen and helium.
Uranus and Neptune are also called ice giants.
The gas methane makes Uranus and Neptune look blue.
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are not gas planets but rocky planets.

abschnitte.text: The gas planets lie in the outer part of the solar system, far from the Sun. **Jupiter** is the largest, followed by **Saturn**, **Uranus** and **Neptune**. All four are much bigger than the Earth. The inner planets Mercury, Venus, Earth and **Mars**, on the other hand, are made of rock. All gas planets have rings; Saturn's are the most magnificent.

A gas planet has no surface you could stand on. The deeper you go, the denser and hotter the gas becomes. The pressure rises so much that the gas becomes liquid. So a **space probe** cannot land; it would be crushed by the pressure. **Jupiter** and **Saturn** consist mainly of **hydrogen** and **helium**, like the Sun.

**Uranus** and **Neptune** contain a lot of frozen water, ammonia and methane. That is why they are also called **ice giants**. The gas **methane** in their outer layers absorbs red light. That is why the two planets look blue. Uranus has the **coldest atmosphere** in the solar system; it gets colder than minus 220 degrees there.

Gas planets have a great many moons. In 2025, **Saturn** had the most known moons, well over a hundred. Because the gas planets are so far from the Sun, one orbit takes a very long time. **Neptune** is the outermost planet. It needs about 165 Earth years to go once around the Sun.

gewusst: Saturn has such a low density that it would float in a giant bathtub full of water.
Since its discovery in 1846, Neptune has only gone around the Sun about once.

teile.einleitung: The parsec is a unit of length in astronomy for very large distances. One parsec is about 3.26 light years. Experts like to use it because it comes directly from a parallax measurement.
wichtigste: From a distance of one parsec, one astronomical unit appears at an angle of one arcsecond.
One parsec is about 3.26 light years.
One parsec is about 206,265 astronomical units, or about 31 trillion kilometres.
The name is made from “parallax” and “second”.
The centre of the Milky Way is about 8 kiloparsecs away.
The Virgo Cluster of galaxies is about 16.5 megaparsecs away.

abschnitte.text: Imagine looking at the Earth and the Sun from a great distance. The distance between them is one **astronomical unit** (AU), about 150 million kilometres. A **parsec** is the distance from which this gap appears at an angle of exactly one **arcsecond**. An arcsecond is tiny: one degree has 3,600 arcseconds. The symbol for parsec is **pc**.

The word **parsec** is short for “**par**allax of one arc**sec**ond” (in German “Parallaxe einer Bogensekunde”). So the unit links angle measurement and distance. The name was suggested in 1913 by the British astronomer Herbert Hall Turner. If you measure a **parallax** in arcseconds, you get the distance in parsecs simply as the **reciprocal**. The light year, on the other hand, is not something you measure directly.

One parsec is about **3.26 light years**. An arcsecond is the 206,265th part of a radian, which is why a parsec is about **206,265 AU** long. In kilometres that is about **31 trillion** kilometres. A light year, by comparison, is only about 9.5 trillion kilometres. The nearest star, **Proxima Centauri**, is about 1.3 parsecs away, just over 4 light years.

For even larger distances, prefixes are added. A **kiloparsec** (kpc) is a thousand parsecs, a **megaparsec** (Mpc) a million parsecs. The centre of the **Milky Way** is about **8.2 kiloparsecs** from the Sun, which is about 27,000 light years. This number is known from measurements of the orbits of stars around the central black hole. The **Virgo Cluster** of galaxies, with over a thousand galaxies, is about **16.5 megaparsecs** away, about 54 million light years.

gewusst: No star apart from the Sun is closer than one parsec.
In books and films, the parsec is sometimes wrongly used as a unit of time, but it is a length.

teile.einleitung: Nicolaus Copernicus was an astronomer and cathedral canon who lived from 1473 to 1543. He put the Sun instead of the Earth at the centre of the model of the world. In doing so, he changed the picture people had of the sky.
wichtigste: Copernicus lived from 1473 to 1543.
He studied in Kraków and in Italy, including in Bologna and Padua.
In Warmia he was a cathedral canon and also looked after administration and finances.
In his model, the Earth and the planets circle the Sun.
The Earth turns once a day on its axis.
His main work, “De revolutionibus orbium coelestium”, appeared in 1543.
Element 112 is called copernicium in his honour.

abschnitte.text: Copernicus was born in **1473** in Thorn, today Toruń in Poland. He first studied in **Kraków** and then went to **Italy**. In Bologna and Padua he studied **church law** and **medicine**, among other things. Later he became a **cathedral canon** in Frombork in **Warmia**. Besides astronomy, he looked after administration and finances and also worked as a doctor.

For a long time people believed that the **Earth** stood still at the centre of the world and everything turned around it. Copernicus suggested a different model: the **Sun** is in the middle, and the Earth circles it like the other planets. This is called the **heliocentric view of the world**, after the Greek word for Sun. In this way, some of the movements of the planets could be explained more simply.

How did Copernicus explain that the Sun and stars rise and set every day? The **Earth turns** once a day on its own **axis**. That makes the whole sky seem to move. However, Copernicus still held on to perfect **circular orbits**. So he still needed small extra circles. Only later did Johannes Kepler show that the orbits are **ellipses**.

Copernicus worked on his book for many years but hesitated for a long time to publish it. In **1539**, the young mathematician **Georg Joachim Rheticus** from Feldkirch visited him and urged him to have the work printed. In **1543** it appeared in **Nuremberg** under the title “**De revolutionibus orbium coelestium**”, in English “On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres”. Copernicus died in the same year.

At first, Copernicus's ideas were accepted by only a few people. Later, **Kepler** and **Galileo** built on them. Today people speak of a **Copernican revolution** when a view of the world changes fundamentally. In 2010, the artificially made **element 112** was given the name **copernicium**.

gewusst: Feldkirch, the home town of Rheticus, is in Vorarlberg, right on the border with Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
Even before his main work, Copernicus had handed out his idea to friends in a short handwritten text.

teile.einleitung: A neutron star is the incredibly dense remnant of an exploded giant star. Although it can have more mass than our Sun, it is only the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.
wichtigste: Neutron stars form in supernova explosions of very massive stars.
A typical neutron star has a radius of about 10 to 12 kilometres.
It consists mainly of neutrons packed extremely tightly together.
The degeneracy pressure of the neutrons stops it from collapsing further.
Many neutron stars spin very fast and send out radiation as pulsars.
Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsar in 1967.
Magnetars are neutron stars with an extremely strong magnetic field.

abschnitte.text: A neutron star forms when a star with at least about eight solar masses runs out of fuel at the end of its life. Its core then collapses under its own gravity in fractions of a second. The outer layers are flung into space in an enormous **supernova**. What remains is a tiny, super-dense core, the **neutron star**. In the process, electrons and protons are squeezed together into neutrons.

A typical neutron star has a radius of only about 10 to 12 kilometres, about the size of the city of Zurich. Even so, it usually has about 1.4 to 2 solar masses. It is stopped from collapsing further mainly by the **degeneracy pressure** of the neutrons, a result of quantum physics. The theoretical upper limit for its mass is called the **Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit** and lies at about two to three solar masses. If the remnant is heavier, a black hole forms.

Newly formed neutron stars spin extremely fast. This is explained by the **conservation of angular momentum**: when a huge star shrinks to a few kilometres, it spins much faster. A figure skater who pulls in her arms during a pirouette spins faster for the same reason. The pulsar in the **Crab Nebula** spins about 30 times a second. The fastest known neutron stars manage over 700 turns a second.

Many neutron stars send out beams of radiation from their magnetic poles. Because they spin, this beam sweeps regularly over the Earth like the light of a **lighthouse**. Such neutron stars are called **pulsars**. The first was discovered in 1967 by the doctoral student **Jocelyn Bell Burnell** in Cambridge with a radio telescope. Because the signals were so regular, the source was at first jokingly called “LGM-1”, for “little green men”.

**Magnetars** are neutron stars with an extremely strong magnetic field, trillions of times stronger than the Earth's. In 2017, researchers observed two neutron stars colliding for the first time. They measured **gravitational waves** and at the same time light from the explosion. Such collisions create heavy elements such as gold and platinum. So some of the gold in jewellery probably comes from such collisions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The enormous explosion of a star at the end of its life.
An electrically neutral particle from the atomic nucleus.
A fast-spinning neutron star whose radiation reaches us at regular intervals.
A neutron star with an extremely strong magnetic field.
A measure of the turning movement of a body, which is conserved.

gewusst: A teaspoon of neutron star matter would weigh about as much as a large mountain on Earth.
The gravity at the surface of a neutron star is so strong that the highest mountains there would only be a few millimetres high.
The supernova that formed the Crab Nebula was observed by Chinese astronomers in 1054.

teile.einleitung: The seasons are the four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn and winter. They happen because the Earth's axis is tilted as the Earth circles the Sun. That is why in our part of the world it is warm and light in summer and cold and dark in winter.
wichtigste: There are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter.
There are seasons because the Earth's axis is tilted.
When it is summer here, it is winter in Australia.
Here, spring begins in March.
At the equinox, day and night are about the same length.
Here, the longest day is around 21 June and the shortest around 21 December.
Near the equator, instead of four seasons there are often rainy and dry seasons.

abschnitte.text: The Earth's axis is **tilted** by about 23.4 degrees. During a year, the Earth circles the Sun, and the axis always points in the same direction. That is why sometimes the northern hemisphere and sometimes the southern hemisphere is tilted more towards the Sun. The hemisphere facing the Sun has summer, the other has winter.

abschnitte.titel: The Sun's height and the length of the day
abschnitte.text: In summer, the Sun is high in the sky at midday; its rays strike steeply and warm more strongly. The days are also long, so the ground and air heat up for a long time. In winter, the Sun is low; its rays hit at a shallow angle and spread over a larger area. The distance from the Sun, on the other hand, hardly matters, because in January the Earth is actually closest to the Sun.

Astronomically, spring begins here around 20 March with the **equinox**, when day and night are about the same length. Summer begins around 21 June with the **summer solstice**, the longest day. Autumn begins around 22 or 23 September, and winter around 21 December with the shortest day. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss count the seasons more simply by whole months; for them, spring lasts from March to May.

In the **southern hemisphere**, the seasons are exactly the other way round. When it is summer here, it is winter in Australia, South Africa or Argentina. That is why many people in Australia celebrate Christmas on the beach in midsummer. In the tropics at the equator it stays warm all year; there people mainly distinguish between the **rainy season** and the dry season.

Plants and animals have adapted to the seasons. In spring, trees blossom and migrating birds such as swallows return from Africa. In autumn, the leaves change colour and fall, and animals such as marmots get ready for **hibernation**. In the Swiss Alps, the seasons also decide when the cattle are driven up to the alpine pastures in early summer and brought down again in autumn.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line through the North and South Poles, around which the Earth turns.
A day in spring or autumn when day and night are about the same length.
The day with the longest or shortest daylight of the year.
The northern or southern half of the Earth.

gewusst: At the poles, day and night each last about half a year.
On 21 June it is light for about 16 hours in Zurich, but on 21 December only about 8 hours.
Mars has seasons too, because its axis is tilted at a similar angle to the Earth's.

teile.einleitung: Exoplanets are planets that orbit not our Sun but other stars. In 1995, the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz discovered the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star. Today thousands of them are known, and researchers are looking for a second Earth.
wichtigste: Exoplanets are planets outside our solar system.
In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz from Geneva found the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star.
For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
The Kepler telescope found most of its planets with the transit method.
The radial velocity method measures the Doppler shift in the star's light.
The nearest known exoplanet, Proxima Centauri b, is about 4.2 light years away.
The University of Bern leads the ESA mission CHEOPS, which has been measuring exoplanets precisely since 2019.

abschnitte.text: An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun. Exoplanets are very hard to see because their star shines millions of times more brightly. That is why they are usually found indirectly, from their effect on the star. By 2025, about 6,000 exoplanets had been confirmed (as of about 2025).

In 1995, **Michel Mayor** and **Didier Queloz** from the University of Geneva discovered the planet 51 Pegasi b. It was the first exoplanet found orbiting a Sun-like star. It is a so-called **hot Jupiter**: a gas giant that orbits very close to its star in only about four days. In 2019, the two researchers received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this.

When a planet passes in front of its star as seen from us, the star becomes a little dimmer. This passage is called a **transit**. If the planet has a tenth of the star's radius, it covers a hundredth of the star's disc, and the brightness drops by about 1 per cent. From 2009 to 2018, the space telescope **Kepler** found thousands of planets with this method.
