A planet pulls on its star with its gravity, so that the star wobbles slightly to and fro. When the star moves towards us, its light becomes a little bluer; when it moves away, it becomes redder. This regular **Doppler shift** of the spectral lines can be detected with very precise instruments. With this radial velocity method, Mayor and Queloz found 51 Pegasi b, and researchers in Geneva build world-famous spectrographs for it.

Planets in the **habitable zone** are particularly exciting; this is the area around a star where liquid water is possible on a planet. One example is Proxima Centauri b, the nearest known exoplanet, about 4.2 light years away. The space telescope **CHEOPS**, led by the University of Bern, has been measuring the size and orbits of known exoplanets since 2019. The James Webb Space Telescope even studies the atmospheres of some exoplanets.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet that orbits a star other than the Sun.
The passage of a planet in front of its star.
The area around a star where there can be liquid water on a planet.
A gas giant that orbits very close to its star and is therefore very hot.
The distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

gewusst: The very first exoplanets were found in 1992 around a pulsar, a dead, fast-spinning star.
There are exoplanets on which a year is shorter than a day on Earth.
Probably almost every star in the Milky Way has at least one planet.

teile.einleitung: Cryovolcanism literally means “ice volcanism”. On some icy moons and dwarf planets, it is not hot molten rock that erupts but water, ammonia or methane. These ice volcanoes reveal that there are still liquid substances inside such bodies.
wichtigste: Cryovolcanoes bring up **cryomagma**, which consists mainly of water, often mixed with ammonia or methane.
In 2005, the space probe Cassini discovered fountains at the south pole of Saturn's moon Enceladus.
In 1989, Voyager 2 observed geysers on Neptune's moon Triton.
On the dwarf planet Ceres, the mountain Ahuna Mons is considered a cryovolcano.
On Enceladus, tidal friction caused by Saturn's gravity provides the heat needed.
Ammonia lowers the freezing point of water considerably, like antifreeze.

abschnitte.text: On Earth, hot **lava** made of molten rock flows out during an eruption. Far out in the solar system it is much too cold for that. There the crust of many moons is made of ice that is as hard as stone. If it gets a little warmer underneath, water can become liquid and push upwards. This material is called **cryomagma**. A mixture of water and ammonia stays liquid down to about minus 97 degrees and can therefore erupt more easily.

Saturn's small moon **Enceladus** is the best-known example. In 2005, the probe **Cassini** saw fountains of water vapour and ice particles at its south pole. They shoot out of long cracks called **tiger stripes**. Some of the material forms Saturn's thin E ring. The heat comes from **tidal friction**: Saturn's gravity constantly kneads the moon on its slightly oval orbit.

Cassini flew through the fountains several times and studied them. The probe found **molecular hydrogen** and tiny grains of **silica**. Such grains only form when hot water comes into contact with rock. That is why researchers suspect **hydrothermal vents** at the bottom of an ocean beneath the ice. So Enceladus is considered an exciting place to search for conditions that could make life possible.

In 1989, **Voyager 2** saw dark plumes on Neptune's moon **Triton** rising about 8 kilometres high. There, heat from the Sun probably drives nitrogen gas through the icy crust. The probe **Dawn** found the roughly 4 kilometre high **Ahuna Mons**, made of salty ice, on the dwarf planet **Ceres**. **New Horizons** discovered the hills **Wright Mons** and **Piccard Mons** on Pluto, which are considered possible ice volcanoes.

Jupiter's moon **Europa** probably also has an ocean beneath its ice. The **Hubble Space Telescope** provided clues to plumes of water vapour above its south pole. But these plumes have not yet been confirmed for certain. New space probes are to study Europa more closely in the coming years.

gewusst: The material from the fountains of Enceladus spreads so far that it forms a whole ring of Saturn.
On Triton, even the weak heat of the Sun probably drives gas through the ice, although the Sun is very far away there.

teile.einleitung: The Earth also casts a shadow into space, just like a ball in sunlight. When this shadow falls on the Moon, there is a lunar eclipse. Sometimes you can even see it in the sky at twilight.
wichtigste: The Earth casts a shadow on the side facing away from the Sun.
In a lunar eclipse, the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line, with the Earth in the middle.
Everyone who has the Moon in their sky at that moment can see the eclipse.
In a total lunar eclipse the Moon glows reddish; people call it a blood moon.
Over 2,000 years ago, the round shadow of the Earth already showed that the Earth is a sphere.
You can watch a lunar eclipse without protective glasses.

abschnitte.text: In a **lunar eclipse**, the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line. The Earth is in the middle. Its shadow then falls exactly on the Moon. Because the Moon lies in the Earth's shadow, the eclipse can be seen everywhere on the night side of the Earth where the Moon is in the sky. A lunar eclipse only happens at full moon.

In a **total lunar eclipse**, the Moon does not disappear completely. It glows dark red. The reason is the Earth's **atmosphere**: it bends some sunlight into the shadow. Mainly red light reaches the Moon in this way. That is why many people then call the Moon a **blood moon**.

The edge of the Earth's shadow on the Moon is always **curved**. In ancient Greece, over 2,000 years ago, people already concluded from this that the Earth is a **sphere**. Only a sphere casts a round shadow in every position. This was one of the first pieces of evidence for the shape of our planet.

You can see the Earth's shadow even without an eclipse. After sunset it appears as a **dark blue band** low in the sky, on the side opposite the Sun. Above this band, a **pink strip** often glows. It is called the **Belt of Venus**. You can see both best on a clear evening with an open view, for example from a hill.

Unlike a solar eclipse, you need **no protective glasses** for a lunar eclipse. The Moon does not shine as brightly as the Sun. So you can simply look at it with the naked eye. With binoculars, the colours look even more beautiful. A total lunar eclipse can last for more than an hour.

gewusst: During a lunar eclipse, the Moon sees the sunsets of all places on Earth at the same time, which is why it glows red.
The Belt of Venus has nothing to do with the planet Venus; it is just named after the Roman goddess.

teile.einleitung: The Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope is a NASA space telescope. It observes gamma rays, the most energetic form of light. With it, scientists study black holes, exploding stars and even thunderstorms on Earth.
wichtigste: The telescope was launched in June 2008, at first under the name GLAST.
It is named after the physicist Enrico Fermi.
The main instrument is called the Large Area Telescope, plus the Gamma-ray Burst Monitor.
It measures gamma rays from about 20 MeV to over 300 GeV.
In 2010, the huge Fermi bubbles were found above and below the centre of the Milky Way.
Most of the identified sources are blazars.
Fermi showed that thunderstorms produce antimatter.

abschnitte.text: The telescope was launched in **June 2008**, still under the name **GLAST**. Shortly afterwards it was named after the physicist **Enrico Fermi**. Gamma rays do not get through the Earth's atmosphere. That is why they have to be observed from space. Fermi orbits the Earth and constantly looks at the whole sky as it does so.

The main instrument is the **Large Area Telescope**, LAT for short. It covers about a fifth of the sky at once and measures gamma rays from about **20 MeV to over 300 GeV**. In thin **tungsten foils**, a gamma ray photon turns into an electron and a positron. This process is called **pair production**. From the tracks of the two particles, the instrument works out the direction and energy. The second instrument is the **Gamma-ray Burst Monitor**, which detects short gamma ray flashes.

In 2010, researchers discovered something surprising in the data. Above and below the centre of the Milky Way there are **two huge gamma ray bubbles**. These **Fermi bubbles** each stretch about 25,000 light years. They probably go back to earlier activity at the centre of the Milky Way. But most of the sources in Fermi's catalogues are **blazars**. These are active galactic nuclei with a jet pointing almost exactly towards us.

abschnitte.titel: Gamma ray burst and gravitational waves
abschnitte.text: In 2017, gravitational waves from two merging **neutron stars** were measured. About **1.7 seconds** later, the Gamma-ray Burst Monitor recorded a gamma ray burst from the same direction. Both signals had been travelling for about 130 million light years. This showed that **gravitational waves** travel at practically the speed of light.

Fermi also observes the Earth. In 2011, the Gamma-ray Burst Monitor picked up signals from **positrons**. Positrons are particles of **antimatter**. They were created in thunderstorms and guided out into space along the Earth's magnetic field. This showed that thunderstorms produce antimatter.

gewusst: At even higher energies, Cherenkov telescopes on the ground take over the observations.
Fermi has found thousands of gamma ray sources in the sky.

teile.einleitung: The Lunar Roving Vehicle was a vehicle that astronauts drove around in on the Moon. It is often simply called the moon buggy. It was used on the last three Apollo Moon landings.
wichtigste: The Lunar Roving Vehicle is often called the **moon buggy**.
It had **four** wheels made of a mesh of wire.
It ran on electricity from **batteries**.
A moon buggy was driven for the first time on **Apollo 15** in 1971.
There was room for two astronauts in the moon buggy.
Its top speed was about 18 km/h.

abschnitte.text: On the first Moon landings, the astronauts went on foot. That way they did not get far. So for the last three missions the **Lunar Roving Vehicle**, the **moon buggy**, was built. It was used on **Apollo 15**, **16** and **17** in 1971 and 1972. It was first driven on **Apollo 15**. With it, the astronauts could explore much larger areas.

There is no air on the Moon, so a petrol engine cannot run. That is why the moon buggy ran on **electricity from batteries**. Each of the **four wheels** had its own small electric motor. It was steered with a lever instead of a steering wheel. Its top speed was **about 18 km/h**, which was quite fast on the bumpy ground of the Moon.

Normal rubber tyres would not have worked well on the Moon. The extreme heat and cold and the sharp Moon dust are too difficult for them. So the wheels were made of a **mesh of wire**. Metal strips were attached to it to give grip in the dust. The wheels were light and gave a little on stones.

There was room for **two astronauts** side by side in the moon buggy. There was also storage space for tools, cameras and rock samples. So that it fitted on the lunar module, the moon buggy was attached to its side **folded up**. On the Moon it unfolded almost by itself. A television camera on the vehicle sent pictures back to Earth.

After each mission, the moon buggy was left behind on the Moon, because bringing it back would have been far too heavy. That is why **three moon buggies** are still standing on the Moon today. On Apollo 17, the astronauts parked it so that the camera could film the lunar module taking off. This film went around the world.

gewusst: The moon buggy weighed about 210 kilograms on Earth, but because of the weak gravity on the Moon you only felt a sixth of that.
A mudguard on the Apollo 17 moon buggy broke off and was mended with maps and tape.

teile.einleitung: Lunar craters are round hollows on the surface of the Moon. Almost all of them were formed by lumps of rock from space crashing into it. Even with binoculars you can see many of them.
wichtigste: Most lunar craters were formed by impacts of lumps of rock.
A crater looks like a round bowl with a raised rim.
Because there is no wind or water on the Moon, craters last a very long time.
The Moon has no protective atmosphere, so small lumps hit it too.
Many craters are named after famous scientists, such as Copernicus or Kepler.
At half moon you can see craters particularly well, because they cast long shadows.

abschnitte.text: Countless lumps of rock fly around in space. When one of them falls onto the Moon, it hits at an enormous speed. Rock is flung to the side, and an **impact crater** forms. A crater is a round **hollow** with a raised **rim**. Large craters often have a **central peak** in the middle, which was pushed up during the impact.

abschnitte.titel: Why the Moon has so many
abschnitte.text: The Earth has a thick **atmosphere**. Small lumps burn up in it as shooting stars before they reach the ground. The Moon has no such atmosphere, so small lumps hit it too. In addition, there is **no wind and no water** on the Moon. On Earth, craters are worn away by rain, rivers and wind or overgrown by plants. On the Moon, on the other hand, they last for billions of years.

A particularly well-known crater is **Tycho** in the south of the Moon. Compared with others, it is still fairly young. Long, bright **rays** spread out from it. This is material that was flung far across the surface during the impact. At full moon you can see these rays especially clearly.

Even with simple **binoculars** you can make out many craters. With a telescope you can see even more detail. It is best to observe at **half moon**. Then the sunlight falls at an angle on the border between light and dark. The crater rims cast long **shadows**, and the landscape looks three-dimensional. At full moon, on the other hand, the light shines from the front and the craters look flat.

Many lunar craters bear the names of well-known **scientists**, for example **Copernicus**, **Kepler** or Tycho, named after Tycho Brahe. Today the names are given by the International Astronomical Union. Scientists from Switzerland are among them too: one crater is called **Euler**, after the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler.

gewusst: On the far side of the Moon, which we never see, there are even more craters than on the near side.
The Moon's largest known impact basin lies near the south pole and is about 2,500 kilometres wide.

teile.einleitung: Tidal locking means that a celestial body turns once on its own axis in exactly the time it takes to go once around another body. That is why the Moon always shows us the same side.
wichtigste: With tidal locking, a moon always shows its planet the same side.
The Moon turns once on its axis and goes once around the Earth in about 27 days.
The Earth's tidal force has slowed down the Moon's spin.
Over time, about 59 per cent of the Moon's surface can be seen from the Earth.
The far side of the Moon is lit by the Sun just as much as the near side.
Jupiter's four Galilean moons are also tidally locked.

abschnitte.text: The Moon takes about **27 days** to turn once on its axis. It takes exactly as long to go once around the Earth. That is why we always see the same side. This is called **tidal locking**. Because the Moon wobbles a little in its orbit, about **59 per cent** of its surface can be seen over time. This wobbling is called **libration**.

In the past, the Moon spun faster. The Earth's **tidal force** deformed it slightly and slowed its spin. This went on until the spin matched the orbit. The Moon also slows down the Earth with its **tides**. That is why the **days on Earth** are slowly getting longer, though only by tiny fractions of a second per century.

abschnitte.titel: The far side of the Moon
abschnitte.text: The far side of the Moon remained a mystery for a long time. Only in 1959 did the Soviet probe **Luna 3** photograph it for the first time. People often speak of the “dark side of the Moon”. But that is wrong, because the far side also gets sunlight when it is new moon for us. In 2019, **China** made the first soft landing on the far side with the Chang’e 4 probe.

Tidal locking is common in the solar system. Jupiter's four **Galilean moons** also always show their planet the same side. With **Mercury** it is a bit different. It turns on its axis exactly three times during two orbits of the Sun. Experts speak of a **resonance**. With Pluto and its moon Charon, both are even locked to each other.

gewusst: Pluto and Charon always show each other the same side. From one side of Pluto, Charon would always be visible, from the other side never.
About 400 million years ago a year had about 400 days, because the Earth spun faster then. Growth rings in old corals show this.

teile.einleitung: The European Space Agency, ESA for short, is the joint space agency of many European countries. It builds satellites, sends space probes into space and trains astronauts. Switzerland has been part of it from the start.
wichtigste: ESA was founded in 1975, and its headquarters are in Paris.
Switzerland is one of the founding members.
ESA is not an organisation of the EU.
Satellites and space probes are controlled from the ESOC control centre in Darmstadt.
Astronauts train at the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne.
At the beginning of 2025, Slovenia became the 23rd full member state.
The ESA probe Huygens landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005.

abschnitte.text: The convention founding **ESA** was signed in Paris on **30 May 1975**. Its predecessors were two organisations, **ESRO** for research satellites and **ELDO** for rockets. In 2025, ESA had **23 member states**; the latest to join was Slovenia. There are also some associate states. ESA is not an organisation of the European Union, even though it works closely with it.

In 1975, **Switzerland** was one of the **founding states** of ESA. Because ESA does not belong to the EU, Switzerland is a full member. Swiss universities and companies build parts for many missions. The best-known Swiss astronaut is **Claude Nicollier**, who flew into space several times. In November 2022, ESA selected the doctor **Marco Sieber** as a career astronaut. He is the second Swiss ESA astronaut.

ESA's **headquarters** are in **Paris**. Its centres are spread over several countries. Satellites and space probes have been controlled from the **ESOC** control centre in **Darmstadt** since 1967. At the European Astronaut Centre **EAC** in **Cologne**, astronauts train for their flights. Launches take place mainly from the spaceport in Kourou in French Guiana in South America.

ESA has built many important missions. The **Huygens** probe travelled to Saturn together with the American space probe Cassini. In January 2005 it landed on Saturn's moon **Titan**. The **Rosetta** probe accompanied a comet for years. With the **Ariane** family of rockets, Europe launches its own satellites into space. Many ESA satellites also observe the Earth's weather and climate.

gewusst: The landing of Huygens on Titan is still the landing of a probe furthest from the Earth.
Several instruments on ESA probes were developed at the University of Bern.

teile.einleitung: Communications satellites transmit television, phone calls and internet data over long distances. They circle the Earth and pass on radio signals from one place to another.
wichtigste: Many television satellites orbit geostationary at a height of about 36,000 kilometres.
A geostationary satellite seems to stand still in the sky.
A signal takes about 0.24 seconds to go there and back.
Arthur C. Clarke suggested the idea as early as 1945.
In 1962, Telstar 1 transmitted live television pictures across the Atlantic for the first time.
Three geostationary satellites cover almost the whole Earth.

abschnitte.text: Many television satellites orbit **geostationary** above the equator, at a height of about 36,000 kilometres. They go around the Earth exactly as fast as the Earth turns. So from below it looks as if they are standing still. That is why a **satellite dish** can always point in the same direction. In Switzerland, the dishes usually point south.

The signals from a satellite arrive only very weakly on the ground. A **parabolic antenna** is curved like a concave mirror. It reflects the signals onto one point and focuses them there. At this point sits the **receiver**. This makes the weak signal strong enough for television pictures.

Radio signals travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second. To a geostationary satellite and back is about 72,000 kilometres. That takes about **0.24 seconds**. In phone calls via satellite you notice this small **delay**. Each geostationary satellite sees about a third of the Earth, so three satellites evenly spaced are enough for almost the whole Earth apart from the poles.

As early as 1945, the writer **Arthur C. Clarke** described satellites that stay above one point of the Earth. In his honour, the geostationary orbit is sometimes called the **Clarke orbit**. From 1960, the huge balloon satellite **Echo 1**, about 30 metres across, simply reflected radio signals back. In July 1962, **Telstar 1** was launched. It was the first to transmit live television pictures between America and Europe.

In the middle of the ocean, in the desert or high in the mountains there are often no **mobile phone masts**. A **satellite phone** sends its signal directly to a satellite and so works almost everywhere. Ships, expeditions and rescue teams use such devices. Today there are also many satellites in low orbits that bring fast internet to remote areas.

gewusst: Arthur C. Clarke is also known as the author of the science fiction classic “2001: A Space Odyssey”.
There is only one ring of geostationary orbit above the equator, so the places in it are allocated internationally.

teile.einleitung: Kepler was a NASA space telescope that searched for planets around other stars. It found thousands of these exoplanets and showed that planets are very common in the universe.
wichtigste: Kepler was launched in March 2009.
It circled the Sun in its own orbit, trailing behind the Earth.
In its main mission, it looked at a field between the constellations Cygnus and Lyra.
After a breakdown in 2013, the mission continued as K2.
Kepler found over 2,600 confirmed exoplanets.
In October 2018 it was switched off because its fuel had run out.

abschnitte.text: NASA launched Kepler in March 2009. It was meant to find out how common **Earth-sized planets** are around other stars. It is named after **Johannes Kepler**, who found the laws of planetary motion in the 17th century. Kepler circled the Sun in its own orbit and slowly moved away from the Earth. That way, neither the Earth's shadow nor the Earth's light disturbed the measurements.

Kepler searched for planets with the **transit method**. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star becomes a tiny bit dimmer. Kepler measured the brightness of over a hundred thousand stars very precisely. To do this, it stared for years at a fixed field between the constellations **Cygnus** and **Lyra**. This also let it catch planets with longer orbital periods several times.

Kepler found over 2,600 confirmed **exoplanets** and thousands more candidates. That made it the most successful planet hunter of its time. In 2014, **Kepler-186f** was announced, the first roughly Earth-sized planet in the **habitable zone** of a star. In this zone there could be liquid water. Whether Kepler-186f is really habitable is not known.

To point itself precisely, Kepler used **reaction wheels**. In 2013 the second of four wheels failed, and a fixed field could no longer be held. The mission continued as **K2**: Kepler observed different fields along the **ecliptic** one after the other. At the end of October 2018 the fuel had run out, and NASA ended the mission. Since 2018 the search has been continued by the telescope **TESS**, which watches almost the whole sky.

gewusst: The drop in brightness caused by an Earth-sized planet is less than one ten-thousandth.
Kepler's data are still being analysed today, and new planets are still being found in them.

teile.einleitung: The Great Red Spot is a huge storm on the planet Jupiter. It is bigger than the whole Earth and has been observed for a very long time.
wichtigste: The Great Red Spot is a huge storm on Jupiter.
It is bigger than the Earth.
It has been observed without a break since 1878.
It has been getting smaller for many years.
The storm turns anticlockwise, and one turn takes a few days.
Why it is red has not yet been fully explained.

abschnitte.text: The Great Red Spot lies in Jupiter's **southern hemisphere**. It is an enormous **storm**, similar to a high-pressure area on Earth, only much bigger. The Earth would fit inside it comfortably. The astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini may already have seen it in the 17th century. But people have only been observing it **without a break** since **1878**.

The storm turns **anticlockwise**. It takes **a few days** for one whole turn. At the edge of the spot, winds blow at **several hundred km/h**. That is faster than the strongest hurricanes on Earth. The storm also reaches far down into Jupiter's atmosphere. The space probe **Juno** measured this.

The spot used to be much bigger. Over a hundred years ago, several Earths would have fitted inside it side by side. For many years it has been **shrinking** and becoming rounder. Today it is only a little bigger than the Earth. Nobody knows for sure whether it will one day disappear completely.

The colour of the spot varies between pale pink and strong reddish orange. Researchers do **not yet know exactly** where the red comes from. Substances from deep down are probably carried upwards. Sunlight then changes them so that they turn reddish. With a telescope you can also observe the spot from Switzerland when Jupiter is well placed in the sky.

gewusst: A storm on Earth usually lasts only days or weeks, but the Great Red Spot has existed for well over a hundred years.
There are many smaller storms on Jupiter; one of them is called the “Little Red Spot”.

teile.einleitung: A coronal mass ejection is an enormous eruption on the Sun. The Sun flings a huge cloud of electrically charged gas into space, which can also hit the Earth.
wichtigste: A typical ejection contains about a billion tonnes of plasma.
The clouds fly at hundreds to thousands of kilometres per second.
They usually take one to four days to reach the Earth.
If their magnetic field points south, they cause strong geomagnetic storms.
At solar maximum they happen several times a day.
The SOHO probe has been observing them since 1996 with the instrument LASCO.

abschnitte.text: The outermost layer of the Sun is called the **corona**. Sometimes magnetic fields there tear open and fling a huge cloud of **plasma** into space. Plasma is a hot gas made of electrically charged particles. A typical **coronal mass ejection**, CME for short, contains about 10 to the power of 12 kilograms, about a billion tonnes. The cloud takes a piece of the Sun's magnetic field with it.

Speeds from about 20 to over 3,000 kilometres per second have been measured, about 500 on average. So an ejection usually takes **one to four days** to cover the roughly 150 million kilometres to the Earth. Very fast ejections make it in less than a day. If an ejection is faster than disturbances can spread in the **solar wind**, it pushes a **shock wave** ahead of it. At this shock wave, particles are accelerated to high energies.

If an ejection hits the Earth, it can cause a **geomagnetic storm**. It becomes especially strong if the magnetic field it carries points **south**. Then it points the opposite way to the Earth's magnetic field, and the fields can join up; this is called **reconnection**. In this way a lot of energy gets into the **magnetosphere**. The results can be auroras, but also disruption to satellites, radio and power grids.

A **coronagraph** covers the bright disc of the Sun so that you can see the faint corona. The **SOHO** probe has been observing ejections since 1996 with its coronagraphs called **LASCO**; tens of thousands have been catalogued this way. If an ejection appears as a ring around the Sun, it is called a **halo CME**. It is then flying straight towards us or away from us. From 2006, NASA's two **STEREO** probes observed ejections from two angles; contact with STEREO-B was lost in 2014.

The Sun has an activity cycle of about eleven years. At **solar maximum**, about three ejections a day are observed on average. At **solar minimum** it is only about one every five days. That is why space weather services watch the Sun constantly, so that they can warn of strong storms.

gewusst: Strong ejections can bring auroras so far south that you can even see them in Switzerland, as in May 2024.
A halo CME heading towards the Earth is particularly important for space weather.

teile.einleitung: The Moon landing of 1969 was one of the greatest moments in human history. With the Apollo 11 mission, humans set foot on another celestial body for the first time. Hundreds of millions of people followed the event live on television.
wichtigste: The first crewed Moon landing took place in 1969 with the Apollo 11 mission.
Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon, and Buzz Aldrin followed as the second.
Michael Collins stayed in the capsule in orbit around the Moon.
The astronauts set up a solar wind sail from the University of Bern.
By 1972, six Apollo missions had landed on the Moon.
Altogether, 12 people have walked on the Moon.
With the Artemis programme, the USA wants to send people to the Moon again.

abschnitte.text: In the 1950s and 1960s, during the **Cold War**, the USA and the Soviet Union also competed in space. The Soviet Union sent the first satellite into space in 1957 and the first human, Yuri Gagarin, in 1961. Then in 1961, US President John F. Kennedy announced that a man would be put on the Moon within the same decade. For this, NASA started the **Apollo programme**. Hundreds of thousands of people worked on it.

On 16 July 1969, **Apollo 11** was launched on the huge Saturn V rocket in Florida. On board were Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. On 20 July, the lunar module “Eagle” landed in the Sea of Tranquillity, a flat plain on the Moon. A few hours later, early in the morning of 21 July Swiss time, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to step onto the Moon. His sentence about one small step for a man and one giant leap for mankind became world-famous.

Armstrong and **Buzz Aldrin** spent about two and a half hours outside the lunar module. They collected about 22 kilograms of Moon rock and put up an American flag. They also set up experiments, including a seismometer and a laser mirror. The first experiment they set up was the **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern, a foil that caught particles of the solar wind. The Bern experiment, led by Johannes Geiss, also flew on later Apollo missions.

After Apollo 11, five more successful landings followed by December 1972. Only Apollo 13 had to turn back after an explosion on board, but the crew returned safely. Altogether, **12 people** have walked on the Moon, all of them men from the USA. On the later missions, the astronauts even drove around in a **moon buggy**. The last person on the Moon was Eugene Cernan of Apollo 17.

The Moon landing showed what people can achieve with science and cooperation. The **Moon rock** brought back is still being studied today and helped to explain how the Moon formed. Many technical developments from the Apollo programme, for example in computers, found their way into everyday life. With the **Artemis programme**, NASA, together with partners such as the European Space Agency ESA, plans to bring people to the Moon again. For the first time, a woman is also to walk on the Moon.

begriffe.erklaerung: The American space programme that took people to the Moon.
The landing craft in which the astronauts flew from lunar orbit down to the Moon and back.
A stream of tiny particles that constantly flows out from the Sun.
The long period of tension between the USA and the Soviet Union after the Second World War.

gewusst: The computers on the Apollo spacecraft had much less computing power than a modern smartphone.
The Bern solar wind sail was set up before the American flag.
Michael Collins circled the Moon alone and at times, behind the far side, had no radio contact at all with the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Lunar seas are the large, dark patches you can see on the Moon even with the naked eye. Despite their name, there is no water there: they are dry plains of solidified lava.
wichtigste: Lunar seas are flat, dry plains without water.
They formed from lava that flowed into large basins long ago and solidified.
Early researchers thought the dark patches were seas, hence the name.
The Latin word for a lunar sea is “mare”.
Apollo 11 landed in the Sea of Tranquillity in 1969.
The largest dark area is the Ocean of Storms.
Lunar seas have fewer craters than the bright highlands.

abschnitte.text: A few hundred years ago, researchers looked at the Moon with the first telescopes. They thought the dark patches were **seas** and the bright areas land. The name has stuck, even though there is no water there. In Latin, a lunar sea is called a **mare**, in the plural **maria**. The lunar seas are flat, dry plains of rock.

A very long time ago, large lumps crashed into the Moon and tore open huge **basins**. Later, liquid **lava** rose from inside the Moon and filled these basins. It hardened and today forms the dark plains. The rock is called **basalt** and is darker than the rock of the bright **highlands**. That is why the lunar seas look **dark grey** from the Earth.

The **Sea of Tranquillity** (Mare Tranquillitatis) is famous because **Apollo 11** landed there in 1969. The plain was flat and good for landing. The largest dark area is so big that it is called the **Ocean of Storms** (Oceanus Procellarum). Seen from the northern hemisphere, it lies on the left side of the Moon. Other names include the **Sea of Rains** and the **Sea of Serenity**.

The lunar seas are **younger** than the bright highlands. Since they formed, fewer lumps have had the chance to hit them. That is why they have **fewer craters** and look smoother. Researchers make use of this: the more craters an area has, the older it usually is.

Almost all the large lunar seas are on the side that always faces the Earth. Their dark areas form the pattern in which many people see a face, the **Man in the Moon**. In other countries people see other figures in it, for example a hare.

gewusst: On the far side of the Moon there are hardly any large lunar seas.
Many names of the lunar seas date from the 17th century and describe weather or moods, such as rain, tranquillity or serenity.

teile.einleitung: During a lunar eclipse, the Moon passes through the Earth's shadow and becomes dark or even copper red. This only happens at full moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon are almost exactly in a line. Unlike a solar eclipse, you can watch it without any protective glasses.
wichtigste: During a lunar eclipse, the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.
A lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon.
A total lunar eclipse can be seen from the whole night side of the Earth.
During a total eclipse the Moon glows faintly reddish and is often called a blood moon.
The red light comes about because the Earth's atmosphere bends red sunlight into the Earth's shadow.
Because the Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees against the Earth's orbit, there is not an eclipse at every full moon.
You can safely watch a lunar eclipse with the naked eye.

abschnitte.text: Like every lit-up body, the Earth casts a **shadow** into space. During a lunar eclipse, the Earth is exactly between the Sun and the Moon. The Moon then moves through the Earth's shadow and no longer gets any direct sunlight. This is only possible at **full moon**, because only then is the Moon opposite the Sun. A total eclipse can last for over an hour.

Even during a total eclipse, the Moon usually does not disappear completely. The **Earth's atmosphere** bends some of the sunlight into the Earth's shadow. Blue light is scattered more strongly, and mainly red light gets through, as at sunset. That is why the Moon glows faintly copper red. In everyday language it is then called a **blood moon**.

There are three kinds of lunar eclipse. In a **total** eclipse, the whole Moon enters the Earth's umbra, the full shadow. In a **partial** eclipse, only part of the Moon is covered by the umbra. In a penumbral eclipse, the Moon only grazes the outer, lighter penumbra, so you hardly notice anything. How dark a blood moon becomes also depends on how much dust is in the Earth's atmosphere at the time.

The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees against the Earth's orbit around the Sun. That is why the full moon usually passes just above or below the Earth's shadow. Only when the full moon is near the **nodes**, where the two orbits cross, is there an eclipse. There are usually two to three lunar eclipses of some kind each year. Astronomers can calculate them precisely many centuries in advance.

A total lunar eclipse can be seen from the whole **night side** of the Earth, as long as the Moon is above the horizon. That is why a great many people can watch at the same time. You do not need protective glasses, but binoculars make the spectacle even more beautiful. The Greek scholar Aristotle already realised from the round shadow of the Earth on the Moon that the Earth is a sphere. In earlier times, lunar eclipses frightened many people because they were seen as a bad sign.

begriffe.erklaerung: The darkest part of a shadow, into which no direct sunlight falls at all.
The lighter outer area of a shadow, into which some sunlight still falls.
An everyday name for the reddish glowing Moon during a total lunar eclipse.
An event in which one celestial body moves into the shadow of another.

gewusst: Anyone standing on the Moon during a lunar eclipse would see a solar eclipse caused by the Earth, framed by a red ring.
In 1504, Christopher Columbus is said to have used a lunar eclipse he had calculated in advance to impress local people in Jamaica.
A lunar eclipse can be seen for much longer than a solar eclipse, because the Earth's shadow is much bigger than the Moon.

t1foky1l.t: Distance from the Earth to the Sun

teile.einleitung: The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from the Earth. This distance is so important that it is used as a unit of measurement in astronomy. It also makes sure that it is neither too hot nor too cold on Earth.
wichtigste: The Sun is on average about 150 million kilometres from the Earth.
That is about 400 times as far as the Moon.
This distance is called the astronomical unit, AU for short.
The Earth circles the Sun in an almost round orbit.
At the beginning of January, the Earth is closest to the Sun.
The right distance makes liquid water possible on Earth.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is on average about **150 million kilometres** from the Earth. The Moon is only about 384,000 kilometres away. So the Sun is about **400 times** as far away as the Moon. That is why the huge Sun looks so small in the sky: the further away something is, the smaller it looks. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us.

Because the distances in the solar system are so large, researchers use a unit of their own. The average distance between the Earth and the Sun is called the **astronomical unit**, **AU** for short. Mars, for example, is on average about 1.5 AU from the Sun, so about one and a half times as far as the Earth. This unit makes distances easy to compare.

A calculation shows how far 150 million kilometres is. An aeroplane flies at about 900 kilometres per hour. Without a break, it would need about 167,000 hours to reach the Sun. That is about **19 years**. A child born at take-off would already be grown up on arrival.

The Earth travels around the Sun in an **orbit**. This path is almost round, but not quite. At the beginning of **January**, the Earth is closest to the Sun, and at the beginning of July it is furthest away. So summer and winter are not caused by the distance. They happen because the **Earth's axis is tilted**, so the Sun's rays hit us at different angles over the course of the year.

The Earth is neither too close to nor too far from the Sun. Venus, which orbits closer, is scorching hot. Mars, which orbits further out, is ice cold. On Earth, however, there can be **liquid water**. This is an important condition for life as we know it.

gewusst: The light you are seeing from the Sun right now left it about eight minutes ago.
In January, the Earth is about 5 million kilometres closer to the Sun than in July.

teile.einleitung: The Earth is our home planet and the only place in the universe where we know there is life. It is the third planet from the Sun and has one moon. From space it looks like a blue marble, because water covers most of its surface.
wichtigste: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
It has a single natural moon.
Water covers about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface.
The Earth takes a year to go once around the Sun.
A layer of air, the atmosphere, surrounds the Earth like a protective cover.
The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
It is the largest of the four rocky planets.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is the third of eight planets in the **solar system**. It is a rocky planet with a diameter of about 12,700 kilometres. Its circumference at the equator is about 40,000 kilometres. It is just the right distance from the Sun for water to be liquid, which is why we speak of the **habitable zone**.

About 71 per cent of the surface is covered with water, mainly by the great **oceans**. The largest of these is the Pacific. The land is spread over seven continents, the largest being Asia. The highest mountain is Mount Everest at 8,849 metres, and the deepest point lies in the Mariana Trench, almost 11 kilometres below sea level.

The Earth is surrounded by a layer of air, the **atmosphere**. It consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen. The atmosphere gives us air to breathe, holds in the heat and, with the **ozone layer**, protects us from dangerous UV radiation. In addition, most small lumps of rock from space burn up in it as shooting stars.

The Earth is built up of layers like an onion. Right on the outside is the thin **Earth's crust**, beneath it the hot mantle and in the middle the core of iron and nickel. In the core it is about as hot as on the surface of the Sun. The liquid outer core creates the **magnetic field**, which protects us from charged particles from the Sun.

The Earth spins once on its own axis in about 24 hours, and this creates day and night. In a year it goes around the Sun. Its only moon is about 384,000 kilometres away and with its pull causes **low and high tide**. Because the Earth's axis is tilted, there are seasons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large round celestial body that circles a star.
The layer of air that surrounds a planet.
The outermost, solid layer of the Earth, on which we live.
An invisible field of force that a compass needle, for example, lines up with.

gewusst: The Earth is not quite round but slightly flattened at the poles.
The Earth is the densest planet in the whole solar system.
Almost 97 per cent of the water on Earth is salty seawater.

teile.einleitung: A model rocket is a small, light rocket that really flies. People build them as a hobby or in lessons and learn a lot about technology and physics.
wichtigste: Model rockets are made of light materials such as cardboard, balsa wood and plastic.
They are usually powered by a small solid-fuel motor.
The motor burns for only a few seconds.
It is ignited electrically from a safe distance.
A launch rod guides the rocket straight upwards at the start.
A parachute brings it gently back to the ground.
Children always launch model rockets together with an adult.

abschnitte.text: A model rocket looks like a big rocket in miniature. It has a slim **body**, a pointed **nose** and **fins** at the bottom. The fins make sure the rocket flies steadily and straight. Because everything has to be very light, it is built from cardboard, balsa wood and plastic. You can glue together and paint many models yourself from a kit.

Model rockets usually fly with a small **solid-fuel motor**. This is a tube containing solid fuel. When it burns, hot gases stream out downwards, and the rocket is pushed upwards. This principle is called **recoil** or thrust. The motor burns for only a few seconds, but in that time the rocket can climb dozens or even hundreds of metres. The motors are bought ready-made; you never make them yourself.

Before launch, the rocket is placed on a thin metal rod, the **launch rod**. It slides along it as it lifts off and so flies in the right direction from the start. It is ignited **electrically**: a cable runs from the motor to a switch. This means you stand far enough away at launch. Beforehand you count down out loud, so that everyone knows it is about to go.

When the motor has burned out, the rocket carries on upwards for a bit. Then a small **ejection charge** goes off. It pushes off the nose and lets a **parachute** fall out. The rocket floats slowly to the ground on the parachute. That way nothing breaks, and you can launch it again with a new motor.

It is best to launch on a large, **open field**. There are no trees, houses or power lines there, and nothing can catch fire easily. In strong wind or when it is very dry, it is better to wait. Because the motor burns very hot, there is always an **adult** with children. They help set up and make sure everyone keeps their distance.

gewusst: Model rockets as a hobby became known in the USA in the 1950s and then spread all over the world.
The motors have letters such as A, B or C: each next letter stands for about twice as much total thrust.

teile.einleitung: Perihelion and aphelion are the two special points on a planet's orbit around the Sun. At perihelion it is closest to the Sun, and at aphelion furthest from it. The Earth has such points too.
wichtigste: Perihelion is the point of an orbit closest to the Sun, and aphelion the point furthest from it.
The Earth reaches its perihelion at the beginning of January and its aphelion at the beginning of July.
At perihelion the Earth is about 147 million km from the Sun, and at aphelion about 152 million km.
The distance varies by only just over 3 per cent and does not explain the seasons.
At perihelion the Earth moves fastest.
Together, perihelion and aphelion are called apsides.

abschnitte.text: The words come from **Greek**. “Peri” means “close to”, “apo” means “away from”, and “Helios” is the Sun. So at **perihelion** a planet is closest to the Sun, and at **aphelion** furthest away. This is because planetary orbits are not perfect circles but **ellipses**. Johannes Kepler found this out.

The Earth's orbit is almost a circle. At **perihelion** at the beginning of **January**, the Earth is about **147.1 million km** from the Sun, and at **aphelion** at the beginning of **July** about **152.1 million km**. So the distance varies by only just over **3 per cent**. Amazingly, just when it is summer in our part of the world, we are furthest from the Sun.

abschnitte.titel: Not the reason for the seasons
abschnitte.text: The small differences in distance are far too small to explain **summer and winter**. The seasons come about because the **Earth's axis is tilted**. In summer, the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun. The Sun is higher in the sky, and the days are longer. In the southern hemisphere it is exactly the other way round.

A planet does not always travel at the same speed. Close to the Sun, the Sun pulls more strongly and the planet moves faster. The Earth is fastest at **perihelion**, at just over **30 km/s**, and at aphelion only about **29 km/s**. This rule is **Kepler's second law**. That is why in our part of the world the winter half of the year is a few days shorter than the summer half.

Together, perihelion and aphelion are called **apsides**. The line joining them is called the **line of apsides**. For orbits around the Earth, people speak of **perigee** (close to the Earth) and **apogee** (far from the Earth). The Moon has them too. When a full moon falls at perigee, people often speak of a **supermoon**, because it looks a little bigger and brighter.

gewusst: Comets often have very stretched orbits: their aphelion can lie far beyond the orbit of Neptune.
The Earth's perihelion is slowly moving through the calendar; in many thousands of years it will be in summer.

teile.einleitung: The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest telescope ever sent into space. It observes mainly infrared light and so looks deep into the past of the universe.
wichtigste: James Webb is considered the successor to the Hubble Telescope.
It observes mainly infrared light, in other words heat radiation.
It was built by NASA, ESA and the Canadian CSA.
It works about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth at the point L2.
The sunshield is about the size of a tennis court.
The first colour pictures appeared in July 2022.

abschnitte.text: Since 1990, the **Hubble Telescope** has been observing mainly visible light. The James Webb Telescope adds observations in the **infrared**. Infrared light is **heat radiation**. With it, the telescope can look through clouds of dust and capture the light of very distant galaxies. It was launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5.

The telescope is named after **James Webb**. He led NASA in the 1960s. During his time in office, the **Apollo Moon programme** was prepared. The telescope was built by NASA together with the European **ESA** and the Canadian Space Agency **CSA**.

To measure faint heat radiation, the telescope itself has to be very cold. That is why it has a huge **sunshield** made of five thin layers of foil. It is about 21 metres long and 14 metres wide, about the size of a tennis court. The shield keeps out the light and heat of the Sun and Earth. The telescope circles the **Lagrange point L2**, about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth on the side facing away from the Sun.

After launch, the telescope had to **unfold** step by step in space. The golden main mirror made of 18 parts and the sunshield had been folded up for the rocket. After that it took months to cool down and to line up the mirrors precisely. In July 2022, NASA showed the first colour pictures. They showed galaxies, nebulae and the light fingerprint of a distant planet.

The telescope has four scientific instruments. The **Paul Scherrer Institute** (PSI) and **ETH Zurich** helped build the instrument **MIRI** for the mid-infrared. Swiss experts developed cables and a shutter mechanism, among other things. MIRI is the instrument that measures the longest wavelengths and therefore has to be especially cold.

gewusst: The main mirror consists of 18 hexagonal parts covered with a thin layer of gold.
Because light takes time to travel, James Webb sees some galaxies as they looked over 13 billion years ago.

teile.einleitung: An ion drive is an electric rocket engine. It only pushes very gently, but it can run for months and uses very little fuel.
wichtigste: The most common fuel for ion engines is the noble gas xenon.
Charged grids accelerate the ions with an electric field.
A neutraliser stops the probe from becoming electrically charged.
The thrust is in the range of millinewtons.
From 1998, Deep Space 1 was the first NASA probe to use an ion engine as its main drive.
In 2010, the Japanese probe Hayabusa brought samples from the asteroid Itokawa to Earth.

abschnitte.text: In the engine, a gas is **ionised**, which means electrons are torn away from its atoms. The atoms are then electrically charged and are called **ions**. There is a high voltage between charged **grids**. The electric field accelerates the ions to a high speed and flings them out at the back. The electricity usually comes from **solar panels**.

The noble gas **xenon** is used most often. It is heavy, easy to ionise and hardly reacts with other substances. It can also be stored densely in tanks. The first **Starlink satellites** used **krypton** in their Hall thrusters. It is much cheaper but gives a little less thrust, and with thousands of satellites, the price matters.

If an engine only pushed out positive ions, the probe would become negatively charged. Then it would attract the ions back again. That is why a **neutraliser** releases electrons into the ion beam. This keeps the probe electrically neutral.

The **thrust** of an ion engine is in the range of **millinewtons**. That is about as much as a sheet of paper pressing on your hand. But an ion drive can run for months or years. This lets the probe achieve a large change in speed, the **delta-v**, with little fuel. For launching from the Earth the thrust is far too weak; chemical rockets are needed for that.

From 1998, NASA's **Deep Space 1** was the first probe to use an ion engine as its main drive, which ran for over 16,000 hours. In 2001 it flew past the comet Borrelly. The Japanese probe **Hayabusa** had four xenon ion engines and landed its sample capsule from the asteroid Itokawa in Australia in 2010. From 2003, the ESA probe **SMART-1** flew to the Moon in a spiral path in about 13 months using a Hall thruster.

gewusst: The ions leave the engine at tens of thousands of kilometres per hour, much faster than the gases of a chemical rocket.
At the end of its mission in 2006, SMART-1 was deliberately steered onto the surface of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: The ecliptic is the imaginary line in the sky along which the Sun moves in front of the stars over the course of a year. Along this line you also find the Moon, the planets and the constellations of the zodiac.
wichtigste: The ecliptic is the apparent yearly path of the Sun in front of the stars.
It is tilted by about 23.4 degrees to the celestial equator.
The Sun moves on by about 1 degree each day.
The planets are always close to the ecliptic.
The constellations along the ecliptic make up the zodiac.
The name comes from the Greek word for eclipse.

abschnitte.text: The Earth travels around the Sun in a year. Seen from the Earth, the Sun therefore stands in front of **different stars** over the course of the year. We cannot see these stars during the day, but it can be calculated. The imaginary line along which the Sun moves is called the **ecliptic**. The Sun takes about 365 days for the 360 degrees. So it moves on by **just under 1 degree** each day.

abschnitte.titel: At an angle to the celestial equator
abschnitte.text: The **celestial equator** is the Earth's equator extended out onto the sky. The Earth's axis is tilted by about **23.4 degrees** compared with the Earth's orbit. The ecliptic is tipped by the same angle against the celestial equator. The two lines cross at two points. Around **20 March**, the Sun is at the **vernal equinox point** and moves from the southern to the northern sky. Then day and night are about the same length everywhere.

The Greek word **“ekleipsis”** means **eclipse**. Solar and lunar eclipses only happen when the Moon is close to the ecliptic. The Moon's orbit is slightly tilted against the ecliptic. Only when a new moon or full moon happens exactly as the Moon crosses the ecliptic are the Sun, Earth and Moon in a line.

The solar system is fairly **flat**, like a disc. The orbits of the planets lie almost in the same plane as the Earth's orbit. That is why, seen from the Earth, the planets all move across the sky **close to the ecliptic**. The constellations the ecliptic runs through make up the **zodiac**, for example Aries, Taurus and Gemini. According to today's constellation boundaries, the Sun also passes through **Ophiuchus**, roughly from late November to mid December. Even so, astrology does not count it among its twelve signs of the zodiac.

gewusst: Because the ecliptic is tilted, the Sun in Switzerland stands much higher in the sky at midday in summer than in winter.
The constellation boundaries in the sky were fixed in 1930 by the International Astronomical Union.

t1k1nivu.t: Distance from the Earth to the Moon

teile.einleitung: The Moon is our nearest neighbour in space. Even so, it is very far away: on average about 384,000 kilometres. Here you can find out how this distance is measured and how you can imagine it.
wichtigste: The Moon is on average about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth.
About 30 Earths would fit side by side between the Earth and the Moon.
The Apollo astronauts needed about three days for the journey.
The Moon's orbit is not quite round, so the distance changes.
A full moon at a particularly short distance is called a supermoon.
With laser light and mirrors on the Moon, the distance is measured very precisely.
The Moon moves about 4 centimetres further away every year.

abschnitte.titel: How far away is the Moon?
abschnitte.text: The Moon is on average about **384,000 kilometres** from the Earth. The Earth itself is about 12,700 kilometres thick. So you could place about **30 Earths** side by side between the Earth and the Moon. Even so, the Moon is much closer than the Sun. It is the nearest celestial body of all.

The American **Apollo spacecraft** needed about **three days** to get to the Moon. A car travelling at 100 km/h on an imaginary road would take much longer. 384,000 kilometres divided by 100 kilometres per hour makes 3,840 hours. That is about 160 days, so a good five months without a break. Light, on the other hand, covers the distance in just over a second.

The Moon's orbit around the Earth is not a perfect circle but slightly oval. That is why the Moon is sometimes a bit closer and sometimes a bit further away. If it is particularly close at full moon, people speak of a **supermoon**. It then looks a little bigger and brighter than usual. But the difference is hard to see with the naked eye.

During the Apollo missions, astronauts placed **mirrors** on the Moon. Researchers on Earth send **laser light** to these mirrors. They measure how long the light takes to get there and back. Because the speed of light is known exactly, the distance can be calculated from this. This is how the distance to the Moon is measured to within a few centimetres.

The measurements show something amazing: every year the Moon moves about **4 centimetres** further away from the Earth. That is about as much as a fingernail grows in a year. The reason is the **tides**, the interplay of low tide and high tide. You notice nothing of this in everyday life, but over a very long time it makes a big difference.

gewusst: All the other planets of the solar system together would just about fit into the gap between the Earth and the Moon.
The mirrors on the Moon have been used for measurements for over 50 years.

teile.einleitung: Gravitational waves are tiny ripples in space and time that form when very heavy bodies move violently. Albert Einstein predicted them in 1916, but they were only measured directly in 2015. Since then, researchers can not only see the universe but also, in a way, hear it.
wichtigste: Gravitational waves are distortions of space and time that spread out like waves.
According to today's measurements, they travel at the speed of light.
The first directly measured signal, GW150914, came from two black holes merging.
Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 2017.
Each arm of a LIGO detector is 4 kilometres long.
With GW170817, the same event was observed with light as well for the first time.
ESA is planning the space observatory LISA with arms 2.5 million kilometres long.

abschnitte.text: According to Einstein's general theory of relativity, masses bend space and time. When huge masses move very fast, waves form in this **spacetime**, just as a stone makes ripples in a pond. These **gravitational waves** squeeze and stretch everything they pass through by a tiny amount. They travel at the speed of light.

Einstein predicted the waves in 1916 but thought they were too weak ever to be measured. In 1974, Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered the **Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar**, two neutron stars orbiting each other. Their orbital period is slowly getting shorter, exactly as expected if they are giving off gravitational waves. This was the first indirect proof, and it earned the Nobel Prize in 1993.

The two **LIGO** detectors in the USA each have two arms, 4 kilometres long, in the shape of an L. Laser beams in them measure whether the lengths of the arms change by a tiny amount. A gravitational wave changes the length by less than a thousandth of the diameter of a proton. Similar detectors are **Virgo** in Italy and KAGRA in Japan.

On 14 September 2015, LIGO recorded the signal **GW150914**, caused by two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light years away. Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 2017. In the same year, the merger of two neutron stars was measured with **GW170817**. For the first time, telescopes also observed the same event electromagnetically, in other words as light, and found signs of newly formed gold.

With **LISA**, ESA is planning a gravitational wave observatory in space. Three satellites are to form a huge triangle with arms 2.5 million kilometres long. This will make it possible to measure slower waves, for example from huge black holes merging at the centres of galaxies. Swiss researchers, for example at ETH Zurich and the University of Zurich, are involved in LISA.

begriffe.erklaerung: Space and time together, as Einstein describes them.
A celestial body with such strong gravity that not even light can escape.
A very small, extremely dense remnant of an exploded star.
A measuring device that uses laser light to detect the tiniest changes in length.

gewusst: If you turn the GW150914 signal into sound, it sounds like a short, rising chirp.
In the GW150914 merger, about the mass of three suns was turned into gravitational waves in fractions of a second.
Gravitational waves pass through everything, including the Earth, without us feeling it.

teile.einleitung: Molecular clouds are huge, cold and dark clouds of gas and dust in space. New stars form in them. They are among the most important places for understanding where stars and planets come from.
wichtigste: Molecular clouds consist mainly of molecular hydrogen (H₂), plus helium and dust.
Inside they are only about 10 to 20 kelvin, just above absolute zero.
Because H₂ hardly gives off any radiation in the cold, the clouds are mapped with carbon monoxide (CO).
Giant molecular clouds reach up to a few million solar masses.
If a cloud exceeds the Jeans mass, it collapses under its own gravity.
The Orion Nebula is the nearest large region where massive stars form.

abschnitte.text: The main ingredient is **molecular hydrogen**, two hydrogen atoms joined together (H₂). There is also helium, tiny **dust grains** and traces of many other molecules. Experts have already found well over a hundred different molecules in space, for example water, ammonia and even alcohol. The dust shields off the light of the stars. That is why it is so cold inside and the molecules are not destroyed.

Molecular clouds are dark in normal light. At 10 to 20 kelvin, the hydrogen itself gives off practically no radiation, because the H₂ molecule has no **dipole moment**. The molecule **carbon monoxide** (CO), on the other hand, gives off easily measurable lines in the millimetre range. With radio telescopes, the shape and movement of the clouds can be mapped precisely in this way. So CO acts like a glowing paint that shows where the gas is.

Two forces battle against each other in a cloud: the **gas pressure** pushes outwards, and **gravity** pulls inwards. The **Jeans criterion** says: above a certain limit, the Jeans mass, gravity wins. Then the cloud begins to collapse. This can be set off, for example, by the **shock wave of a supernova**, which squeezes the gas together. In the densest places it gets hot, and a new star forms.

**Giant molecular clouds** are dozens to hundreds of light years across. Whole star clusters form from them. The **Orion Nebula** in Orion's sword is about 1,300 light years away and can be seen with the naked eye in winter. In the **Eagle Nebula** M16 are the “Pillars of Creation”, dense fingers of gas and dust. The Hubble image from 1995 made them famous all over the world.

There are also very small, dense and dark clouds, the **Bok globules**. They are named after the astronomer Bart Bok. In front of a bright nebula they appear as black spots. Single stars or small groups of stars can form in them.

gewusst: Our Sun also formed in a molecular cloud about 4.6 billion years ago.
Molecular clouds are among the coldest places in the whole universe.

teile.einleitung: Galileo Galilei was an Italian natural scientist who lived from 1564 to 1642. He was one of the first to explore the sky with a telescope. His discoveries supported the view of the world with the Sun at the centre and brought him into conflict with the Church.
wichtigste: With the telescope, Galileo discovered mountains and craters on the Moon.
He realised that the Milky Way consists of countless stars.
For him, the phases of Venus were evidence for the heliocentric view of the world.
He found out that without air all bodies fall at the same speed.
In 1633 he was sentenced by the Inquisition to house arrest for life.
In 1992, Pope John Paul II declared that the Church had wronged him.

abschnitte.text: Galileo Galilei was born in **1564** in **Pisa** and died in **1642** near Florence. He was a mathematician, physicist and astronomer. Galileo carried out many **experiments** and demanded that claims be tested by observation. That is why he is considered one of the founders of modern natural science.

From 1609, Galileo pointed a **telescope** at the sky. On the **Moon** he saw light and shadow and concluded that there were **mountains and craters**. So the Moon was not a perfectly smooth sphere. He resolved the **Milky Way** into countless individual, faint **stars**. He also discovered four large moons around Jupiter, which today are called the **Galilean moons**.

Galileo saw that **Venus** shows **phases** like the Moon, appearing sometimes full and sometimes thin. The easiest way to explain this is if Venus circles the **Sun**. For Galileo, this was evidence for the **heliocentric view of the world**, in which the Sun is in the middle. But at that time the Church taught that the Earth was at the centre.

Galileo also studied how bodies **fall**. He realised that without **air resistance** all bodies fall at the same speed, no matter how heavy they are. In air, a feather only falls more slowly because the air slows it down. This finding was very important for later **physics**. Centuries later, it was demonstrated on the Moon with a hammer and a feather.

In **1633**, Galileo stood before the **Inquisition**, a court of the Church. He had to renounce the heliocentric view of the world. He was sentenced to **house arrest for life** and spent the rest of his life near Florence. The famous sentence **“And yet it moves”** is said to have been spoken after the trial. But it was only recorded long after his death, and Galileo probably never said it. In **1992**, Pope **John Paul II** publicly acknowledged that the verdict had been a mistake.

gewusst: In Italian, the famous sentence is “Eppur si muove”.
A NASA space probe that explored Jupiter was named Galileo.

teile.einleitung: A magnetar is a neutron star with an unimaginably strong magnetic field. It is the strongest magnetic field known in the universe. Magnetars give off X-rays and gamma rays and can have enormous outbursts.
wichtigste: The magnetic field strength of a magnetar is about 10^9 to 10^11 tesla.
The energy for its radiation comes mainly from the **decay of the magnetic field**.
**Soft gamma repeaters** and **anomalous X-ray pulsars** are now counted as magnetars.
On 27 December 2004, the magnetar **SGR 1806-20** had a giant flare.
In 2020, a magnetar in the Milky Way was linked with a **fast radio burst**.
Robert Duncan and Christopher Thompson proposed the model in 1992.

abschnitte.text: When a very large star explodes at the end of its life, a **neutron star** can be left behind. It is only about the size of a city but heavier than the Sun. Some neutron stars have a particularly strong magnetic field. They are called **magnetars**. The model for them was proposed by **Robert Duncan** and **Christopher Thompson** in **1992**.

The magnetic field strength of a magnetar is about **10^9 to 10^11 tesla**. For comparison: the Earth's magnetic field, which a compass lines up with, is many trillions of times weaker. A magnetar gets its energy mainly from the **decay** of this magnetic field. This produces strong **X-rays** and **gamma rays**.

Many radio pulsars spin several times a second. Magnetars, on the other hand, rotate **slowly**, about **once every few seconds**. Their strong magnetic field slows them down. A magnetar also does not stay active for long. After **about 10,000 years**, its magnetic field has weakened so much that it hardly stands out any more. For astronomy, that is a very short time.

In the past, two puzzling kinds of objects in the sky were known. **Soft gamma repeaters** repeatedly send out flashes of gamma rays. **Anomalous X-ray pulsars** regularly give off X-rays. Today we know that both groups belong to the **magnetars**. So they are just two different sides of the same kind of star.

On **27 December 2004**, the magnetar **SGR 1806-20** had a giant flare. Even though it lies far away in the Milky Way, the radiation measurably disturbed the Earth's **ionosphere**. This is a layer high up in the atmosphere. In **2020**, a magnetar in the Milky Way was linked with a **fast radio burst** for the first time. Such short flashes had long been a mystery.

gewusst: A neutron star is so dense that a teaspoon of its material would weigh many millions of tonnes on Earth.
In a tenth of a second, the flare of SGR 1806-20 released more energy than the Sun gives off in many thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: The universe is expanding: galaxies are moving away from each other because the space between them is growing. This expansion of the universe began with the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago. The further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us.
wichtigste: The universe has been expanding since the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago.
In 1927, Georges Lemaître worked out the expansion from the theory of relativity and observations.
In 1929, Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are flying away from us faster.
The Hubble constant is given in kilometres per second per megaparsec.
Because of the expansion, the light of distant galaxies becomes redder; this is called redshift.
Different measurements of the Hubble constant contradict each other; this is the Hubble tension.
For a few billion years, the expansion has been speeding up because of dark energy.

abschnitte.text: The galaxies are not flying away through a fixed space; **space itself** is expanding. You can imagine it like a raisin cake in the oven: the dough rises, and all the raisins move away from each other. From every raisin, it looks as if all the others are flying away. That is why there is no centre of the expansion either.

The Belgian physicist and priest **Georges Lemaître** worked out the expansion in 1927 from Einstein's general theory of relativity and observations. He is also considered the father of the idea of the **Big Bang**. In 1929, the American Edwin Hubble published measurements that showed: the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away. Today this relationship is called the **Hubble-Lemaître law**.

The **Hubble constant** H0 tells you how fast the expansion is today. It is given in kilometres per second per megaparsec; one megaparsec is about 3.26 million light years. If it is 70, a galaxy at a distance of 100 megaparsecs is moving away at 7,000 km/s. The reciprocal, 1 divided by H0, is called the Hubble time and with this value comes to about 14 billion years, similar to the age of the universe.

As light travels through the growing universe, its waves are stretched too and so become redder. This **redshift** z measures how much the light has been stretched. If a line at 500 nm is observed at 1,000 nm, z equals 1, and the universe was half as big when the light was sent out. At z equals 3, the universe was only a quarter as big as today when the light was sent out.

Different measuring methods give slightly different values for H0, about 67 or 73 km/s per megaparsec. This contradiction is called the **Hubble tension**, and it has still not been solved. In addition, the expansion has been speeding up for about 5 to 6 billion years, which is explained by **dark energy**. Space telescopes such as Euclid and James Webb are to help solve these puzzles.

begriffe.erklaerung: The beginning of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.
The light of distant galaxies is stretched into longer, redder waves.
A huge unit of distance of about 3.26 million light years.
A number that tells you how fast the universe is expanding today.

gewusst: Despite the expansion, the Andromeda Galaxy is coming towards us, because gravity is stronger over short distances.
Very distant galaxies are now moving away from us faster than light, because space itself is expanding.
Einstein himself at first believed in an unchanging universe and only accepted the expansion later.

teile.einleitung: A heat shield protects space capsules and space shuttles as they enter an atmosphere. Thousands of degrees of heat are produced. Without a heat shield, a spacecraft would burn up.
wichtigste: On entering the atmosphere, the air in front of the spacecraft is strongly compressed and becomes red hot.
An ablative heat shield chars and evaporates, carrying heat away as it does so.
Return capsules have a blunt shape so that less heat reaches the capsule.
The Space Shuttle carried over 20,000 heat protection tiles made of silica fibres.
Apollo and Orion use the material Avcoat, the Dragon capsule PICA-X.
In 1995, the Galileo probe survived an entry at Jupiter at about 47 km/s.

abschnitte.text: A space capsule returning from Earth orbit is travelling at about 28,000 km/h. On entering the **atmosphere**, it hits the air at this speed. In front of the capsule a **shock wave** forms, in which the air is strongly compressed. This air becomes thousands of degrees hot and glows. So the heat comes mainly from squeezing the air, not just from friction.

Return capsules have a **blunt** underside instead of a pointed nose. This puts the shock wave **further forward**, and less heat reaches the capsule. Many capsules have an **ablative heat shield**. Its material slowly **chars** and **evaporates**, carrying heat away as it does so. The Apollo capsules and the new Orion capsule use **Avcoat** for this. SpaceX uses the material **PICA-X** for the **Dragon** capsule.

The **Space Shuttle** was meant to fly many times. So its heat protection was not allowed to evaporate. It carried **over 20,000 heat protection tiles**. Most of them were made of **silica fibres**, a kind of glass. These tiles conduct heat so poorly that you can touch their edges shortly after they have been glowing. The hottest places, the nose and the **leading edges of the wings**, were protected by **reinforced carbon-carbon**.

Probes to other planets need heat shields too. In 1995, the **Galileo atmospheric probe** had to survive the toughest entry so far, at **Jupiter**. It plunged into the atmosphere at about **47 km/s**. A large part of its heat shield evaporated. But the probe survived the entry and then sent measurements from Jupiter's atmosphere back to Earth.

gewusst: During entry, radio contact with the capsule is often lost for a few minutes, because the glowing air disturbs the radio waves.
The blunt shape for return capsules was developed in the USA in the 1950s; it was a surprising discovery.

teile.einleitung: Lagrange points are special places in space. There, the gravity of two celestial bodies and the movement of a small probe balance each other so that the probe keeps its position relative to the two. Space agencies like to use these points for telescopes.
wichtigste: In a system of two bodies orbiting each other there are **five** Lagrange points.
L4 and L5 are stable if the two main bodies have very different masses.
L1 and L2 of the Sun-Earth system lie about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth.
The James Webb Space Telescope works at the point L2.
The solar observatory SOHO has been watching the Sun from L1 since 1996.
In 1767, the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** found the three points that lie on a line.

abschnitte.text: Imagine the Sun and the Earth turning around each other together. At certain places, their **gravity** together with the circular movement acts in such a way that a small body moves along with them. It then always stays in the same place relative to the Sun and the Earth. Such places are called **Lagrange points**. There are exactly **five** of them, called L1 to L5.

The **Basel** mathematician **Leonhard Euler** found as early as **1767** the three points that lie on a line with the two bodies: L1, L2 and L3. A few years later, the mathematician **Joseph-Louis Lagrange** also described the points L4 and L5. These lie on the orbit of the smaller body, 60 degrees ahead of it and behind it. In the end, all five points were named after Lagrange.

L1 and L2 of the Sun-Earth system each lie **about 1.5 million kilometres** from the Earth. L1 lies between the Earth and the Sun. From there, the **SOHO** observatory of ESA and NASA has been watching the Sun without a break since 1996. L2 lies on the other side, behind the Earth as seen from the Sun. The **James Webb Space Telescope** works there, because the Sun, Earth and Moon are always in the same direction and it can easily shield itself from them.

L1, L2 and L3 are **unstable**. It is like a ball on a hill: small disturbances grow. That is why a probe at L2 regularly needs small **course corrections** with its engines. L4 and L5, on the other hand, are **stable** if the two main bodies have very different masses. There a body stays put like a ball in a hollow.

Many asteroids have gathered at the stable points L4 and L5 of the **Sun-Jupiter** system. They are called **Trojans**. They travel around the Sun on the same orbit as Jupiter, one group ahead of it and one behind it. Many of them are named after heroes from the Greek legend of the Trojan War.

gewusst: At L1 and L2, the probes usually circle the point in large orbits instead of sitting exactly on it.
Trojans have also been found alongside other planets such as Mars or Neptune.

teile.einleitung: Galaxies are not spread evenly through space. Many are linked by their gravity into large groups, the galaxy clusters. They are among the largest connected structures in the universe.
