wichtigste: Galaxy clusters contain hundreds to thousands of galaxies.
Groups have up to about 50 bright galaxies; larger collections are called clusters.
Most of the mass is dark matter.
Hot gas between the galaxies glows mainly in X-ray light.
Massive clusters act as gravitational lenses.
The nearest large cluster is the Virgo Cluster, about 54 million light years away.
Clusters together form even larger superclusters.

abschnitte.text: Galaxies often occur together. Smaller collections with up to about **50** bright galaxies are called **groups**. Our Milky Way, for example, belongs to the **Local Group**. Larger collections with **hundreds to thousands** of galaxies are called **galaxy clusters**. The nearest large cluster is the **Virgo Cluster** in the constellation Virgo. It is about 54 million light years away and contains well over a thousand galaxies.

Between the galaxies of a cluster lies very thin but extremely **hot gas**. It is tens of millions of degrees hot. At such temperatures it gives off mainly **X-rays**. This gas contains more normal matter than all the stars of the cluster put together. The cosmic **background radiation** is also changed as it passes through the gas. Fast electrons give it energy; this is called the **Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect**.

About **80 to 90 per cent** of the mass of a cluster is **dark matter**. It is invisible and can only be detected by its gravity. A strong clue is the **Bullet Cluster**. There, two clusters collided. The hot gas was slowed down, while the dark matter flew through. Measurements show: most of the mass is not where most of the gas is.

The huge mass of a cluster **bends** the space around it. This deflects the light of galaxies behind it. This creates distorted **arcs** and even **multiple images** of the same galaxy. This is called the **gravitational lensing effect**. Researchers use it to measure the mass of clusters and to see very distant galaxies.

Galaxy clusters and groups line up into even larger structures. They are called **superclusters**. The Virgo Cluster, for example, lies at the centre of the **Virgo Supercluster**. The superclusters stretch through space along long threads, the **filaments**. Between them lie huge, almost empty spaces, the **voids**.

gewusst: On a large scale, the universe looks like foam or a huge spider's web of galaxies.
The Local Group with our Milky Way is only a small group at the edge of the Virgo Supercluster.

teile.einleitung: The Little Dipper is a star pattern in the northern sky that looks like a smaller version of the Plough. At its end sits the famous Pole Star.
wichtigste: The Little Dipper belongs to the constellation of the Little Bear.
It usually consists of seven stars: four in the box and three in the handle.
The Pole Star sits at the end of the handle.
The Little Dipper is very close to the north celestial pole.
In our part of the world it never sets.
Many of its stars are faint and hard to see in towns.

abschnitte.text: The Little Dipper is not a constellation of its own but the noticeable part of the constellation of the **Little Bear**. Like the Plough, it usually consists of **seven stars**. Four stars form the **box** and three the **handle**. The Plough looks similar but is bigger and brighter.

The last star of the handle is the **Pole Star**. It is also the brightest star of the Little Dipper. The Pole Star is almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole, at the **north celestial pole**. So if you find it, you know where north is. Sailors and walkers used it to find their way long ago.

Because the Little Dipper hangs from the Pole Star by its handle, it circles very tightly around the north celestial pole. It turns all the way round once during the night but never disappears below the horizon. So in Switzerland you can see it on every clear night of the year. Such stars are called **circumpolar**.

Apart from the Pole Star and two other stars, the stars of the Little Dipper shine only **faintly**. In towns the light of the street lamps outshines them. You see it best in a dark place, for example in the countryside or in the mountains. A good trick: first look for the bright **Plough**. The Plough and the Little Dipper lie almost the wrong way round to each other; their handles point in opposite directions.

gewusst: If you extend the back edge of the Plough's box about five times, you reach the Pole Star.
The Pole Star is not the brightest star in the sky, but it is probably the best known.

teile.einleitung: There are billions of stars, and many of them have planets. So there really ought to be other civilisations somewhere. Even so, no trace of them has been found to this day. This contradiction is called the Fermi paradox.
wichtigste: The Fermi paradox describes the contradiction between the likelihood of civilisations and the absence of any trace of them.
In 1950 at Los Alamos, Enrico Fermi asked: “Where is everybody?”
The idea of the “Great Filter” comes from the economist Robin Hanson.
The zoo hypothesis suggests that aliens deliberately leave us alone.
The Rare Earth hypothesis considers complex life to be very rare.
The Kardashev scale ranks civilisations by their energy use.
So far there is no proof for any of the explanations.

abschnitte.text: In 1950, the physicist **Enrico Fermi** was having lunch with colleagues at the **Los Alamos** research laboratory in the USA. They were talking about UFOs and space travel. Then Fermi suddenly asked: “Where is everybody?” This question gave the **Fermi paradox** its name. Fermi was a famous scientist. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1938 and in 1942 led the building of the first nuclear reactor in Chicago.

Our Milky Way has billions of stars and is over 10 billion years old. A civilisation travelling at **1 per cent of the speed of light** would need about **10 million years** to cross the galaxy, which is about 100,000 light years wide. That is short compared with the age of the galaxy. So civilisations could long since have spread out. Even so, there is no sign of them. That is the **contradiction** this is all about.

One possible explanation is the **Great Filter**. In 1996, the economist **Robin Hanson** suggested that a very difficult step prevents life from developing into space travellers. Perhaps life only rarely arises. Perhaps civilisations often fail before they travel into space. It is an open question whether this step lies behind us or still ahead of us.

According to the **zoo hypothesis**, advanced civilisations watch us but deliberately do not interfere. This would be similar to people not disturbing animals in a nature reserve. The **Rare Earth hypothesis** by Ward and Brownlee from 2000 says: simple life could be common, but complex life very rare. It would need many lucky coincidences, such as a large moon. There is no evidence for any of these ideas.

In 1964, the scientist **Nikolai Kardashev** ranked possible civilisations by their **energy use**. He distinguished between civilisations that use the energy of a planet, of a whole star or of a whole galaxy. Such large civilisations ought to be easy to see. The fact that none are found makes the puzzle even bigger. Researchers keep looking, for example with radio telescopes for signals from space.

gewusst: Fermi himself never wrote down his famous question; colleagues passed it on later.
The search for signals from aliens with radio telescopes is called SETI.

teile.einleitung: The International Space Station ISS is a huge research laboratory that orbits the Earth at a height of about 400 kilometres. People have been living and working there without a break since November 2000. It is the largest structure humans have ever put into space.
wichtigste: The ISS orbits the Earth at a height of about 400 kilometres.
It takes about 90 minutes to go once around the Earth.
It flies at about 7.7 km per second and so covers about 460 km in one minute.
The ISS has been continuously inhabited since November 2000.
The partners are the USA, Russia, Europe through ESA, Japan and Canada.
The people float because they are in free fall around the Earth together with the station.
You can sometimes see the ISS with the naked eye as a bright dot in the sky.

abschnitte.text: The ISS is a crewed **space station**, a laboratory and home in space. It is about the size of a football pitch and weighs about 400 tonnes. Usually about seven people live on board at the same time, staying for a few months. They do research in areas such as medicine, biology, physics and materials science.

In 1998, the first part, the Russian **module** Zarya, was taken into space. After that the station was put together piece by piece, a bit like Lego bricks, using rockets and the American Space Shuttle. It has been continuously inhabited since 2 November 2000. Its electricity comes from huge **solar arrays**.

The space agencies of the USA (NASA), Russia, Japan, Canada and Europe take part in the ISS. Europe is represented by **ESA**, whose members include Switzerland. The European laboratory module is called **Columbus** and has been attached to the station since 2008. According to current plans, the ISS is to be operated until about 2030.

The ISS flies at about 7.7 kilometres per second, which is about 28,000 kilometres per hour. So in one minute it covers about 460 kilometres, more than the distance from Geneva to St Gallen. It takes about 90 minutes to go once around the Earth, so the astronauts see about 16 sunrises a day. When it passes over Switzerland in the evening sky, you can see it as a bright, fast-moving dot.

The people on the ISS do not float because there is no gravity there. They are in **free fall** around the Earth together with the station, so they are constantly falling but miss the Earth because of their high speed. That is why they feel **weightless**. To stop their muscles and bones from getting weaker, they exercise every day on special fitness machines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building in space where people live and do research for long periods.
A single part of the space station, for example a laboratory or a living area.
Movement in which only gravity acts and you feel weightless.
The path along which an object circles the Earth.

gewusst: On the ISS, water from sweat and urine is cleaned and drunk again.
The ISS is the most expensive structure humans have ever built.
You can look up on the NASA website when the ISS will fly over where you live.

teile.einleitung: Moonlight is really sunlight. The Moon does not shine by itself but reflects a small part of the sunlight back to the Earth. Even so, a night with a full moon can be amazingly bright.
wichtigste: The Moon does not shine by itself; it is lit up by the Sun.
Light takes only about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to the Earth.
At full moon the night is brightest, and you can even see shadows.
The Moon's surface is rather dark, similar to old tarmac.
Moonlight gives off almost no warmth.
In moonlight, colours look pale and grey.

abschnitte.text: The Moon is a celestial body made of rock and has no light of its own. The **Sun** lights it up, and it reflects part of that light back. But the surface is rather **dark**, similar to old tarmac. It reflects only about an eighth of the light. The Moon only looks so bright because the night sky around it is so dark. Light is very fast: it takes only about **1.3 seconds** to get from the Moon to us.

How bright the night is depends on the **phase of the Moon**. At **full moon**, the whole side facing us is lit, and the most light reaches the Earth. Outside you can then even see **shadows**. Even so, a full moon is many hundreds of thousands of times weaker than sunlight. That is why you feel **no warmth** on your skin.

Next to a thin crescent moon, you can sometimes see the rest of the Moon glowing faintly. This is called **earthshine**. The Earth reflects sunlight into space, and part of it falls on the Moon. This light makes the actually dark part of the Moon a little bright. The artist and scientist Leonardo da Vinci already explained this correctly.

There are two kinds of sensory cells in our eyes: **cones** for colours and **rods** for faint light. In little light, mainly the rods work. They cannot tell colours apart. That is why in moonlight many things look **pale and grey**, even a red flower.

When the bright Moon shines on raindrops, a **moonbow** can form. It is faint and usually looks almost white to our eyes. When thin clouds pass in front of the Moon, you sometimes see a bright glow close around it. This is a **lunar corona**. It forms when the light shines through tiny water droplets in the clouds.

gewusst: In photos with a long exposure, a moonbow shows its colours, which the eye cannot see.
For astronauts on the Moon, the Earth in the sky is much brighter than the full moon is for us.

teile.einleitung: Callisto is one of the four large moons of Jupiter. Its dark, ancient surface is more densely covered with craters than almost any other body in the solar system.
wichtigste: Callisto is the third largest moon in the solar system.
It is almost exactly the same size as the planet Mercury.
Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered bodies.
The huge impact basin Valhalla measures over 3,000 kilometres.
One orbit around Jupiter takes about 16.7 days.
Callisto is almost geologically inactive.

abschnitte.text: Callisto's surface is very old and has hardly changed for billions of years. Every impact has left its mark. That is why there are **craters** crowded right next to each other. The largest impact basin is called **Valhalla**. It consists of many ring-shaped ridges around a bright centre and measures over 3,000 kilometres.

Callisto orbits far out from Jupiter. There, the planet's **tidal forces** are only weak. So Callisto is hardly kneaded or heated, unlike the volcanic moon Io. That is why there is almost no **geological activity**, and the old surface is preserved. Callisto takes about 16.7 days for one orbit, the longest time of the four **Galilean moons**.

Callisto measures about 4,820 kilometres across. The planet **Mercury**, at about 4,880 kilometres, is almost the same width. Only Jupiter's moon **Ganymede** and Saturn's moon **Titan** are bigger. That makes Callisto the **third largest moon** in the solar system. It is made of about half rock and half ice.

Around Jupiter the **radiation** is very strong, especially near the inner moons. Callisto is far enough out for it to be much weaker there. Because it is also geologically quiet, a **NASA study** in 2003 suggested Callisto as a possible place for a future research station. So far, such plans are only ideas for the distant future.

Callisto is named after a **nymph** from Greek legend. According to the legend, she was turned into a **she-bear**. Later she was placed in the sky as the constellation of the **Great Bear**. The moon was discovered by **Galileo Galilei** in 1610.

gewusst: Researchers suspect an ocean of salty water beneath Callisto's icy crust.
Callisto is one of the darkest of Jupiter's large moons, even though it contains a lot of ice.

teile.einleitung: The Magellanic Clouds are two small neighbouring galaxies of our Milky Way. You can only see them from the southern hemisphere, where they appear as bright, misty patches in the night sky. They are among the nearest galaxies of all.
wichtigste: There is a **Large** and a **Small Magellanic Cloud**.
The Large one is about 160,000 light years away, the Small one about 200,000 light years.
Most of the Large Cloud lies in the constellation **Dorado**.
Both are considered **irregular dwarf galaxies**.
The huge **Tarantula Nebula** lies in the Large Cloud.
They are named after the seafarer **Ferdinand Magellan**.

abschnitte.text: If you look at the sky on a dark night in the southern hemisphere, you see two bright, misty patches. They look like small clouds torn off the Milky Way. In reality they are two **galaxies**. Most of the **Large Magellanic Cloud** lies in the constellation **Dorado**. You cannot see the two clouds from Switzerland, because they are too far south.

The clouds are named after the Portuguese seafarer **Ferdinand Magellan**. At the beginning of the 16th century, his expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world. The sailors described the bright patches in the southern sky. Of course, people in the southern hemisphere had known them for much longer and had their own names and stories for them.

The Large Magellanic Cloud is **about 160,000 light years** away, the Small one **about 200,000 light years**. Both are much smaller than the Milky Way. They do not have a beautiful spiral shape but look irregular. That is why they are counted among the **irregular dwarf galaxies**. They belong to the **Local Group**, the Milky Way's group of galaxies.

The **Tarantula Nebula** lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud. It is a huge **star-forming region** in which new stars keep forming from gas and dust. It gets its name because its glowing threads of gas look like the legs of a spider. Inside it is the star **R136a1**. It is considered the most massive known star.

The Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way pull on each other with their gravity. This pulls gas out of the clouds. This has created a long band of **hydrogen gas** that connects the clouds with the Milky Way. It is called the **Magellanic Stream**. You cannot see it with the naked eye, but you can with radio telescopes.

gewusst: In 1987, a supernova lit up in the Large Magellanic Cloud that could even be seen with the naked eye.
R136a1 has many times the mass of our Sun and shines millions of times more brightly.

teile.einleitung: The habitable zone is the area around a star where a planet is neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water. Liquid water is considered an important condition for life as we know it.
wichtigste: In the habitable zone, water can be liquid on the surface of a planet.
It is often also called the Goldilocks zone.
The Earth lies in the Sun's habitable zone, and so does the Moon, but the Moon has no liquid water.
According to many models, Mars lies close to the outer edge.
The brighter a star shines, the further out its habitable zone lies.
The Sun's habitable zone is slowly moving outwards.

abschnitte.titel: Not too hot, not too cold
abschnitte.text: If a planet is too close to its star, the water evaporates. If it is too far away, it freezes into ice. In between lies the **habitable zone**, which means the zone where living things could live. It is often also called the **Goldilocks zone**. In the English fairy tale, Goldilocks chooses the porridge that is neither too hot nor too cold. But lying in this zone is not enough on its own; a planet also needs a suitable atmosphere, for example.

The **Earth** lies in the middle of the Sun's habitable zone. The **Moon** lies in it too, but it has no atmosphere and so no liquid water on its surface. According to many models, **Mars** lies close to the **outer edge**; today it is cold and dry. **Venus** lies close to the inner edge. There, a **runaway greenhouse effect** probably took place: more and more heat was trapped until the water evaporated and Venus became scorching hot.

Where the habitable zone lies depends on the **brightness** of the star. A star that shines four times as strongly as the Sun has its zone about **twice as far** away. This is because the radiation decreases with the square of the distance. For small, faint stars, the zone lies very close to the star. The Sun is also becoming brighter over billions of years. So its habitable zone is slowly **moving outwards**.

Liquid water can also exist outside the habitable zone. Moons of gas giants are kneaded by **tidal friction** and heated inside. So there is probably an ocean beneath the ice of Jupiter's moon **Europa**. Experts also speak of a **galactic habitable zone**. This means the area of the Milky Way where conditions for life could be favourable.

gewusst: In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz from the University of Geneva discovered the first planet around a Sun-like star. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
Today thousands of exoplanets are known, and some of them lie in the habitable zone of their star.

teile.einleitung: Where does our Moon actually come from? Researchers argued about this question for a long time. Today most of them explain its formation with an enormous collision between the young Earth and another celestial body.
wichtigste: The Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago, shortly after the Earth.
According to the collision theory, the young Earth collided with a body called Theia.
According to the usual idea, Theia was about the size of Mars.
The debris formed a ring around the Earth, and the Moon clumped together from it.
Moon rock is very similar to the Earth's mantle.
Older ideas were the fission theory and the capture theory.

abschnitte.text: According to today's usual **collision theory**, the young Earth collided with another celestial body. Researchers call it **Theia**, after the mother of the moon goddess Selene in Greek legend. According to most models, Theia was about the size of **Mars**, so about half as wide as the Earth. In the impact, a lot of rock was flung into space. Theia itself no longer exists today.

abschnitte.titel: From a ring of debris to the Moon
abschnitte.text: The debris that was flung out collected in a **disc** around the Earth. In it, the lumps kept colliding and sticking together. In a relatively short time, the Moon clumped together from them. This happened about **4.5 billion years ago**, shortly after the Earth formed. Dating of Moon rock shows this.

The astronauts of the **Apollo missions** brought rock from the Moon to the Earth. It has almost the same composition as the **Earth's mantle**, the layer of rock beneath the Earth's crust. This fits with the idea that a lot of material was knocked out of the Earth. In the impact, it was mainly light, outer rock that flew into space. Most of the heavy iron stayed in the Earth. That is why the Moon has only a small **iron core** and a low density.

In the past there were other explanations. **George Darwin**, a son of the naturalist Charles Darwin, thought in the 19th century that the Moon had split off from the fast-spinning Earth. But this **fission theory** does not explain why the Earth should have been spinning so fast. According to the **capture theory**, the Moon formed somewhere else and was captured by the Earth. Today this is thought very unlikely, because the Moon and the Earth are too similar in composition.

gewusst: The name Theia fits well: in the legend, Theia is the mother of Selene, the goddess of the Moon.
The Apollo astronauts brought a total of about 380 kilograms of Moon rock to Earth.

teile.einleitung: Comets are lumps of ice, dust and rock that circle the Sun. When they come close to the Sun, they form a glowing tail that can be millions of kilometres long.
wichtigste: A comet is often called a “dirty snowball”.
Near the Sun, ice evaporates and carries dust with it, which forms the tail.
Many comets have two tails: a dust tail and a gas tail.
The glowing cloud around the nucleus is called the coma.
Comet tails can be millions of kilometres long.
The word “comet” originally means something like “hairy star”.

abschnitte.text: The **nucleus** of a comet is made of ice mixed with dust and rock. That is why it is often called a **dirty snowball**. Most of the time a comet is far from the Sun, cold and dark. Only when it comes closer does it begin to shine. The word “comet” comes from Greek and means something like “long-haired”; the tail looks like flowing hair.

Near the Sun, the comet warms up. The ice **evaporates** and carries dust with it. A cloud of gas and dust forms around the nucleus: the **coma**. The **solar wind** and the pressure of sunlight blow the material away. This forms the tail, which always points roughly away from the Sun.

Many comets have two tails. The **dust tail** is yellowish, wide and often slightly curved. The dust simply reflects the sunlight. The **gas tail** is bluish, straight and narrow. Its gas is excited by the Sun and glows by itself. The two tails point in slightly different directions.

Comet tails can be many **millions of kilometres** long. Even so, the gas in them is extremely thin, much thinner than the air on Earth. A famous example is the comet **Hale-Bopp**. In 1997 it shone so brightly that many people saw it with the naked eye in the evening sky for weeks. **Halley's Comet** is also very well known; it comes back about every 76 years.

gewusst: When the Earth flies through a comet's trail of dust, you see many shooting stars.
Halley's Comet will not come close to the Sun again until 2061.

teile.einleitung: Newton's law of gravitation describes how strongly two bodies with mass attract each other. Isaac Newton set it out in the 17th century. It explains why an apple falls and why the Moon circles the Earth.
wichtigste: All bodies with mass attract each other.
The force is proportional to the product of the two masses.
It decreases with the square of the distance: double the distance, a quarter of the force.
In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the attraction in the laboratory with a torsion balance.
The unit of force is called the “newton” (N) after Isaac Newton.
The same force makes apples fall and keeps the Moon in its orbit.

abschnitte.text: According to a well-known story, a **falling apple** set Isaac Newton thinking. He wondered whether the same force also keeps the **Moon** in its orbit. His answer was yes: **gravity** works in the same way on Earth and throughout the universe. In 1687, Newton published his famous work in which he describes the law. For the first time, the orbits of the planets could be calculated with the same rule as falling stones.

According to Newton, **all bodies with mass** attract each other, even two apples. The force is **proportional** to the product of the two masses. If you double the mass of one body, the force also doubles. But with small masses it is tiny. Only with huge bodies like the Earth can you feel it clearly, as **weight**.

The force decreases with the **square of the distance**. At double the distance, that gives 2 · 2 = 4, so the force becomes four times smaller. At three times the distance it is 3 · 3 = 9, so a ninth of the force. This is called an **inverse square law**. As a formula: force equals G times mass 1 times mass 2, divided by the distance squared. G is called the **gravitational constant**.

In **1798**, **Henry Cavendish** used a **torsion balance** to measure the tiny attraction between lead balls. It was a very delicate experiment, because even a draught could disturb it. From his measurements, the **density of the Earth** and the gravitational constant G could be worked out.

With the law, you can calculate how strong gravity is elsewhere. **Jupiter** has over 300 times as much mass as the Earth, but also a radius about 11 times larger. That is why the gravity at the top of its clouds is only about **2.5 times** as strong. On the **Moon** it is only about a sixth. A body with a mass of 1 kg has a weight of just under **10 newtons** on Earth.

gewusst: With Newton's law, an unknown planet was predicted in the 19th century and then actually found: Neptune.
Albert Einstein, who worked in Bern for some years, later developed an even more precise theory of gravity.

teile.einleitung: Eris is a dwarf planet far out at the edge of the solar system. It is almost exactly the same size as Pluto. Its discovery sparked a big argument and led to Pluto no longer being considered a planet today.
wichtigste: Eris is a dwarf planet that is slightly smaller but heavier than Pluto.
A team led by the astronomer Mike Brown discovered Eris.
Because of Eris, experts redefined in 2006 what a planet is.
Eris is named after the Greek goddess of strife and discord.
Its moon is called Dysnomia.
One orbit around the Sun takes about 560 years.
In 2025, Eris was about 96 AU from the Sun.

abschnitte.text: Eris was found by a team led by the American astronomer **Mike Brown**. The researchers worked with images from the observatory on **Mount Palomar** in California. At first the team jokingly called the body **Xena**, after the heroine of a television series. In 2006 it was given its official name. Since then, Mike Brown has jokingly called himself the “Pluto killer”.

At first, Eris seemed to be the same size as **Pluto**. The experts had to decide: is Eris a tenth planet, or does what counts as a planet have to be redefined? In 2006, the International Astronomical Union agreed on a **new definition of a planet**. Since then, Pluto and Eris have been considered **dwarf planets**. Since then our solar system has had eight planets.

In Greek legend, **Eris** is the goddess of strife and **discord**. The name fitted, because the body sparked a big argument among astronomers. Eris has a moon called **Dysnomia**. In the legend, Dysnomia is a daughter of the goddess Eris. With the help of this moon, the mass of Eris could be worked out.

Eris measures about **2,330 kilometres**, Pluto about 2,380 kilometres. So Eris is a little smaller. But it has about **27 per cent more mass** than Pluto. So Eris is more densely built. It is probably made of rock and ice.

Eris orbits very far out. In 2025 it was about **96 AU** from the Sun, so about 96 times as far as the Earth. Its orbit is strongly **elliptical**, which means stretched out. One orbit takes about **560 years**. In addition, the orbit is tilted by about **44 degrees** against the plane of the planets' orbits. That is why Eris was easily missed in earlier searches.

gewusst: Eris is one of the most distant known dwarf planets in the solar system.
Without the discovery of Eris, Pluto might still be considered a planet today.

teile.einleitung: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. It is a huge gas planet without a solid surface and the fifth planet from the Sun. It is famous for its colourful bands of cloud and the Great Red Spot, an enormous storm.
wichtigste: Jupiter is the fifth and largest planet in the solar system.
It is a gas giant made mainly of hydrogen and helium.
The Great Red Spot is a huge storm.
A day on Jupiter lasts only about 10 hours.
Its largest moon, Ganymede, is even bigger than the planet Mercury.
Jupiter takes almost 12 years to go once around the Sun.
After the Moon and Venus, Jupiter is often the brightest object in the night sky.

abschnitte.titel: The giant of the solar system
abschnitte.text: Jupiter's diameter is about eleven times that of the Earth. It is over 300 times as heavy as the Earth and heavier than all the other planets put together. As a **gas giant**, it is made mainly of hydrogen and helium and has no solid surface. It is named after Jupiter, the father of the gods in Roman religion.

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and orbits beyond the asteroid belt. It is about five times as far from the Sun as the Earth. It takes almost 12 Earth years to go once around the Sun. But it spins on its axis faster than any other planet: a **Jupiter day** lasts only about 10 hours.

Because of the fast spin, the clouds form light and dark **bands** around the planet. The **Great Red Spot** is a huge storm that has been raging for at least 150 years, perhaps even for over 300 years. It is bigger than the Earth but has been slowly shrinking for decades. Inside, the enormous pressure makes hydrogen liquid and even metallic.

Jupiter has almost 100 known moons (as of about 2025). In 1610, Galileo Galilei discovered the four largest with a telescope; they are called the **Galilean moons**: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. **Ganymede** is the largest moon in the solar system and bigger than the planet Mercury. Io has active volcanoes, and an ocean of liquid water is suspected beneath Europa's shell of ice.

Space probes such as Voyager, Galileo and, since 2016, Juno have explored Jupiter close up. In April 2023, the ESA probe **JUICE** was launched to study Jupiter's icy moons. The University of Bern is also involved in JUICE with a measuring instrument. Even with binoculars you can see Jupiter as a bright disc with its four large moons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large planet made mainly of gas, with no solid surface.
A huge, long-lasting storm on Jupiter.
The four largest moons of Jupiter, discovered by Galileo Galilei.
An uncrewed spacecraft that explores celestial bodies.

gewusst: About 1,300 Earths would fit inside Jupiter.
Jupiter also has faint rings, but they are hard to see.
With its strong gravity, Jupiter deflects many comets and asteroids, and some even crash into it.

teile.einleitung: Europa is one of the four large moons of the planet Jupiter. Its surface is made of ice, and beneath it there is probably a huge ocean. That is why Europa is considered one of the best places in the solar system to search for life.
wichtigste: Europa is the smallest of Jupiter's four Galilean moons.
At about 3,120 kilometres, it is a little smaller than our Moon.
The surface consists of a bright crust of water ice.
Beneath the ice there is probably an ocean with about twice as much water as all the seas on Earth.
Long lines on the surface are cracks in the icy crust.
Few craters show that the surface is geologically young.
NASA's Europa Clipper probe set off for this moon in October 2024.

abschnitte.text: Europa is one of the four **Galilean moons** that Galileo Galilei discovered in 1610. With a diameter of about **3,120 kilometres**, it is the smallest of the four. It is also a little smaller than our Moon. It is named after a figure from Greek legend: the Phoenician princess **Europa**. In the legend, Zeus carries her off to Crete in the shape of a bull. Our continent is also named after her.

The surface of Europa is made of **water ice**. This bright crust reflects a lot of sunlight. In pictures you can see many long, often reddish **lines**. These are **cracks** in the icy crust. They form because Jupiter's **tidal forces** keep stretching the ice until it breaks.

On old surfaces, many impact craters collect over time. But on Europa there are only very **few craters**. From this, researchers conclude that the surface is **geologically young**. So the icy crust keeps renewing itself. Old craters are covered over or disappear.

Beneath the icy crust there is probably an **ocean of salt water**. It is probably many dozens of kilometres deep. According to NASA estimates, it could contain about **twice as much water** as all the Earth's oceans put together. And this even though Europa is smaller than our Moon. The ocean cannot yet be proven quite directly, but many measurements point to it.

**Liquid water** is an important condition for life as we know it. That is why Europa is considered one of the best places to search for extraterrestrial life. Simple living things could exist in the ocean, but this has not been proven. NASA's **Europa Clipper** probe was launched on 14 October 2024. During many flybys, it is to check whether Europa could be friendly to life.

gewusst: Europa is one of the smoothest bodies in the whole solar system.
The European probe JUICE is also to study Europa on its journey to Jupiter.

teile.einleitung: Cosmology is the science of the universe as a whole. It asks how the universe came into being, how old it is, what it is made of and how it will develop in the future. So it deals with the biggest questions people can ask.
wichtigste: Cosmology studies the origin, structure and development of the whole universe.
According to measurements by the Planck satellite, the universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
The most important model is the Big Bang theory, according to which the universe came from an extremely hot and dense state.
The universe has been expanding since the Big Bang, as Edwin Hubble showed in the 1920s.
The cosmic background radiation is an afterglow of the Big Bang and today has about 2.7 kelvin.
According to the cosmological principle, the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales.
Most of the universe consists of dark matter and dark energy, which we do not yet understand exactly.

abschnitte.text: The word **cosmology** comes from Greek: “kosmos” means order or world, and “logos” means study. Cosmology is part of astronomy and physics. It does not look at individual stars but at the whole **universe** with all its galaxies. In doing so, it combines observations with telescopes and satellites with physical theories such as Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity.

According to the **Big Bang theory**, the universe was unimaginably hot and dense at the beginning. Since then it has been expanding and cooling down. The Big Bang was not an explosion at a particular place; space itself began to expand everywhere. In the first minutes, the light atomic nuclei formed in **primordial nucleosynthesis**. About 25 per cent of the mass of normal matter became helium-4 at that time, and the rest was almost all hydrogen.

About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe had cooled down enough for electrons and atomic nuclei to join to form atoms. This process is called **recombination**. Since then the universe has been transparent to light. This ancient light reaches us today as the **cosmic background radiation** from all directions. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered it more or less by chance in 1964 with a large horn antenna in the USA and later received the Nobel Prize for it.

In the 1920s, the astronomer Edwin Hubble observed that almost all galaxies are moving away from us. The further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away. This shows that the universe is **expanding**, a bit like a yeast dough with raisins that move apart as it rises. Since 1998 it has also been known that the expansion is speeding up. The suspected cause is the mysterious **dark energy**.

Only about 5 per cent of the universe consists of normal matter, which stars, planets and people are made of. About a quarter is **dark matter**, which cannot be seen but holds galaxies together with its gravity. Most of it is dark energy. The theory of **cosmic inflation** says that the young universe blew up extremely fast for a tiny moment. Among other things, it is meant to solve the horizon problem, in other words to explain why very distant regions are almost exactly the same temperature.

Important data come from satellites such as COBE, WMAP and Planck, which have measured the background radiation very precisely. The **cosmological principle** is a basic assumption: on very large scales the universe looks the same everywhere and the same in every direction. The Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky found the first clues to dark matter as early as 1933. Today, teams at ETH Zurich, EPFL and the universities of Geneva and Zurich also research cosmological questions, for example for the European space telescope **Euclid**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The beginning of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state.
Faint light from the early days of the universe that today comes from all directions.
Invisible matter that can only be detected by its gravity.
A very short phase in which the young universe is thought to have expanded extremely fast.
The same in all directions.

gewusst: A small part of the noise on old tube televisions with no station tuned in came from the cosmic background radiation.
Penzias and Wilson at first thought the signal was interference caused by pigeon droppings in their antenna.
When we look at very distant galaxies, we are looking into the past, because their light has been travelling for billions of years.

teile.einleitung: LIGO is a huge measuring facility in the USA that detects gravitational waves. These are tiny vibrations of space and time that Albert Einstein had predicted. In 2015, LIGO achieved the first direct detection.
wichtigste: LIGO stands for **Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory**.
The two detectors are located in **Hanford** and **Livingston** in the USA.
On 14 September 2015, LIGO detected gravitational waves for the first time.
The signal GW150914 came from two merging black holes.
The detectors work on the principle of a **Michelson interferometer**.
The Italian detector **Virgo** observes together with LIGO.

abschnitte.text: When very heavy bodies such as **black holes** circle each other and merge, they create **gravitational waves**. These waves travel at the speed of light. They stretch and squeeze space by a very tiny amount. Albert Einstein had already predicted them over 100 years ago in his theory of relativity. But they could only be measured much later.

Each LIGO detector has two long arms at right angles to each other. A **laser beam** is split and sent through both arms. At the end, **mirrors** reflect the light back, and the two beams are brought together again. This measuring principle is called a **Michelson interferometer**. To make the light path even longer, the light travels back and forth between the mirrors many times.

A typical gravitational wave changes the length of an arm by **less than a thousandth of the diameter of a proton**. A proton is a tiny building block of an atomic nucleus. To measure something like this, the facility has to be protected from vibrations, for example from lorries or waves on the sea. That is why there are two sites far apart: only a signal that arrives at both almost at the same time is real.

On **14 September 2015**, both detectors recorded the same signal. It was given the name **GW150914**. It came from two black holes that merged far away. In the process, **about three solar masses** were turned into the energy of gravitational waves. For this discovery, three researchers received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in 2017.

Today LIGO works closely with the **Virgo** detector in Italy. There is also a detector in Japan. With several facilities, it is easier to work out which direction a wave is coming from. In 2017, this made it possible to observe the merger of two **neutron stars**, which could also be seen at the same time with telescopes as a flash of light.

gewusst: The arms of the LIGO detectors are each 4 kilometres long.
The gravitational waves of GW150914 had been travelling for over a billion years before they reached the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Galaxies can collide and even merge with each other. This takes hundreds of millions of years. Their shapes change greatly, and often a great many new stars form.
wichtigste: In a galaxy collision, hardly any stars crash directly into each other.
The reason is the huge distances between the stars.
Squeezed gas often sets off a lot of star formation.
Close encounters create long tidal tails.
The Antennae Galaxies and the Cartwheel Galaxy are well-known examples.
The Milky Way once swallowed the dwarf galaxy Gaia-Enceladus.
If the Milky Way and Andromeda merge, an elliptical galaxy will probably form.

abschnitte.text: You might think that when two galaxies collide, stars would keep crashing into each other. But that is not the case. Compared with their size, stars are **extremely far** apart. Even when two galaxies merge, direct hits between stars are extremely rare. The galaxies glide through each other, so to speak.

It is different with the **gas** in the galaxies. In a collision, gas clouds are **squeezed** and collapse. This creates a great many new stars at once. A galaxy with such a burst of star formation is called a **starburst galaxy**. At the end of a collision, the central **black holes** also sink to the middle, form a pair and can merge.

In close encounters, gravity pulls out long bands of stars and gas. They are called **tidal tails**. A well-known example is the **Antennae Galaxies**, which are in the middle of merging. Their two long tails look like the feelers of an insect. In the **Cartwheel Galaxy**, a smaller galaxy flew right through a larger one. This sent out a spreading ring in which many new stars are forming.

Our Milky Way has also grown through mergers. ESA's **Gaia** space probe measures the orbits of a great many stars. In its data, a group of stars with strikingly similar orbits was found. They come from a dwarf galaxy that merged with the Milky Way about 8 to 11 billion years ago. This galaxy is called **Gaia-Enceladus**.

The nearby **Andromeda Galaxy** is moving towards the Milky Way. In a few billion years, the two galaxies could collide. According to newer calculations, it is not quite certain whether and when they will really merge. If it happens, simulations usually produce a large **elliptical galaxy**. Some people jokingly call it **“Milkomeda”**.

gewusst: Even today, the Milky Way is swallowing small dwarf galaxies near it.
For humans, a galaxy collision would hardly be noticeable; you would just see the night sky slowly change.

teile.einleitung: The Orion Nebula is a glowing cloud of gas and dust in the constellation Orion. It is one of the most active areas near us where new stars are forming. Under a dark sky you can even see it without a telescope.
wichtigste: The Orion Nebula is about 1,350 light years from the Earth.
In the Messier catalogue it has the number M 42.
With the naked eye you see it as a faint, blurry patch.
Many new stars are forming in the nebula; about 3,500 mostly young stars have been counted.
At the centre is the Trapezium, a group of four bright, young stars.
The radiation of hot young stars makes the gas glow.

abschnitte.text: The Orion Nebula lies in Orion's **sword**, below the three belt stars. Under a dark sky you can see it with the **naked eye**. It looks like a slightly blurred star. With binoculars or a small telescope you can make out a glowing cloud. In the sky it appears about twice as wide as the **full moon**.

Measurements give a distance of about **1,350 light years** for the Orion Nebula. So its light has been travelling to us for over a thousand years. Its diameter is about **24 light years**. Charles Messier listed it as the 42nd object in his catalogue, which first appeared in 1774. That is why it is called **M 42**. The nebula is part of a much larger, dark **molecular cloud** in Orion.

Particularly many **new stars** are **forming** in the Orion Nebula right now. About **3,500** mostly young stars have been counted in it. They will probably one day become an **open star cluster**. The Hubble Space Telescope also found many young stars in the nebula with discs of gas and dust. **Planets** can later form from such discs.

At the centre of the nebula is a group of four bright, young stars. They form a small four-sided shape and are therefore called the **Trapezium**. **Galileo** already saw three of them close together in 1617. These stars are very hot and are among the most important sources of light in the nebula.

Young, very hot stars in the nebula give off **high-energy radiation**. This excites the **gas** so that it glows by itself. That is why the Orion Nebula is called an **emission nebula**. In photos it glows red and pink from the hydrogen, with greenish and bluish tones as well. To the eye it only looks grey or slightly greenish, because our eyes can hardly see colours in low light.

gewusst: The Orion Nebula is the brightest star-forming region that can be seen in the night sky from Central Europe.
The stars in the Orion Nebula are only about one to a few million years old, which is very young for stars.

teile.einleitung: Comets are celestial bodies made of ice, dust and rock that circle the Sun in long, stretched orbits. When they come close to the Sun, they form a glowing cloud and a long tail. In the past they were seen as bringers of misfortune; today they are important witnesses from the time when the solar system formed.
wichtigste: The nucleus of a comet consists mainly of ice, dust and rock.
Near the Sun, a glowing cloud of gas forms around the nucleus: the coma.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.
Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years.
Many long-period comets come from the Oort Cloud at the edge of the solar system.
In 2014, the ESA probe Rosetta landed a lander on a comet for the first time.
Comets are also called dirty snowballs.

abschnitte.text: A comet is a small celestial body that circles the Sun. Its **nucleus** is made of ice, dust and rock and is usually only a few kilometres across. That is why comets are also called dirty snowballs. The word comet comes from the Greek word for hairy star, because of the tail that looks like flowing hair.

When a comet comes close to the Sun, its ice warms up and evaporates. This creates a glowing cloud of gas around the nucleus, the **coma**. The solar wind and sunlight push gas and dust backwards, and so the **tail** forms, which can be millions of kilometres long. Because it is blown away by the Sun, it always points away from the Sun, even when the comet is moving away from it.

Short-period comets usually come from the **Kuiper Belt** beyond Neptune. Long-period comets come from the **Oort Cloud**, a huge cloud of icy bodies at the very edge of the solar system. A well-known comet is **Halley's Comet**, which returns about every 76 years. It was last seen in 1986, and it will next come in 2061.

In 2014, the ESA space probe **Rosetta** reached the comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko. In November 2014, its small lander Philae became the first spacecraft to land on a comet. The University of Bern built the measuring instrument ROSINA for Rosetta, which studied the comet's gases. Among other things, simple organic substances were found that could be building blocks for life.

Bright comets are rare, but then they are a wonderful sight. In 1997, the comet Hale-Bopp could be seen with the naked eye for months. When the Earth flies through a comet's trail of dust, we see many **shooting stars**, for example the Perseids in August. In the past, many people thought comets were signs of war or misfortune.

begriffe.erklaerung: The solid part of a comet, made of ice, dust and rock.
A glowing cloud of gas around the nucleus of a comet near the Sun.
A long streak of gas and dust that points away from the Sun.
A huge cloud of icy bodies at the edge of the solar system.

gewusst: Many comets have two tails, a bluish one of gas and a yellowish one of dust.
Halley's Comet is shown on the famous Bayeux Tapestry from the Middle Ages.
The nucleus of the comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko looks like a giant rubber duck.

teile.einleitung: Edwin Hubble was an American astronomer who greatly changed our picture of the universe. He showed that there are many other galaxies besides the Milky Way, and he sorted them by their shape.
wichtigste: Edwin Hubble was born in 1889 in the US state of Missouri.
He first studied law at Oxford.
He made his most important discoveries at the Mount Wilson Observatory in California.
In 1924 he used Cepheids to prove that the Andromeda Nebula is a separate galaxy.
He arranged the galaxies in the tuning fork diagram.
Since 2018, the law describing how galaxies move away from us has been called the Hubble-Lemaître law.

abschnitte.text: Edwin Hubble was born in **1889** in **Missouri** in the USA. With a scholarship, he first studied **law** at **Oxford** in England. Only afterwards did he turn fully to astronomy. He spent his research career in the USA, above all at the **Mount Wilson Observatory** in California. The 2.5 metre **Hooker Telescope** stood there, the largest in the world at the time.

Experts used to argue about whether the blurry “nebulae” in the sky belonged to the Milky Way. In the **Andromeda Nebula**, Hubble found variable stars called **Cepheids**. They change their brightness in a fixed rhythm. From the rhythm you know their true brightness and can work out the distance. In **1924**, Hubble used this to show that Andromeda lies far outside our Milky Way. That made it clear: there are **many galaxies**.

Hubble classified galaxies by their **shape**. He arranged them in a picture that looks like a tuning fork lying on its side. On the left, at the **handle**, are the **elliptical galaxies**. Then the scheme splits into two prongs: the normal **spiral galaxies** and the **barred spirals**, which have a bright bar through the middle. This scheme is still used today.

Together with his colleague **Milton Humason**, Hubble measured the light spectra of distant galaxies. Humason had started out as a mule driver at Mount Wilson and became a very skilled observer. The measurements showed: the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us. The Belgian **Georges Lemaître** had already described this relationship in 1927. That is why the International Astronomical Union recommended the name **Hubble-Lemaître law** in **2018**.

Hubble died in 1953. The **Hubble Space Telescope** was named in his honour. It was launched into space in 1990 and has been orbiting the Earth ever since. The Swiss astronaut **Claude Nicollier** helped to repair it. The telescope has delivered many famous pictures of distant galaxies.

gewusst: Hubble's discoveries helped to establish the idea of an expanding universe.
Hubble never received the Nobel Prize, because at that time astronomy was not yet considered for the Nobel Prize in Physics.

teile.einleitung: Laika was a dog from Moscow who went down in the history of space travel in 1957. She was the first animal to circle the Earth in orbit. Her flight showed that living things can survive the launch and weightlessness.
wichtigste: Laika was the first animal in Earth orbit.
The **Soviet Union** sent her into space in November 1957.
Before she was chosen, Laika lived on the streets.
She flew on board the satellite **Sputnik 2**.
Laika did not return to Earth alive.
In 1960, the dogs **Belka and Strelka** flew into space and came back healthy.

abschnitte.text: Laika was a small mixed-breed dog who lived **on the streets of Moscow**. Researchers in the **Soviet Union** liked to choose such dogs for their experiments. They thought they were especially tough because they were used to cold and hunger. Small dogs also fitted well into the cramped cabins. Before the flight, the animals were trained to stay in a small space for a long time.

On 3 November 1957, Laika was launched on board **Sputnik 2**. Only a month earlier, the Soviet Union had put the very first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, into space. Laika lay in a small cabin with an air supply and food. Instruments sent data about her heartbeat and breathing to Earth. This made her the **first animal in Earth orbit**.

**No return** was planned for Laika. At that time it was not yet possible to bring a capsule safely back to Earth. Laika died during the flight, probably after a few hours, because the cabin got too hot. The satellite burned up in the atmosphere a few months later. Many people around the world were sad about her fate, and there was a lot of discussion about whether such experiments were right.

In **1960**, the two dogs **Belka and Strelka** flew into space. They circled the Earth for a day and **came back healthy**. This showed that living things can survive a space flight and land safely. Only a year later, in 1961, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human to fly into space.

gewusst: Since 2008, a monument in Moscow has honoured Laika: she stands on a rocket that turns into a hand.
Strelka later had puppies, and the Soviet Union gave one of them to the family of the American President Kennedy.

teile.einleitung: The Local Group is the small group of galaxies to which our Milky Way belongs. Besides two large spiral galaxies, it includes many small dwarf galaxies. Gravity holds these galaxies together.
wichtigste: The **Milky Way** and the **Andromeda Galaxy** hold most of the visible mass.
The third largest member is the **Triangulum Galaxy** M33.
The great majority of the members are **dwarf galaxies**.
The Local Group has a diameter of a few million light years.
It belongs to the **Virgo Supercluster**.
The term “Local Group” was coined by the astronomer **Edwin Hubble**.

abschnitte.text: Galaxies are huge collections of billions of stars. They often occur in groups. Our own group is called the **Local Group**. Its diameter is **a few million light years**. The astronomer **Edwin Hubble** coined the term in the 1930s. He had previously shown that there are other galaxies outside the Milky Way.

Two spiral galaxies hold most of the visible mass: the **Milky Way** and the **Andromeda Galaxy**. The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light years away and on dark nights can even be seen with the naked eye as a faint patch. The third largest member is the **Triangulum Galaxy**, also called **M33**. It is also a spiral galaxy, but much smaller.

The great majority of the members are **dwarf galaxies**. They have far fewer stars than the large galaxies. Many of them orbit the Milky Way or the Andromeda Galaxy. Well known are the two **Magellanic Clouds**, which can be seen well from the southern hemisphere. New, very faint dwarf galaxies keep being discovered.

The universe is expanding, and most galaxies are moving away from each other. With the members of the Local Group, this is not the case. They are **bound to each other by gravity**. The Andromeda Galaxy is even coming towards us. Some galaxies are also swallowed: the **Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy** is currently being torn apart and taken in by the Milky Way.

The Local Group itself is only a small part of a much bigger structure. It belongs to the **Virgo Supercluster**. At its centre lies the large **Virgo Cluster** of galaxies with over a thousand galaxies. So the universe is built up like a web: galaxies form groups, groups form clusters, and clusters form superclusters.

gewusst: The Andromeda Galaxy is one of the most distant objects you can see with the naked eye without a telescope.
The Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy could collide in a few billion years.

teile.einleitung: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and also the closest to the Sun. It races around the Sun in only about 88 days. Its grey surface, covered with craters, is reminiscent of our Moon.
wichtigste: Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system.
It is the planet closest to the Sun.
A year on Mercury lasts only about 88 Earth days.
Mercury has no moon.
Its surface is full of craters.
On Mercury it is scorching hot during the day and icy cold at night.
Mercury is named after the swift messenger of the Roman gods.

abschnitte.text: Mercury has a diameter of about 4,900 kilometres. That makes it only a little bigger than our Moon and smaller than Jupiter's moon Ganymede. It is a **rocky planet** with a very large iron core that makes up a large part of its interior. Mercury has a weak **magnetic field**. It has no moon.

Mercury is on average about 58 million kilometres from the Sun. It takes only about 88 days to go once around the Sun, which makes it the fastest planet. It is named after **Mercury**, the nimble messenger of the Roman gods. Its orbit is more elliptical than those of the other planets. The slow turning of its orbit, the **precession of the perihelion**, could only be fully explained by Albert Einstein with the general theory of relativity.

Mercury has almost no **atmosphere** that could store heat. That is why it gets hotter than 400 degrees Celsius on the day side, hot enough to melt lead. On the night side the temperature drops to about minus 170 degrees. Mercury turns very slowly on its axis. A whole day from sunrise to sunrise lasts about 176 Earth days there, which is two Mercury years.

Mercury's surface is full of **craters** caused by impacts of asteroids and comets. The largest is the **Caloris Basin**, about 1,500 kilometres across. There are also long cliffs that formed when the planet shrank a little as it cooled. In deep craters at the poles, which never get sunlight, there is probably water ice.

Because Mercury is so close to the Sun, it is hard to observe from the Earth. You can only see it low on the horizon shortly after sunset or before sunrise. In the 1970s, the space probe **Mariner 10** was the first to fly past it. From 2011 to 2015, the probe **Messenger** orbited it. Since 2018, the European and Japanese mission BepiColombo has been on its way, in which researchers from the University of Bern are also involved with a laser altimeter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet with a solid surface of rock, like Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
A bowl-shaped hollow, usually formed by an impact.
The time a planet takes to go once around the Sun.
The layer of gas around a celestial body.

gewusst: Although Mercury is closest to the Sun, Venus is hotter, because its thick atmosphere stores the heat.
About 13 times a century, Mercury passes in front of the Sun as a small black dot as seen from the Earth.
On Mercury, a day lasts longer than a year.

teile.einleitung: Light pollution means that it is too bright at night because of artificial light. Street lamps, advertising boards and lit-up buildings brighten the sky. This spoils the view of the stars and also disturbs many animals.
wichtigste: Light pollution means too much artificial light at night.
When it is very bright at night, you see far fewer stars.
The **Milky Way** can hardly be seen any more in towns and cities.
Insects are particularly strongly attracted by lamps.
Migrating birds find their way less well at night in bright light.
Lamps that shine downwards help against light pollution.

abschnitte.text: Above a town at night you can often see a **bright glow** in the sky. It is called a **light dome** or skyglow. It forms because light from lamps shines upwards and is reflected by dust and water droplets in the air. This dome of light can be seen from many kilometres away. In Switzerland, with its many villages and towns, there are only a few completely dark places left.

The brighter the sky is, the **fewer stars** you see. The faint stars simply disappear in the light. Especially the **Milky Way**, the bright band of countless stars, can hardly be made out in towns and cities. Many children have never seen it. In Switzerland today, you usually see the most stars **in remote mountain valleys**, far from large towns.

Many **insects** are drawn to lamps at night as if by magic. They circle the light until they are exhausted, or they become easy prey. In a single summer night, a great many insects can die at one lamp. They are then missing from nature, because insects pollinate plants and are food for birds, bats and other animals.

Many **migrating birds** fly south or back again at night. Among other things, they find their way by the stars. Bright light from towns and lit-up buildings can **confuse** them. Some then take detours or crash into glass walls. Other night-active animals such as bats or glow-worms also suffer from too much light.

There are simple measures against light pollution. Lamps should shine **downwards** and not into the sky. Lights should only be on where they are needed and only for as long as necessary. Warm, yellowish light attracts fewer insects than cold, bluish light. In Switzerland, some municipalities switch off part of their street lighting at night. This also saves electricity and money.

gewusst: Glow-worms find each other with their own glow, which can hardly be seen any more in the light of lamps.
The dome of light over a large city can often be seen from many kilometres away.

teile.einleitung: Why does an apple fall down from a tree and not up? The reason is the Earth's pull, also called gravity. It keeps us on the ground, holds the air around the Earth and even keeps the Moon in its orbit.
wichtigste: The Earth pulls all things towards it; this force is called the Earth's pull or gravity.
Isaac Newton explained gravity over 300 years ago.
The Earth's pull keeps the Moon in its orbit.
Without air, a feather and a hammer fall at the same speed.
On Jupiter you would be about two and a half times as heavy as on Earth.
On Mars you weigh only just over a third.
The Earth's gravity holds on to the Earth's atmosphere.

abschnitte.text: When a ripe apple falls from a tree, the Earth pulls it towards itself. This force is called the **Earth's pull** or **gravity**. It acts on everything: on stones, water, animals and on us humans. That is why we stand firmly on the ground. If you throw a ball into the air, it always comes back down.

The scientist **Isaac Newton** lived in England over 300 years ago. He explained why things fall and why planets circle the Sun. A well-known story says that a falling apple gave him the idea. It is not certain whether it really happened like that. But Newton realised that the same force makes the apple fall and steers the Moon around the Earth.

The Earth also pulls on the **Moon**. That is why it does not fly off into space but circles around us. The **air** is also held in place by the Earth's gravity. Without it, our atmosphere would escape into space. We would then not be able to breathe.

On Earth, a feather falls more slowly than a hammer. But this is not because of gravity; it is because of the **air**, which slows down the light feather. An astronaut on an Apollo mission did an experiment on the Moon. He dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time. Because there is no air on the Moon, **both landed at the same time**.

How strongly a celestial body pulls depends on its mass and size. Huge **Jupiter** pulls strongly: you would be about two and a half times as heavy there as on Earth. Smaller **Mars** pulls more weakly; you weigh only just over a third there. On the **Moon** you weigh only about a sixth. That is why the astronauts could make big jumps there.

gewusst: Without the Earth's gravity there would be no rivers, because water only flows downhill thanks to gravity.
The Sun's gravity keeps all the planets in their orbits.

teile.einleitung: The heliocentric model puts the Sun at the centre. The Earth and the other planets circle around it. Nicolaus Copernicus made this idea known in the 16th century and changed the way people thought.
wichtigste: “Helios” is the Greek word for Sun.
In the heliocentric model, the planets circle the Sun.
The switch to this view of the world is called the Copernican revolution.
In 1616, Copernicus's main work was put on the Index of Forbidden Books.
Isaac Newton used the law of gravitation to explain why the planets circle the Sun.
In 1838, Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel was the first to measure the parallax of a star.

abschnitte.text: The word **heliocentric** comes from “Helios”, the Greek word for **Sun**. According to this view, the Earth goes around the Sun in a year and turns on its own axis every day. The cathedral canon **Nicolaus Copernicus** published his main work on this in 1543. Without his knowledge, a **preface** was added to the book. It said that the model was only an **aid to calculation** and not a description of reality. The switch from the old to the new view of the world is called the **Copernican revolution**.

Mars sometimes traces a **loop** in the sky and seems to move backwards. The heliocentric model explains this simply. The Earth moves faster on its **inner orbit** than Mars. When it **overtakes** Mars, Mars seems to fall behind for a while. The positions of **Mercury** and **Venus** fit with this too. Their orbits lie **inside the Earth's orbit**, which is why you never see them high in the sky at midnight, but only in the evening or morning near the Sun.

The new view of the world met with resistance, including in the Church. In **1616**, Copernicus's main work was put on the **Index of Forbidden Books**. Galileo Galilei supported the new teaching with observations through his telescope. He had to answer for this before a Church court. Johannes Kepler realised that the planets move around the Sun not in circles but in **ellipses**.

In 1687, **Isaac Newton** used his **law of gravitation** to explain why the planets circle the Sun. The Sun pulls on them, just as the Earth pulls on a falling apple. But direct proof of the Earth's movement was missing for a long time. In **1838**, **Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel** was the first to measure the **parallax** of a star. This is a tiny apparent shift that arises because the Earth is on different sides of the Sun over the course of the year.

gewusst: Even in ancient times, the Greek Aristarchus of Samos suggested that the Sun is at the centre, almost 1,800 years before Copernicus.
Today we know that the Sun is not the centre of the universe either. It is one of billions of stars in the Milky Way.

teile.einleitung: Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer and mathematician who lived from 1571 to 1630. He found out the laws by which the planets move around the Sun.
wichtigste: According to Kepler's first law, the planets move in ellipses.
The Sun is at one focus of the ellipse.
According to the second law, a planet is faster when it is close to the Sun.
The third law links the orbital period and the distance from the Sun.
Kepler analysed mainly Tycho Brahe's data on Mars.
His Rudolphine Tables appeared in 1627.

abschnitte.titel: A life devoted to the stars
abschnitte.text: Johannes Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt in Württemberg. He worked as a maths teacher in Graz and later in **Prague** at the court of **Emperor Rudolf II**. There he analysed the very precise observations of the Danish astronomer **Tycho Brahe**. The data on **Mars** helped him most, because its orbit is clearly elliptical. Kepler died in Regensburg in 1630.

The **first law** says: planets move in **ellipses**, not in perfect circles. The Sun is at one of the two **foci**. According to the **second law**, the line between the Sun and a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the planet is faster close to the Sun. The **third law** says: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the distance. A planet four times as far away as the Earth takes 8 years, because 4 cubed is 64 and the square root of 64 is 8.

Kepler published the first two laws in 1609 in the “Astronomia nova”. The third followed in 1619 in **“Harmonices mundi”**, the “Harmony of the World”. In 1627 the **Rudolphine Tables** appeared, named after Emperor Rudolf II. With them, the positions of the planets could be predicted much more accurately than with earlier tables.

Kepler also studied **optics**, the science of light. He described a telescope made of two **converging lenses**. It shows the image upside down, but it has a larger field of view than Galileo's telescope. Such telescopes are still used in astronomy today.

From 1615, Kepler's mother **Katharina Kepler** was accused of **witchcraft**. At that time such accusations were taken very seriously and could end dangerously. Johannes Kepler took on her defence himself. After a long trial, she was released in 1621.

gewusst: NASA named a space telescope for searching for planets after Johannes Kepler.
Kepler also wrote an early story about a journey to the Moon, the “Somnium”.

teile.einleitung: Cosmic rays consist of very high-energy particles that hit the Earth from space. In the atmosphere they create whole showers of new particles, some of which reach the ground.
wichtigste: Victor Franz Hess discovered cosmic rays in 1912 on balloon flights.
The primary rays consist of about nine tenths protons.
Mainly muons arrive at the ground.
Cosmic rays constantly create carbon-14.
The “Oh-My-God particle” of 1991 had about 3 · 10^20 electronvolts.
The University of Bern has been measuring the rays on the Jungfraujoch since 1958.

abschnitte.text: Around 1912, the physicist **Victor Franz Hess** rose to great heights in balloons. He found that **ionising radiation** increases with height instead of decreasing. So it had to come from above, from space. For this discovery, Hess received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1936.

**Primary cosmic rays** hit the atmosphere from outside. They consist of about nine tenths **protons** and about one tenth helium nuclei. Heavier nuclei and electrons are rare. In the air, the particles collide with atoms and create **particle showers**, the **secondary radiation**. When **pions** decay, **muons** are produced, which make up most of the charged radiation at the ground.

A muon lives only about 2.2 microseconds. In this time, even at the speed of light, it would only get about 660 metres. Even so, many muons from many kilometres up reach the ground. The reason is **time dilation** from the theory of relativity: because they fly at almost the speed of light, their time passes much more slowly from our point of view. So muons are an everyday proof of Einstein's theory.

**Neutrons** from cosmic rays turn nitrogen-14 into **carbon-14** in the atmosphere. This isotope gets into all living things through plants. After death it slowly decays. With **radiocarbon dating**, this makes it possible to work out the age of wood, bones or fabrics.

abschnitte.titel: Extreme energies and measurements in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In the energy spectrum there is a bend at about 3 · 10^15 electronvolts, the **knee**, and at much higher energies the **ankle**. Protons above about 5 · 10^19 eV lose energy through collisions with photons of the background radiation; this is the **GZK limit**. In 1991, the Fly's Eye experiment in Utah measured the **“Oh-My-God particle”** with about 3 · 10^20 eV, roughly the energy of a thrown baseball. The Physics Institute of the **University of Bern** has run **neutron monitors** on the **Jungfraujoch** since 1958. The height of about 3,500 metres makes the measurements particularly sensitive.

gewusst: Every second, muons from cosmic rays fly through your body without you noticing.
On high-altitude flights, cosmic rays are much stronger than on the ground.

teile.einleitung: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a huge collection of a few hundred billion stars, gas and dust. Our Sun belongs to it too. On dark nights you can see the Milky Way as a bright, milky band across the sky.
wichtigste: The Milky Way is the galaxy in which our solar system lies.
It is a barred spiral galaxy with several spiral arms.
The Milky Way contains a few hundred billion stars.
Its diameter is over 100,000 light years.
At its centre is the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.
Our solar system lies in the Orion Arm, far from the centre.
The Sun takes about 230 million years to go once around the centre.

abschnitte.text: A **galaxy** is a huge island of stars in space, held together by gravity. Our galaxy is called the **Milky Way**. The name comes from Greek legend, according to which the goddess Hera spilt milk across the sky. The English word “galaxy” comes from the Greek word for milk. The Milky Way contains a few hundred billion stars, as well as huge clouds of gas and dust.

The Milky Way is a **barred spiral galaxy**. Seen from the side, it would be a flat disc with a bulge in the middle. Seen from above, it has a bar-shaped core from which several **spiral arms** extend. The disc has a diameter of over 100,000 light years but is only a few thousand light years thick. It turns slowly around its centre.

Our solar system lies in a smaller spiral arm, the **Orion Arm**. The Sun is about 26,000 light years from the centre, so more on the outskirts of the galaxy. It circles the centre at over 200 kilometres per second. Even so, it takes about 230 million years for one lap. When the Sun was last at its present position, the first dinosaurs were just living on Earth.

abschnitte.titel: The heart of the Milky Way
abschnitte.text: At the centre of the Milky Way sits a **supermassive black hole** called **Sagittarius A***. It has about four million times as much mass as the Sun. Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020 because they had precisely measured the movement of stars around this object. In 2022, the Event Horizon Telescope published the first image of its shadow. Seen from us, the centre lies in the constellation Sagittarius.

You see the Milky Way best on moonless nights far from towns, for example in the Alps. In Switzerland it is particularly impressive in summer, when the bright centre is low in the south. Because of **light pollution**, many people today can no longer see it from home at all. As early as 1609, Galileo Galilei realised with his telescope that the milky band consists of countless individual stars. The European space probe Gaia has measured the positions of over a billion stars in the Milky Way.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge island of billions of stars, gas and dust.
A curved, bright area of a spiral galaxy where many young stars form.
An object with such strong gravity that not even light can escape.
Artificial light at night that outshines the starry sky.

gewusst: In about 4 to 5 billion years, the Milky Way is expected to collide with the Andromeda Galaxy.
There is so much space between the stars that hardly any stars crash directly into each other in such galaxy collisions.
The Magellanic Clouds are small companion galaxies of the Milky Way that can be seen with the naked eye in the southern sky.

teile.einleitung: A fireball is a particularly bright shooting star. It shines more brightly than all the planets and stars in the sky. Sometimes you can even hear it, and sometimes pieces of it fall to Earth.
wichtigste: A fireball is a particularly bright shooting star.
It forms when a larger lump from space burns up in the air.
Very bright fireballs are also called bolides.
Large fireballs can make a bang like thunder.
Remains can fall to the ground as meteorites.
In 2013, a huge fireball exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk.
If you see a fireball, you should report it to an observatory.

abschnitte.text: A **fireball** is a very bright **shooting star**. It shines more brightly than all the planets and stars. Normal shooting stars are caused by tiny grains from space, often no bigger than a grain of sand. With a fireball, the lump is **bigger**. When it enters the atmosphere at high speed, it is strongly heated and shines much more brightly. Experts also call very bright fireballs **bolides**.

Fireballs often glow **greenish**, yellow or **orange**. The colour depends on the substances in the lump and in the air. Some fireballs burst into many pieces in the sky. Large fireballs travel faster than sound. This can create a **bang** that sounds like thunder. It can often only be heard some time after the flash.

With large fireballs, not everything burns up. The remains can fall to Earth. Such stones from space are called **meteorites**. They are very valuable for research. They tell us a lot about how our solar system formed.

On **15 February 2013**, a lump from space exploded high above the Russian city of **Chelyabinsk**. The fireball was easy to see in the bright morning. The **shock wave** broke many windowpanes in the city. Later, numerous meteorite pieces were found in the area. It was one of the largest such events of the last hundred years.

If you see a fireball, you can report it to an **observatory** or to a fireball reporting centre. The place, time, direction and brightness are important. Researchers collect reports from many places. This lets them calculate the **flight path**. Sometimes this makes it possible to find out where meteorites might be lying.

gewusst: A fireball can be so bright that for a moment it makes the night almost as bright as day.
In Switzerland too, cameras run by observatories and amateur astronomers watch the night sky for fireballs.
