teile.einleitung: The Hohmann transfer is a particularly economical way of moving a spacecraft from one circular orbit to another. It is named after the German engineer Walter Hohmann and is still used today for satellites and flights to planets.
wichtigste: Walter Hohmann described the change of orbit in 1925 in the book “Die Erreichbarkeit der Himmelskörper” (The Attainability of Celestial Bodies).
Between two circular orbits, the Hohmann transfer needs exactly two engine burns.
The flight path is half an ellipse that touches the inner and the outer circular orbit.
A Hohmann flight from the Earth to Mars takes about 8.5 months.
Favourable launch windows to Mars open about every 26 months.
Many communications satellites travel to their destination via a geostationary transfer orbit.

abschnitte.text: Walter Hohmann was actually a **civil engineer** in Essen. In his spare time he worked out how you could fly to other celestial bodies with little fuel. In 1925 he published the book “Die Erreichbarkeit der Himmelskörper” (The Attainability of Celestial Bodies). In it he described the path that is now called the **Hohmann transfer**. At that time there was not a single rocket that could fly into space.

A spacecraft first circles in an inner orbit. The **first burn** makes it faster and lifts it into a long orbit, the **transfer ellipse**. Its lowest point, the **periapsis**, lies on the inner orbit, and its highest point, the **apoapsis**, on the outer one. You fly exactly half an ellipse. At the highest point comes the **second burn**, which makes the new orbit circular.

For the journey from the Earth to Mars, the transfer ellipse has a **semi-major axis** of about 1.26 **astronomical units**. Using Kepler's **third law**, this gives a flight time of about 259 days, about 8.5 months. Mars has to be exactly at the end point of the path when the spacecraft arrives. This suitable position of the Earth and Mars only repeats about every 780 days, roughly every 26 months. That is why Mars missions often launch in the same year.

Television and communications satellites orbit at a height of about 36,000 kilometres. The launch rocket usually puts them into a **geostationary transfer orbit**, a Hohmann ellipse. At the highest point, the satellite fires its own engine and makes the orbit round. From a height of 300 kilometres, this change needs about 3.9 kilometres per second of change in speed, the so-called **delta-v**. The flight along the ellipse takes about five hours.

In many cases the Hohmann transfer needs the least fuel, but it is not the fastest way. If the outer orbit is more than about twelve times as far away as the inner one, a **bi-elliptic transfer** with three burns is even more economical. But it takes much longer. Modern missions often combine Hohmann orbits with **flybys** of planets that give extra momentum.

gewusst: When Hohmann wrote his book, no human and no machine had yet been in space.
The flight time on a transfer orbit is always exactly half the orbital period of the ellipse.

teile.einleitung: Io is a moon of the planet Jupiter and the most volcanically active body in the whole solar system. Its surface glows yellow, orange and red and is constantly changing.
wichtigste: Io is one of Jupiter's four Galilean moons.
The heat for the volcanoes comes from Jupiter's tidal forces.
Sulphur gives Io its yellow to orange colour.
In 1979, Voyager 1 discovered the first active volcanoes on Io.
Io goes around Jupiter in just under two days.
Io is a little bigger than our Moon.

abschnitte.text: There are hundreds of active **volcanoes** on Io. One of the best known is **Loki Patera**, a hollow about 200 kilometres wide full of lava. It is one of the strongest sources of heat on Io and is named after the Norse god Loki. Because Io has only weak gravity and almost no atmosphere, gas and dust fly very far. Some **plumes** rise several hundred kilometres high, up to about 500 kilometres.

Where does the heat come from? Jupiter and the other moons constantly pull Io in different directions. These **tidal forces** knead the inside of the moon. This creates heat, just as a wire gets warm if you bend it back and forth many times. This energy powers the volcanoes.

Io's volcanoes give off a lot of **sulphur** and **sulphur dioxide**. These substances colour the surface yellow, orange, red and white. Unlike Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, Io has almost no **water**. The heat drove it away long ago; Io is a dry, rocky moon.

In 1979, the space probe **Voyager 1** flew past Jupiter. In its pictures, the engineer **Linda Morabito** noticed a cloud above the edge of Io. It was the plume of an erupting volcano. This was the first time active volcanoes had been discovered outside the Earth. Later probes such as Galileo and Juno observed Io more closely.

Io has a diameter of about 3,640 kilometres. Our Moon measures about 3,470 kilometres, so Io is only a little bigger. Io takes about 1.8 days, about 42 hours, to go once around Jupiter. That is the fastest orbit of the four **Galilean moons**, which Galileo Galilei discovered in 1610.

gewusst: Io was the first celestial body apart from the Earth on which active volcanoes were found.
Io's surface is renewed so quickly by new lava that hardly any impact craters can be found.

teile.einleitung: Landing is one of the most dangerous parts of a space flight. The space capsule has to slow down from an enormous speed to almost zero in a short time. A heat shield, parachutes and sometimes braking rockets make sure the crew gets home safely.
wichtigste: On entering the atmosphere, the outside of the capsule becomes red hot.
Shortly before landing, **parachutes** slow the capsule down.
The American Apollo capsules landed in the sea after the flight to the Moon.
A landing on water is called a **splashdown**, after which a ship picks up the astronauts.
The Russian Soyuz capsule usually lands on the steppe of Kazakhstan.
Shortly before impact, small braking rockets fire on the Soyuz.

abschnitte.text: A capsule returning from the space station is travelling very fast. When it hits the **atmosphere**, the air in front of it is strongly compressed and becomes hot. The outside of the capsule becomes **red hot**. A **heat shield** on the underside protects the crew. It slowly burns away at the surface and carries the heat away with it. Radio contact is often lost for a few minutes during this time.

The air already slows the capsule down a lot. But that is not enough for a gentle landing. That is why **parachutes** open further down. First come smaller drogue parachutes, then the large main parachutes. They slow the capsule down so much that it touches down on the water or the ground at a low speed.

The American **Apollo capsules** landed **in the sea** after the flight to the Moon. Such a landing on water is called a **splashdown**. Water cushions the impact well. Afterwards a **ship** picks up the capsule and the astronauts. Today's American capsules also usually land in the sea off the coast of the USA.

The Russian **Soyuz capsule** usually lands on land, on the wide **steppe of Kazakhstan**. Because the ground is hard, an extra trick is needed. Shortly before impact, **small braking rockets** fire at the bottom of the capsule. They brake away the last bit of speed. Even so, the cosmonauts feel a hard jolt when they touch down.

After a long stay in space, astronauts often **cannot walk properly** straight away. Their bodies have got used to **floating**. The sense of balance has to readjust, and the muscles and bones have become weaker. That is why helpers assist the crew out of the capsule. After a few days to weeks, most of them have got used to gravity again.

gewusst: A heat shield protects the capsule by slowly burning away and so carrying the heat off.
Large ships of the US Navy were used to bring back the Apollo astronauts.

teile.einleitung: Luminosity tells you how much energy a star gives off per second. It is one of the most important quantities in astronomy. With it, you can compare stars and understand how much energy reaches the planets.
wichtigste: The Sun has a luminosity of about 3.8 · 10²⁶ watts.
The **solar constant** is about 1,361 watts per square metre.
Luminosity grows with the square of the radius and the fourth power of the temperature.
The amount of radiation received decreases with the square of the distance.
About 4 billion years ago, the young Sun shone with only about 70 per cent of today's strength.
In **Davos** there is the World Radiation Centre, which calibrates instruments for measuring sunlight.

abschnitte.text: **Luminosity** is the total power a star gives off as radiation. For the Sun it is **about 3.8 · 10²⁶ watts**. That is 38 followed by 25 zeros. Astronomers often give the luminosity of other stars in **solar luminosities**. So a star with 9 solar luminosities gives off nine times as much energy as our Sun.

Luminosity depends on the **size** and the **surface temperature** of a star. It grows with the **square of the radius**. That is why a star with three times the radius and the same temperature as the Sun has 9 solar luminosities. Temperature has an even stronger effect: it enters with the **fourth power**. If the temperature doubles with the same radius, the luminosity rises by a factor of 16.

The Sun's radiation spreads out over bigger and bigger spheres. That is why the **irradiance** decreases with the **square of the distance**. Outside the Earth's atmosphere, at the Earth's average distance, about **1,361 watts per square metre** is measured. This value is called the **solar constant**. At Jupiter, about 5.2 AU away, only about 1/27 of it arrives, because 5.2 times 5.2 is roughly 27.

For **main sequence stars**, which burn hydrogen like the Sun, luminosity depends strongly on **mass**. It grows roughly with the **3.5th power** of the mass. So a star twice as heavy shines about eleven times as brightly. The Sun is also slowly changing. About 4 billion years ago it had only about **70 per cent** of its present luminosity.

In **Davos** in the canton of the Grisons there is the **Physikalisch-Meteorologisches Observatorium Davos**. It serves as the **World Radiation Centre**. There, instruments for measuring sunlight from many countries are compared with each other and calibrated. This makes measurements all over the world comparable. The observatory also builds instruments that measure the Sun's radiation on satellites.

gewusst: Very massive stars shine so strongly that they use up their fuel in a few million years, while the Sun shines for billions of years.
How the Earth did not freeze completely even though the young Sun was weaker is still a research topic today.

teile.einleitung: The Global Positioning System, GPS for short, is a system of satellites that lets you find your position anywhere on Earth. It is built into mobile phones, cars, watches and aeroplanes.
wichtigste: GPS was built by the USA and is operated by them.
The system has been fully in operation since 1995.
On board the satellites are very precise atomic clocks.
A receiver measures how long the radio signals take to arrive.
For position and height, it needs signals from at least 4 satellites.
There are other systems, such as Galileo from Europe and BeiDou from China.

abschnitte.text: **GPS** was built by the US Department of Defense, at first for the military. Today everyone can use it free of charge. About **30 satellites** orbit the Earth at a height of about 20,000 kilometres. They are spread out so that you can receive several at once almost everywhere. The system has been fully in operation since **1995**.

Each satellite constantly sends out a radio signal with the exact **time**. For this it has an **atomic clock** on board that is extremely accurate. The receiver measures the **travel time** of the signal, in other words how long it was on its way. From this it calculates the distance to the satellite. Because radio signals travel almost 300,000 kilometres per second, the time has to be accurate to billionths of a second.

If the receiver knows its distance from several satellites, it can calculate its position. For the location on the map and the **height**, it needs three distances. But the clock in a mobile phone is much less accurate than an atomic clock. So it needs a **fourth satellite** to correct its clock error. With signals from **at least 4 satellites**, the device knows its position, height and the exact time.

Besides GPS there are other **satellite navigation systems**. Russia operates **GLONASS**, and China the **BeiDou** system. Europe has built the **Galileo** system, and **Switzerland** takes part in it too. Modern mobile phones often receive several systems at once and so become more accurate. In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Topography **swisstopo** uses satellite signals for very precise surveying.

gewusst: Without corrections based on Einstein's theory of relativity, GPS would be several kilometres out after just one day.
GPS provides not only the position but also a very precise time, which power grids and banks, for example, use.

teile.einleitung: Giordano Bruno was an Italian thinker of the 16th century. He taught that the universe is infinite and that the stars are distant suns. Because of his teachings, he was executed in Rome in 1600.
wichtigste: Giordano Bruno was born in 1548 in Nola near Naples.
As a young man he belonged to the Dominican order.
He taught that the universe is infinitely large.
For him, the stars were distant suns that might have planets of their own.
In 1592 he was arrested in Venice, and in 1600 he was executed in Rome.
Today there is a monument to him on the square Campo de’ Fiori in Rome.

abschnitte.text: Giordano Bruno was born in **1548** in **Nola**, a town near Naples. As a young man he joined the **Dominican** order. He read many books and thought very independently. Soon his views brought him into conflict with the order. He left the monastery and fled from Italy.

Bruno travelled through many countries in Europe. In **1579** he lived for a short time in **Geneva**. There too he got into an argument with the Church, which in Geneva was Reformed at the time. Afterwards he taught in France, England and Germany, among other places. Everywhere he wrote books and debated with scholars. But he often had to move on, because his ideas caused offence.

Bruno knew the teaching of **Copernicus**, according to which the Earth goes around the Sun. But he went even further. For him, the universe was **infinitely large** and had no centre. He thought the **stars** in the night sky were **distant suns** that could have planets of their own. He had no measurements for this but arrived at this view by thinking. Today we know that many stars really do have planets.

In 1591, Bruno returned to Italy. In **1592** he was arrested in **Venice** and later handed over to the **Inquisition** in Rome. The Inquisition was a Church court that acted against departures from the faith. Bruno spent about eight years in prison and refused to take back his teachings. In **1600** he was executed in Rome on the square **Campo de’ Fiori**. A monument to him has stood there since 1889.

gewusst: Bruno's conviction had mainly to do with his views on faith, not only with his ideas about the universe.
A crater on the far side of the Moon is named after Giordano Bruno.

teile.einleitung: Michel Mayor is a Swiss astrophysicist from Lausanne. Together with Didier Queloz, in 1995 he discovered the first planet outside our solar system around a Sun-like star. For this, the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
wichtigste: Michel Mayor was born in **Lausanne** in 1942.
He did research and taught at the **University of Geneva** for most of his career.
In 1995, with **Didier Queloz**, he discovered the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star.
He helped develop the measuring instrument **CORAVEL** and led the building of **HARPS** at La Silla.
In 2005 he received the **Shaw Prize**, and in 2017, with Queloz, the **Wolf Prize in Physics**.
In 2019, Mayor and Queloz shared one half of the **Nobel Prize in Physics**; the other half went to James Peebles.

abschnitte.text: Michel Mayor was born in **1942** in **Lausanne**. He studied physics and became an astrophysicist. He did research and taught at the **University of Geneva** for most of his career. With his help, the observatory there became a world-famous centre for the search for planets around other stars.

You usually cannot see a planet around a distant star directly. But the planet pulls the star a tiny bit to and fro with its gravity. This wobble can be measured in the star's light. In the **1970s**, Mayor helped develop the instrument **CORAVEL**, which measured the speeds of stars precisely. Later he led the building of the spectrograph **HARPS** at the **La Silla** Observatory in **Chile**.

In **1995**, Michel Mayor and his doctoral student at the time, **Didier Queloz**, discovered a planet around the star **51 Pegasi**. It was the first planet found around a **Sun-like star**. The planet is a gas giant and goes around its star in only about four days. The discovery was a sensation. Since then, thousands of **exoplanets** have been found.

Mayor received many prizes for his work. In **2005** he was given the **Shaw Prize**, which is awarded in **Hong Kong**. In **2017**, Mayor and Queloz received the **Wolf Prize in Physics** together. Two years later, in **2019**, came the highest honour: the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. Mayor and Queloz shared one half, and the other half went to the cosmologist **James Peebles**.

abschnitte.titel: No second Earth to move to
abschnitte.text: After the Nobel Prize, Mayor was often asked whether people could one day move to an exoplanet. In **2019** he stressed that this was **unrealistic because of the huge distances**. Even the nearest stars are so far away that a journey with today's technology would take an unimaginably long time. So we should take good care of our own Earth.

gewusst: The planet around 51 Pegasi is so close to its star that a year there lasts only about four Earth days.
With Didier Queloz, a second Swiss astronomer also received the Nobel Prize in 2019.

teile.einleitung: A gravitational lens is a large mass in space that bends the light of more distant objects. Like a magnifying glass, it can distort, multiply or brighten images. Albert Einstein predicted this effect.
wichtigste: Large masses bend light, as Einstein's general theory of relativity says.
At the edge of the Sun, the bending is about 1.75 arcseconds.
In 1919, the bending of light was confirmed during a total solar eclipse.
In 1937, Fritz Zwicky suggested that whole galaxies act as gravitational lenses.
If the source, lens and observer lie exactly in a line, an Einstein ring forms.
Gravitational lenses help in the search for exoplanets and dark matter.

abschnitte.text: According to Albert Einstein's **general theory of relativity**, a large mass bends the space around it. Light passing close by follows this curve and is bent. At the edge of the Sun, the bending is about **1.75 arcseconds**, which is a tiny angle. In **1919**, during a **total solar eclipse**, researchers measured the positions of stars close to the Sun. They were slightly shifted, exactly as Einstein had calculated.

The astronomer **Fritz Zwicky** grew up in the canton of **Glarus** and worked in the USA. In **1937** he suggested that whole **galaxies** can act as gravitational lenses. For a long time this could not be observed. In 1979 the first case was discovered: a quasar that appeared twice in the sky. A **quasar** is the extremely bright core of a distant galaxy.

If the source, lens and observer lie exactly in a line, the light is distorted into an **Einstein ring**. If they are slightly out of line, you often see several images of the same source. In the **Einstein Cross** Q2237+030, a quasar appears four times. A gravitational lens bends all colours equally, because the bending does not depend on the **wavelength**. So, unlike with a glass lens, there are no colour errors.

In the **microlensing method**, a single star acts as a lens for a star behind it. If it has a planet, you see a short extra brightening. This is how **exoplanets** are found. In the **Bullet Cluster**, lensing measurements show where most of the mass is, namely not where the visible gas is. This is considered important evidence for **dark matter**. From the differences in travel time between images of a lensed supernova, you can even work out the **Hubble constant**, which tells you how fast the universe is expanding.

gewusst: Fritz Zwicky also helped introduce the term “supernova” and already suspected invisible mass in galaxy clusters in the 1930s.
Thanks to gravitational lenses, telescopes can see galaxies that would otherwise be far too faint.

teile.einleitung: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and our outer neighbour. Because of its reddish colour, it is called the “Red Planet”. No other planet is explored so intensively by robots, and perhaps one day people will travel there.
wichtigste: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
It is called the “Red Planet” because its dust contains rusty iron oxide.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
On Mars stands Olympus Mons, the highest known volcano in the solar system.
Mars is about half the size of the Earth and much colder.
A Martian year lasts about 687 Earth days.
Researchers explore Mars with robotic vehicles and satellites.

abschnitte.text: Mars has a diameter of about 6,800 kilometres, which makes it about half the size of the Earth. Its red colour comes from **iron oxide**, a kind of rust in the dust and rock. The planet is named after **Mars**, the Roman god of war. In the night sky it can be seen as a strikingly reddish point of light. A day on Mars lasts about 24 hours and 37 minutes, almost as long as ours.

On Mars stands **Olympus Mons**, a huge volcano that rises about 22 kilometres above its surroundings. That makes it more than twice as high as Mount Everest. There is also an enormous system of canyons, **Valles Marineris**, which is thousands of kilometres long. At the poles there are ice caps of water ice and frozen carbon dioxide. Dried-up river valleys show that liquid water once flowed on Mars.

The **atmosphere** of Mars is very thin and consists mainly of carbon dioxide. People could not breathe there without a spacesuit. The average temperature is about minus 60 degrees Celsius. Sometimes huge **dust storms** sweep across the planet, covering it almost completely for weeks. Because Mars is further from the Sun, a Martian year lasts about 687 Earth days.

Mars has two small, irregularly shaped moons: **Phobos** and **Deimos**. They were discovered in 1877 by the American astronomer Asaph Hall. Their names mean “fear” and “terror”, after the companions of the Greek god of war. Phobos is only about 22 kilometres across and orbits very close to Mars. Both moons are probably captured asteroids or debris from an impact.

Researchers explore the surface with **rovers**, remote-controlled robotic vehicles. Well-known ones are Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance, which landed in 2021. The small helicopter Ingenuity flew with it, the first aircraft on another planet. From orbit, the camera **CaSSIS** of the University of Bern photographs Mars in colour and at high resolution. An important question is whether simple life once existed on Mars.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remote-controlled robotic vehicle that drives around on another celestial body.
A compound of iron and oxygen, known in everyday life as rust.
The largest known volcano in the solar system, on Mars.
The layer of gas that surrounds a planet.

gewusst: A sunset on Mars looks bluish, exactly the opposite of a sunset on Earth.
On Mars you weigh only about 38 per cent as much as on Earth and could jump almost three times as high.
Depending on the positions of the planets, radio signals take about 3 to more than 20 minutes from the Earth to Mars.

teile.einleitung: Neptune is the eighth and outermost planet of our solar system. This deep blue ice giant is so far away that you can only see it with a telescope. The strongest winds known on any planet blow on it.
wichtigste: Neptune is the planet furthest from the Sun.
It is an ice giant and about four times as big as the Earth.
Neptune looks blue because methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light.
The strongest winds in the solar system blow on Neptune.
It is named after Neptune, the Roman god of the sea.
Voyager 2 is the only space probe that has flown past Neptune.
In 1846, Neptune became the first planet to be calculated first and then found.

abschnitte.text: Neptune has a diameter of about 49,000 kilometres, just under four times the Earth's diameter. Together with Uranus, it is one of the **ice giants**. Beneath its envelope of hydrogen and helium gas lies a thick layer of water, ammonia and **methane**. The methane absorbs red light, which is why Neptune looks blue. It is named after **Neptune**, the Roman god of the sea.

The strongest **winds** in the solar system blow on Neptune, at over 2,000 kilometres per hour. In 1989, Voyager 2 discovered a huge storm, which was called the **Great Dark Spot**. A few years later it had disappeared, but other storms appeared. At the top of the clouds it is extremely cold, at about minus 200 degrees Celsius. Where the energy for the fierce winds comes from has not yet been fully explained.

Neptune is on average about 4.5 billion kilometres from the Sun, about 30 times as far as the Earth. Since Pluto was declared a dwarf planet in 2006, Neptune has been the **outermost planet**. It takes about 165 years to go once around the Sun. Since it was discovered, it has only gone around the Sun about once. Sunlight takes about four hours to reach it.

Neptune is the first planet that was calculated first and then found. Astronomers had noticed that Uranus was not moving around the Sun exactly as it should. From this, the Frenchman **Urbain Le Verrier** calculated where an unknown planet would have to be. On 23 September 1846, Johann Gottfried Galle at the Berlin Observatory found the planet almost exactly at the predicted position. It was a great triumph for physics.

Neptune has several thin, dark **rings** and over a dozen known moons. The largest moon is called **Triton**. It circles Neptune in the opposite direction and is probably a captured body from the Kuiper Belt. On Triton there are geysers that blow out nitrogen. In 1989, the space probe **Voyager 2** was the only one to fly past Neptune and delivered the best close-up pictures so far.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large planet made mainly of water, ammonia and methane, such as Neptune and Uranus.
A gas that gives Neptune its blue colour.
The largest moon of Neptune.
The time for one whole lap around the Sun.

gewusst: A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years, so a child on Neptune would never reach its first birthday.
Galileo Galilei saw Neptune as early as 1612 but thought it was a star.
Deep inside Neptune, it might perhaps rain diamonds.

teile.einleitung: Marco Sieber is a Swiss doctor and astronaut. In 2022 he was accepted into the astronaut corps of the European Space Agency ESA. That makes him only the second Swiss person after Claude Nicollier to receive astronaut training.
wichtigste: Marco Sieber was born in **Biel** in 1989.
Before becoming an astronaut, he worked as a **doctor**.
In **November 2022** he was accepted into ESA's European Astronaut Corps.
He was chosen from over 22,500 valid applications.
He is the second Swiss person to receive astronaut training.
He completed his basic training at the European Astronaut Centre in **Cologne**.

abschnitte.text: Marco Sieber was born in **1989** in **Biel** in the canton of Bern. He studied medicine and worked as a **doctor**. Medical knowledge is very valuable in space travel. There is no hospital in space, and the crew has to be able to help itself with health problems. Doctors also research how the body changes in weightlessness.

Alongside his job, Marco Sieber was active in the **Swiss Armed Forces**. In the **Special Forces Command** he was a **parachutist**. In **2018** he was **chief medical officer of Swisscoy** in **Kosovo**. Swisscoy is Switzerland's contribution to an international peacekeeping mission there. Such experience in difficult situations is helpful for astronauts.

In 2021, **ESA** was looking for new astronauts. **Over 22,500 valid applications** were received. After many tests, examinations and interviews, Marco Sieber was selected in **November 2022** and accepted into the **European Astronaut Corps**. He is the **second Swiss person** to receive astronaut training. The first was **Claude Nicollier**, who flew into space several times on the Space Shuttle.

Marco Sieber completed his **basic training** at the **European Astronaut Centre in Cologne** in Germany. There, the future astronauts learn a lot about space technology, space stations and science. They practise working underwater, where weightlessness can be imitated. Survival training is also part of the course.

gewusst: From all the applications, ESA chose only five new career astronauts in 2022, and one of them was Marco Sieber.
Biel, Marco Sieber's home town, is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Moon does not look the same every evening: sometimes it is a thin crescent, sometimes a half circle, sometimes a full round disc. These changing shapes are called the phases of the Moon. They come about because we see the half of the Moon lit by the Sun from ever-changing angles.
wichtigste: The phases of the Moon are the Moon's changing shapes of light.
They come about because our view of the half of the Moon lit by the Sun keeps changing.
It takes about 29.5 days from one full moon to the next.
The four main phases are new moon, waxing half moon, full moon and waning half moon.
At new moon, the Moon can hardly be seen from the Earth.
Between new moon and full moon, the Moon is said to be waxing.
We always see the same side of the Moon because it turns on its axis as fast as it goes around the Earth.

abschnitte.titel: How do the phases come about?
abschnitte.text: The Sun always lights up exactly one half of the Moon, just as a lamp lights up a ball. As the Moon goes around the Earth, we see this bright half from changing angles. That is why its shape seems to change. So the phases of the Moon have nothing to do with the **Earth's shadow**; that is a common mistake. You can try this out yourself at home with a lamp and a ball.

A whole cycle from new moon to new moon is called a **synodic month** and lasts about 29.5 days. At **new moon**, the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, and we are looking at its dark side. After that a thin crescent grows, and the Moon waxes. After about a week, the waxing **half moon** is reached, when half of the visible disc is lit. After about two weeks, the full moon is opposite the Sun, and after that the Moon wanes again.

In Switzerland and other German-speaking countries there is a memory trick. If you can add a line to the crescent so that a small handwritten “z” is formed, the Moon is waxing (in German “zunehmend”). If the crescent looks like an “a” in old handwriting, it is waning (in German “abnehmend”). The waxing Moon is mainly seen in the evening, the waning Moon more in the second half of the night and in the morning. In the southern hemisphere, for example in Australia, the crescent looks exactly the other way round.

The Moon turns once on its axis in the same time it takes to go around the Earth. This is called **tidal locking**. That is why it always shows us the same side with the familiar dark patches. But the far side of the Moon is not always dark; at new moon it is even fully lit. It was first photographed in 1959 by the Soviet space probe Luna 3.

abschnitte.titel: Phases of the Moon in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Many calendars follow the phases of the Moon. The word **month** is related to the word Moon. Easter is calculated from the first full moon in spring, and the Islamic calendar is a purely lunar calendar. The date of Chinese New Year also depends on the new moon. At new moon the sky is especially dark, which is why it is the best time to watch the stars.

begriffe.erklaerung: The phase in which the Moon is almost invisible because we are looking at its unlit side.
The phase in which we see the whole lit disc of the Moon.
The phase in which half of the visible disc of the Moon is lit.
A moon turns on its axis at the same rate as it goes around its planet.

gewusst: With a thin crescent moon, you can sometimes see the dark part of the Moon glowing faintly because it is lit by the Earth.
This glow is called earthshine or ashen light.
A second full moon in the same calendar month is sometimes called a “blue moon”, but it is not blue.

teile.einleitung: Orion is one of the best-known constellations. It represents a great hunter from Greek legend. In winter you can see it well in the evening, and with its bright stars it is easy to find.
wichtigste: The constellation Orion represents a hunter.
Three bright stars in a row form Orion's Belt.
The reddish star Betelgeuse forms one shoulder.
The bluish white star Rigel forms one foot.
In winter you can see Orion well in the south in the evening.
Below the belt, in the sword, lies the Orion Nebula.

abschnitte.text: In old **Greek legends**, Orion is a great **hunter**. In the sky you can make out his shoulders, his belt and his legs. Roughly, the constellation has the shape of an **hourglass**: four bright stars form the corners, and the narrow **belt** lies in the middle. According to one legend, Orion was defeated by a scorpion. That is why the constellations Orion and Scorpius are never in the sky at the same time.

At the top left is **Betelgeuse**, which forms one of the hunter's shoulders. Betelgeuse is a huge, cooler star and so shines **reddish orange**. At the bottom right is **Rigel**. It is very hot and shines **bluish white**. So you can tell the temperature of the stars from their colours. The other two corners are called Bellatrix and Saiph.

Three bright stars stand almost in a row. They form the famous **Orion's Belt**. Their names are Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. The belt helps you find other stars: if you extend it down to the left, you come to **Sirius**, the brightest star in the night sky. Extended up to the right, it leads close to the star Aldebaran in Taurus.

Below the belt hangs Orion's **sword**, a row of fainter stars. Under a dark sky you can see a faint, blurry patch in it. This is the **Orion Nebula**, a huge cloud of gas and dust. **New stars** are forming in it right now. Even with binoculars it looks wonderful.

In Switzerland you see Orion best in **winter**. Then it is clearly visible in the **south** in the evening. In summer it is in the daytime sky together with the Sun and cannot be seen at night. Because Orion lies on the celestial equator, it can be seen from almost everywhere on Earth.

gewusst: At the end of 2019 and the beginning of 2020, Betelgeuse became noticeably dimmer for a few months, which caused a stir around the world.
Seen from the southern hemisphere, Orion is upside down.

teile.einleitung: Fritz Zwicky was a Swiss astronomer with roots in the canton of Glarus. He worked in the USA and had many ideas that were far ahead of their time. Important thoughts on dark matter, neutron stars and gravitational lenses came from him.
wichtigste: Fritz Zwicky was born in 1898 in Varna in Bulgaria.
His family came from Mollis in the canton of Glarus.
He studied physics at ETH Zurich.
In 1933 he wrote about “dark matter” in galaxy clusters.
With Walter Baade, he predicted in 1934 that neutron stars are the remains of supernovae.
He discovered over 100 supernovae.
He developed the morphological box, a method for finding new ideas.

abschnitte.text: Fritz Zwicky was born in **1898** in **Varna** in **Bulgaria**. His father lived there as a merchant. At the age of six, Fritz went to his grandparents in Switzerland. He grew up in **Glarus**. His place of citizenship was **Mollis** in the canton of Glarus, where he was later also buried.

abschnitte.titel: Studies and the move to the USA
abschnitte.text: Zwicky studied physics at **ETH Zurich** from 1917 to 1925 and wrote his doctoral thesis there. After that he went to the USA, to the **California Institute of Technology** in Pasadena. He worked there for most of his life. He was considered very clever, but also headstrong and quarrelsome. Many of his ideas were only confirmed decades later.

Zwicky studied how fast galaxies move in a **galaxy cluster**. He noticed that the visible galaxies have far too little mass to hold the cluster together. So in **1933** he wrote about **“dark matter”**. By this he meant invisible mass that adds to the pull. Today dark matter is one of the great puzzles of astronomy.

Together with **Walter Baade**, Zwicky suggested in 1934 that an extremely dense **neutron star** is left behind after a **supernova**, the explosion of a large star. Only decades later were such stars actually found. Zwicky also searched for supernovae himself. With his surveys of the sky he found **123 supernovae**, more than any other astronomer at the time.

In 1937, Zwicky predicted that whole **galaxies** can bend light like a **lens**. Their gravity focuses the light of objects that lie behind them. Such **gravitational lenses** were discovered later. Zwicky also developed a method for systematically finding new ideas: the **morphological box**. You break a problem down into features and combine their possible variations. The method is still used in engineering and design today.

gewusst: Zwicky lived in the USA for decades but remained a Swiss citizen.
The word “supernova” also goes back to Zwicky and Baade.

teile.einleitung: Hayabusa2 is a Japanese space probe that visited the asteroid Ryugu. It collected rock samples there and brought them back to Earth in 2020. Today it is on its way to another target.
wichtigste: Hayabusa2 is a space probe of the Japanese space agency JAXA.
It studied the asteroid Ryugu.
It released hopping rovers and the lander MASCOT.
To take samples, it touched down briefly on Ryugu twice.
The sample capsule landed in Australia in December 2020.
Amino acids and other organic compounds were found in the samples.

abschnitte.text: Hayabusa2 was launched from Japan in December 2014. It is built and controlled by the space agency **JAXA**. In 2018 it reached the asteroid **Ryugu**. It is just under a kilometre across and looks like a spinning top. Asteroids like Ryugu are very old. They show what material the solar system formed from.

Hayabusa2 brought small vehicles with it. On Ryugu the pull is so weak that wheels can hardly grip. So they were **hopping rovers** that moved along in small jumps. There was also the lander **MASCOT**, built by the German Aerospace Center **DLR** and the French space agency **CNES**. MASCOT studied the ground for a few hours and once hopped to a new spot.

The probe touched down briefly on Ryugu **twice** and each time picked up some material. For the second sample, it first created an **artificial crater**. To do this, it fired a **copper projectile** at the asteroid, speeded up by an explosive charge. This brought material from the inside to the surface. This material had been protected from sunlight and was hardly changed.

In **December 2020**, the sample capsule landed in the desert near **Woomera** in **Australia**. Inside were a few grams of rock and dust from Ryugu. Researchers found **amino acids** and other **organic compounds** in the samples. Amino acids are building blocks that living things use to build proteins. The probe itself flew on and is due to reach the small asteroid **1998 KY26** in **2031**.

gewusst: The name Ryugu means “dragon palace” and comes from a Japanese fairy tale.
In Japanese, Hayabusa means “peregrine falcon”. The earlier probe Hayabusa had already brought dust from an asteroid to Earth in 2010.

teile.einleitung: The tidal force arises because the Moon and the Sun do not pull equally strongly on all parts of the Earth. It deforms the seas into two tidal bulges and so creates low and high tide.
wichtigste: The tidal force arises from the different strengths of the pull of the Moon and the Sun.
The effect of the Sun is about half as strong as that of the Moon.
On most coasts there is high water about twice a day.
At new moon and full moon there are spring tides, and at half moon neap tides.
The difference in height between high water and low water is called the tidal range.
Because of the tides, the Moon moves about 3.8 cm further away from the Earth every year.

abschnitte.text: The Moon pulls on the Earth, but not equally strongly everywhere. On the side facing it, it pulls most strongly. There the water piles up into a **tidal bulge**. On the side facing away, the Moon pulls **more weakly than at the centre of the Earth**. The water there is, so to speak, left behind, and a second tidal bulge forms. The Earth turns beneath these two bulges. That is why on most coasts there is high water about **twice a day**.

The Sun also creates a tidal force. It is much heavier than the Moon, but also much further away. So its effect is only **about half as strong**. At **new moon** and **full moon**, the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line. Then the forces add up, and there is a **spring tide**. When the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth, at half moon, there is a weak **neap tide**.

Low and high tide shift by about **50 minutes** from day to day. The reason: the Moon moves on along its orbit around the Earth. So the Earth has to turn a little more than once before the same place is under the Moon again. The difference between high water and low water is called the **tidal range**. It depends greatly on the shape of the coast. In the **Bay of Fundy** in Canada it is up to about **16 metres**.

The tides act like a brake on the Earth's spin. As a result, the **days** are very slowly getting longer. At the same time, the Moon gains momentum and moves away. The distance grows by about **3.8 centimetres** every year. This has been measured with laser beams reflected by mirrors on the Moon. Astronauts set up these mirrors there.

gewusst: The tidal force can be used to generate electricity. In France, a tidal power station has been working at the mouth of the Rance since 1966.
Jupiter's tidal force kneads its moon Io so strongly that it is the most volcanically active place in the solar system.

teile.einleitung: A galaxy is a huge collection of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity. Our Sun belongs to the Milky Way galaxy, which consists of hundreds of billions of stars. According to current estimates, there are hundreds of billions of galaxies or more in the observable universe.
wichtigste: Galaxies are huge star systems held together by gravity.
Our home galaxy is the Milky Way.
The nearest large spiral galaxy is the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light years away.
From the southern hemisphere, you can see the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds with the naked eye.
The main types are spiral galaxies, elliptical galaxies and irregular galaxies.
Since the end of 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope has been observing very distant galaxies in infrared light.
There are hundreds of billions of galaxies or more in the observable universe.

abschnitte.text: A galaxy is an enormous island of stars in space. It contains millions to trillions of stars, plus gas, dust and a lot of **dark matter**. In the middle of many galaxies sits a huge **black hole**. The word galaxy comes from the Greek word for milk.

Our Sun is one of an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars in the **Milky Way**. It is a barred spiral galaxy with a diameter of over 100,000 light years. Our solar system lies in a spiral arm, far from the centre. On dark nights, for example in the Alps far from city lights, you can see the Milky Way as a bright band across the sky.

Edwin Hubble sorted galaxies by their shape. **Spiral galaxies** have glowing arms that wind around a centre. Elliptical galaxies look like blurry eggs and mostly contain old stars. Irregular galaxies have no clear shape, like the Magellanic Clouds.

The **Andromeda Galaxy** is the nearest large spiral galaxy and is about 2.5 million light years away. On clear autumn nights you can even see it with the naked eye as a faint misty patch. From the southern hemisphere you can make out the Large and Small **Magellanic Clouds**, two smaller companion galaxies of the Milky Way. In about 4 to 5 billion years, the Milky Way and Andromeda will probably collide and merge.

For a long time, galaxies were thought to be nebulae inside the Milky Way. Only in the 1920s did Edwin Hubble show that the Andromeda Nebula is a separate galaxy far outside it. The Hubble Space Telescope and, since the end of 2021, the **James Webb Space Telescope** photograph very distant galaxies. Because their light has been travelling for billions of years, we see them as they looked shortly after the Big Bang.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
A galaxy with glowing, winding arms.
The distance light travels in a year.
A group of many galaxies that belong together.

gewusst: The light from the Andromeda Galaxy that you see today set off about 2.5 million years ago, when there were no modern humans yet.
The Sun takes about 230 million years to go once around the centre of the Milky Way.
At the centre of the Milky Way sits the black hole Sagittarius A*, which has about four million times as much mass as the Sun.

teile.einleitung: The Kuiper Belt is a huge zone of small icy bodies right at the edge of our solar system. It lies outside the orbit of Neptune. The dwarf planet Pluto also belongs to it.
wichtigste: The Kuiper Belt lies outside Neptune's orbit, about 30 to 50 AU from the Sun.
It is named after the astronomer **Gerard Kuiper**.
The bodies there are made mainly of ice and rock.
Pluto is the best-known dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt.
In 1992, the first object in the Kuiper Belt apart from Pluto and Charon was discovered.
Many short-period comets come from the Kuiper Belt.

abschnitte.text: Beyond Neptune, the outermost planet, the **Kuiper Belt** begins. Its main part lies about 30 to 50 **AU** from the Sun. One AU, the **astronomical unit**, is the average distance between the Earth and the Sun, about 150 million kilometres. So the Kuiper Belt is very far away. It is reminiscent of the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, but much bigger.

The bodies in the Kuiper Belt are made mainly of **ice and rock**. Because it is so cold out there, even substances such as methane or nitrogen are frozen. Many of these bodies are leftovers from the time when the planets formed. They have hardly changed since then. That is why researchers are very interested in them: they are like building blocks from the childhood of the solar system.

The belt is named after the astronomer **Gerard Kuiper**, who had thought about such bodies. For a long time, only **Pluto** and its moon **Charon** were known there. Only in **1992** did astronomers discover another object. Since then, a great many have been found. Because there are so many similar bodies, Pluto has been considered a **dwarf planet** since 2006 and no longer a planet.

In 2015, the space probe **New Horizons** flew past Pluto and took the first detailed pictures. After that it travelled on into the Kuiper Belt. At the beginning of 2019 it visited the small object **Arrokoth**. In 2026 it was still the most distant object ever explored close up by a space probe. Arrokoth looks like two balls stuck together.

Sometimes a body from the Kuiper Belt is pushed out of its orbit by the gravity of the large planets. Then it can get into the inner solar system. As it approaches the Sun, some of its ice evaporates and it gets a glowing tail. This is how many **short-period comets** form, which return every few years.

gewusst: Arrokoth consists of two parts that once touched very gently and have stuck together ever since.
Sunlight takes several hours to reach the Kuiper Belt.

teile.einleitung: Rocky planets are planets with a solid surface made of rock. In our solar system there are four of them: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. They all lie in the inner part, close to the Sun.
wichtigste: The rocky planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
They lie in the inner solar system, close to the Sun.
The Earth is the largest rocky planet, and Venus is almost the same size.
Only on Earth are there seas of liquid water on the surface.
Mercury races around the Sun fastest.
On Venus, a day lasts longer than a year.

abschnitte.text: Rocky planets have a **core of iron**, a mantle of rock around it and a solid **crust** on the outside. You can land on them, unlike on the gas planets. All four lie in the **inner** solar system, close to the Sun. They are much smaller than Jupiter or Saturn. They are also called **terrestrial planets**.

**Mercury** is the smallest planet and lies closest to the Sun. It needs only **88 days** for one orbit, which makes it the fastest. Mercury has almost no atmosphere that could store heat. During the day it gets hotter than 400 degrees there. At night the temperature drops to **below minus 170 degrees**.

**Venus** is almost exactly the same size as the Earth. But it has a thick, poisonous atmosphere and is hotter than any other planet. Venus turns very slowly and **backwards**. That is why the Sun rises in the **west** there. One turn takes about 243 Earth days, while one orbit of the Sun takes only about 225. So on Venus a **day** is longer than a **year**.

The **Earth** is the largest rocky planet. It is the only planet with seas of **liquid water** on its surface and with life. **Mars** is about half as wide as the Earth. Its ground is full of iron oxide, in other words rust, which is why it looks red. On Mars stands **Olympus Mons**, the highest known volcano in the solar system.

gewusst: Olympus Mons on Mars is more than twice as high as Mount Everest.
It is hotter on Venus than on Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. The thick atmosphere traps the heat.

teile.einleitung: Nucleosynthesis is the name for the formation of atomic nuclei. Almost all the chemical elements that planets, plants and people are made of were formed in the Big Bang, in stars or in star explosions. That is why people also say that we are made of stardust.
wichtigste: Hydrogen, helium and some lithium formed shortly after the Big Bang.
Stars fuse light nuclei into heavier ones and gain energy from this.
Nickel-62 has the highest binding energy per nucleon; beyond it, fusion no longer releases energy.
Heavy elements form through neutron capture in the s-process and the r-process.
Lithium, beryllium and boron are formed to a large extent by cosmic rays.
The B²FH paper of 1957 founded the modern theory of how the elements form.

abschnitte.text: In the cores of stars, atomic nuclei fuse at enormous temperatures. First **hydrogen** becomes **helium**. Later, three helium nuclei fuse into **carbon**. In 1953, Fred Hoyle predicted that for this there must be an excited state of the carbon-12 nucleus at about 7.65 MeV; otherwise there would hardly be any carbon. The state was found in the laboratory shortly afterwards. Massive stars go further: in **carbon burning** above 500 million kelvin, mainly neon, sodium and magnesium are formed.

Every fusion releases energy as long as the nuclei become more tightly bound as a result. **Nickel-62** has the highest **binding energy per nucleon**, just ahead of iron-58 and iron-56. With such heavy nuclei, fusion no longer releases energy. That is why the chain of burning phases ends at iron. Elements heavier than iron have to form in other ways.

Heavy elements form mainly through **neutron capture**. In the **s-process** (slow), atomic nuclei in stars on the **asymptotic giant branch** capture neutrons one after another. Between two captures, an unstable nucleus usually has time to decay. In the **r-process** (rapid), a great many neutrons are captured in a short time. This needs extremely neutron-rich places, for example **merging neutron stars**.

In a **supernova**, a lot of new material is flung into space. The radioactive **nickel-56** decays via cobalt-56 into stable iron-56. The energy released heats the cloud of debris and determines how brightly it shines over weeks and months. The rare light elements **lithium**, **beryllium** and **boron**, on the other hand, form to a large extent through **spallation**: fast particles of cosmic rays smash carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nuclei.

In 1952, Paul Merrill discovered the element **technetium** in the spectra of red giants. Technetium has no long-lived isotopes; even the longest-lived ones have half-lives of only about 4 million years. So it must have formed in the star itself. In 1957, the **B²FH paper** by Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle appeared. In it they described the most important processes by which elements form in stars.

gewusst: The carbon in our bodies and the oxygen we breathe were once formed inside stars.
In the merger of two neutron stars observed in 2017, clues were found that heavy elements were formed.

teile.einleitung: Kepler's laws describe how planets move around the Sun. Johannes Kepler found them at the beginning of the 17th century, and they still apply today to moons, satellites and exoplanets too.
wichtigste: Planets move in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.
The line between the Sun and a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.
The eccentricity tells you how much an ellipse differs from a circle.
Kepler used the observations of Tycho Brahe.
The first two laws appeared in 1609 in the “Astronomia nova”.

abschnitte.text: Planets do not move in perfect circles but in **ellipses**. An ellipse is a stretched circle with two **foci**, and the Sun is at one of them. How much an ellipse is stretched is given by its **eccentricity**. A circle has an eccentricity of 0. The Earth's orbit has only about 0.017, so it is almost circular.

abschnitte.titel: Second law: the law of areas
abschnitte.text: Imagine a line from the Sun to the planet. This line sweeps out equal areas in equal times. This is called the **law of areas**. It follows that a planet moves faster close to the Sun and more slowly far away. That is why the Earth is fastest in January, when it is closest to the Sun.

The third law links the **orbital period** T with the **semi-major axis** a. If you measure T in years and a in **astronomical units** (AU), then for the Sun's planets T² = a³. A body with a equal to 9 AU has T² = 729, so T = 27 years. That is why more distant planets take much longer for one orbit.

In 1594, Johannes Kepler became a maths teacher at the Protestant school in **Graz**. Later he worked in **Prague** with the very precise measurements of the Danish astronomer **Tycho Brahe**. From them, after years of calculation, he worked out his laws. He published the first two in 1609 in the “Astronomia nova” and the third in 1619 in “Harmonices mundi”. Kepler died in **Regensburg** in November 1630.

Kepler described **how** planets move, but could not yet say for sure **why**. About 70 years later, **Isaac Newton** showed that the laws follow from his **theory of gravitation**. Today they are used to calculate the orbits of satellites, space probes and planets around distant stars.

gewusst: The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January, in the middle of winter in the northern hemisphere.
Kepler first looked for circular orbits and worked on the orbit of Mars for years before he found the ellipse.

teile.einleitung: The lunar module was the spacecraft in which astronauts in the Apollo programme landed on the Moon. Each time it carried two people down to the surface and back up into orbit.
wichtigste: The Apollo 11 lunar module was called “Eagle”.
Two astronauts at a time flew down to the Moon in the lunar module.
It stood on four landing legs with round pads as feet.
The lower part stayed on the Moon and served as a launch pad for the return.
From 1969 to 1972, six lunar modules landed, and twelve people in total walked on the Moon.
On Apollo 13, the lunar module saved the lives of the three astronauts.

abschnitte.text: On 20 July 1969, the lunar module **Eagle** of **Apollo 11** landed in the Sea of Tranquillity. On board were Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. Their colleague Michael Collins stayed in orbit around the Moon in the spacecraft **Columbia**. In English the craft was called the **Lunar Module**. It was built by an American aircraft company.

The lunar module consisted of two parts. The **lower part**, the descent stage, had the landing engine and the **four landing legs** with round pads. This stopped the lunar module from sinking into the Moon dust. The **upper part**, the ascent stage, was the cabin for the astronauts. For the return, the lower part served as a **launch pad** and stayed on the Moon. Only the upper part flew back to the spacecraft.

Every kilogram was precious. That is why the lunar module was built very light, and its walls were very thin in some places. To save weight, there were **no seats**: the astronauts **stood** and were held in place with straps. The lunar module also had **no heat shield** and could not land on Earth. The astronauts returned to Earth in a different capsule.

In 1970, an **oxygen tank** exploded on **Apollo 13** on the way to the Moon. The landing had to be called off. The three astronauts moved into the lunar module and used it as a **lifeboat**. They went around the Moon and returned safely to Earth.

The lower parts of all six lunar modules that landed are still standing on the Moon today. A **plaque** is attached to the leg of the Apollo 11 lunar module. On it are the words “We came in peace for all mankind”, in other words the astronauts came peacefully on behalf of all humanity.

gewusst: Shortly before the first landing, only a little fuel was left, because Armstrong had to steer clear of a field of large rocks.
Space probes have photographed the lunar module parts left behind from orbit around the Moon.

teile.einleitung: New Horizons is a NASA space probe that was the first to explore the dwarf planet Pluto close up. After that it flew on into the Kuiper Belt and visited the distant object Arrokoth.
wichtigste: New Horizons was launched in January 2006 on an Atlas V rocket.
At about 16 km/s, it was faster at launch than any probe before it.
In February 2007 it picked up speed at Jupiter.
In July 2015 it flew past Pluto and its large moon Charon.
On 1 January 2019 it visited Arrokoth in the Kuiper Belt.
On board is some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered Pluto.

abschnitte.text: New Horizons was launched in **January 2006**. An **Atlas V rocket** with an extra stage accelerated the light probe to about **16.26 kilometres per second**. That was a record at launch. It passed the Moon's orbit after only about nine hours. In **February 2007** it flew close past **Jupiter**. This **swing-by** increased its speed by about 4 kilometres per second and shortened the journey by about three years.

At the time of the launch, **Pluto** was still considered a planet. In August 2006, the **International Astronomical Union** agreed on a new definition. Pluto does not meet the condition of having cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. Since then it has been called a **dwarf planet**. So the probe set off for a planet and arrived at a dwarf planet.

In **July 2015**, New Horizons flew past Pluto. At that time Pluto was about 4.9 billion kilometres away, and the radio signals took about **4.5 hours** to reach the Earth. The pictures showed a heart-shaped plain, **Sputnik Planitia**. It is filled with **nitrogen ice**, which is divided into cells. Because no craters can be seen there, the surface is geologically young. Pluto's largest moon, **Charon**, is about half Pluto's diameter. Their common centre of gravity lies outside Pluto, which is why they are called a **double system**.

On **1 January 2019**, the probe visited **Arrokoth** in the **Kuiper Belt**, which used to be called 2014 MU69. It is the most distant object ever explored close up by a probe. Arrokoth consists of two flat parts that touched gently and merged. This is called a **contact binary**. It suggests a calm formation in the early solar system.

**Clyde Tombaugh** discovered Pluto in **1930**. He died in 1997, before the probe was launched. A small container with some of his **ashes** is flying through space with New Horizons. So the man who discovered Pluto did travel to his celestial body after all.

gewusst: Because sunlight at Pluto is very weak, New Horizons gets its electricity from a radioisotope battery instead of solar panels.
New Horizons keeps flying further out and will one day leave the solar system.

teile.einleitung: Olympus Mons is a huge volcano on Mars. It is the highest known volcano in the whole solar system. Its base is so wide that the whole of Switzerland would fit on it comfortably.
wichtigste: Olympus Mons is the highest known volcano in the solar system.
It rises about 22 kilometres high, about two and a half times as high as Mount Everest.
Its base is almost 600 kilometres wide.
On the summit is a collapse crater up to 90 kilometres wide.
It is named after Mount Olympus in Greece.
In 1971, the Mariner 9 probe showed that it is a volcano.

abschnitte.text: **Olympus Mons** is a **shield volcano**. This is a volcano with gently rising slopes, similar to the volcanoes on Hawaii. It rises about **22 kilometres** high. That is about two and a half times as high as **Mount Everest**. No other known volcano in the solar system is higher. It lies in a region of Mars where there are several large volcanoes.

The base of the volcano is almost **600 kilometres** wide. Switzerland measures only about **350 kilometres** from west to east. So Olympus Mons would cover the whole country and much more. Because the slopes are so gentle, you would hardly notice on the mountain itself that you were standing on a volcano. At its edge it drops away in many places with steep **cliffs** several kilometres high.

On top of the volcano lies a huge **collapse crater**, a so-called **caldera**. It is up to **90 kilometres** wide. A caldera forms when a chamber of magma under the volcano empties and the ground above it sinks. On Olympus Mons you can see several such sunken hollows lying inside each other.

On **Mars**, **gravity** is weaker than on Earth. That is why a great deal of lava could pile up there into a huge mountain without it sinking under its own weight. In addition, the crust of Mars does not move in plates as on Earth. So the lava kept flowing out at the same place for a very long time, and the mountain kept growing.

Even with telescopes, a bright spot could be seen on Mars at this place. Only the space probe **Mariner 9**, which orbited Mars in **1971**, showed with its pictures that it is an enormous volcano. It gets its name from **Mount Olympus**, a mountain in Greece. According to the old legends, the Greek gods lived there.

gewusst: Olympus Mons is so high that its summit is often above the dust storms of Mars.
Because the mountain is so wide, its summit lies beyond the horizon when seen from a point at its base.

teile.einleitung: A telescope makes things that are far away look closer. In German there are two words for it, “Fernrohr” and “Teleskop”. With telescopes, people have explored the sky and discovered many new things.
wichtigste: A telescope collects light and magnifies distant things.
In German, another word for “Fernrohr” is “Teleskop”.
A simple telescope has curved pieces of glass, the lenses.
In 1609, Galileo Galilei was one of the first to point a telescope at the sky.
Binoculars are a telescope for both eyes.
Never look at the Sun through a telescope without a protective filter.
The Hubble Space Telescope has been orbiting the Earth since 1990.

abschnitte.text: A telescope **collects light** and **magnifies** the image. This lets you see distant things bigger and more clearly. In German, another word for “Fernrohr” is **“Teleskop”**. It comes from Greek and means “looking into the distance”. A **microscope**, on the other hand, magnifies very small things that are close by.

A simple telescope has curved pieces of glass, the **lenses**. They focus the light and magnify the image. At the front is the **objective**, and at the back by the eye is the **eyepiece**. Large telescopes for astronomy often use curved **mirrors** instead of lenses. Such reflecting telescopes can be built very large.

The first telescopes were built in the Netherlands shortly after 1600. **Galileo Galilei** heard about this and built one himself in 1609. He was one of the first to point it at the **sky**. He discovered **craters** on the Moon and four **moons** around Jupiter. Today, even with a small telescope you can see many round craters on the Moon. But there are no houses, trees or rivers there.

**Binoculars**, in Swiss German often called a **“Feldstecher”**, consist of two small telescopes side by side. So you look with **both eyes** at the same time. Binoculars are handy and good for trips to the mountains or for watching birds. You can also see the moons of Jupiter as small dots with them.

You must **never** look at the **Sun** through a telescope **without a protective filter**. The telescope focuses the very bright sunlight, which can seriously injure your eyes at once. A very special telescope is the **Hubble Space Telescope**. It was launched into space in 1990 and has been orbiting the Earth ever since. Because it flies above the atmosphere, it takes very sharp pictures.

gewusst: With his telescope, Galileo saw that the Milky Way consists of countless stars.
Many observatories in Switzerland invite people to public observing evenings.

teile.einleitung: An impact crater forms when a large lump of rock from space crashes into a planet or moon. You can see countless such craters on the Moon, but only a few are well preserved on Earth.
wichtigste: On impact, a lot of rock is thrown out, leaving a crater behind.
Craters are usually round and much bigger than the lump of rock.
Around the crater is a raised crater rim, and large craters often have a central peak.
On Earth, wind, water and plants wear away old craters.
The Nördlinger Ries in Bavaria formed around 15 million years ago.
Mercury is full of craters, almost like our Moon.

abschnitte.text: When a large lump of rock from space hits the ground at high speed, an enormous amount of energy is released. There is a huge explosion, and a lot of rock is thrown out. What remains is a large hole, an **impact crater**. Because so much force is released, the crater is **much bigger** than the lump itself, often about ten to twenty times. Even if the lump hits at an angle, the crater is usually **round**.

On impact, rock is pushed outwards. This creates a raised **crater rim** all around the crater. In large impacts, the ground in the middle springs back, a bit like water when a drop falls into it. A hill forms there, which is called a **central peak**. Many large craters on the Moon have a central peak like this.

abschnitte.titel: Why the Earth has few craters
abschnitte.text: The Earth has been hit many times too. But **rain, rivers, wind and plants** are constantly changing its surface. That is why old craters disappear over time. In addition, smaller lumps burn up in the **atmosphere** before they reach the ground. The Moon and the planet **Mercury** have almost no atmosphere and no weather. So their many craters are preserved for a very long time, and Mercury looks almost like our Moon.

A well-known impact crater lies in our neighbouring country **Germany**: the **Nördlinger Ries** in **Bavaria**. The impact happened around **15 million years ago**. Today the town of **Nördlingen** lies in the middle of the crater. Many people live there, and you can see the crater rim as a ring of hills in the landscape. The crater is about 25 kilometres wide.

gewusst: In Nördlingen there is a church built from rock that was formed during the impact.
The Apollo astronauts practised recognising rock from impacts in the Nördlinger Ries.

teile.einleitung: Cassiopeia is a constellation in the northern sky that is easy to recognise. Its five bright stars form a large W, which depending on its position can also look like an M.
wichtigste: Five bright stars form the W of Cassiopeia.
When the W is upside down, it looks like an M.
Cassiopeia is in the northern sky, close to the Pole Star.
In our part of the world it never sets and can be seen all year round.
It lies opposite the Plough.
In Greek legend, Cassiopeia was a queen.

abschnitte.text: Cassiopeia consists of five bright stars. Together they form a clear **W**. You need exactly five points for a W, which is why the constellation is so easy to remember. During the night, Cassiopeia turns around the **Pole Star**. When the W is upside down, it looks like an **M**.

Cassiopeia is in the **northern sky**, not far from the Pole Star. On the other side of the Pole Star lies the **Plough**. The two are opposite each other: when one is high in the sky, the other is low. Because Cassiopeia is close to the **north celestial pole**, it never sets in Switzerland. So you can see it on every clear night of the year.

abschnitte.titel: In the middle of the Milky Way
abschnitte.text: Cassiopeia lies in the middle of the bright band of light of the **Milky Way**. On dark nights, for example in the mountains, you can see a great many faint stars there. With binoculars you can discover even more, such as small **star clusters**. In towns you usually only see the five bright stars because of the lights.

In Greek legend, Cassiopeia was a **queen**. She was the mother of the princess **Andromeda**. According to the legend, she boasted about her beauty, which angered the sea gods. Her husband **Cepheus** and her daughter Andromeda are also constellations nearby.

gewusst: In 1572, a new, very bright star suddenly lit up in Cassiopeia; it was a supernova, which Tycho Brahe observed.
Very close to Cassiopeia lies the Andromeda Galaxy, which you can even see without binoculars on dark nights.

teile.einleitung: Juno is a NASA space probe that has been orbiting the giant planet Jupiter since 2016. It studies its interior, its clouds, its magnetic field and also some of its moons.
wichtigste: Juno was launched on 5 August 2011 and reached Jupiter on 4 July 2016.
Juno is the first Jupiter probe to work on solar power alone.
Juno flies in a highly elliptical polar orbit.
A titanium box protects the electronics from radiation.
One orbit takes about 53 days instead of the planned 14.
At the end of 2023 and the beginning of 2024, Juno flew close past the volcanic moon Io.

abschnitte.text: In Roman mythology, **Juno** is the wife of Jupiter, the father of the gods. According to the legend, Jupiter veiled himself in clouds, but Juno could see through them. In the same way, the probe is meant to look beneath the planet's cloud cover. Juno was launched on 5 August 2011. On 4 July 2016, the American national holiday, it went into orbit around Jupiter.

Earlier Jupiter probes such as **Galileo** got their electricity from **radioisotope batteries**. Juno is the first probe at Jupiter to work on **solar power** alone. Because sunlight there is very weak, it has three large **solar wings**. It also spins slowly on its axis, which keeps it stable.

Jupiter is surrounded by strong **radiation belts**. Juno flies in a highly **elliptical polar orbit** over the poles. This brings it very close above the clouds but avoids the strongest parts of the radiation belts. The sensitive electronics sit in a **titanium box** about one centimetre thick. It shields them from the high-energy particles.

Originally one orbit was to last only 14 days. But before the necessary manoeuvre in 2016, **helium valves** in the main engine did not work properly. So NASA decided not to shorten the orbital period. Since then, one orbit has taken about 53 days. Even so, the mission has been very successful and has been extended several times.

Juno measured Jupiter's gravity very precisely. The data point to a large, **diluted core** in which heavy elements are mixed with hydrogen. A small, compact rocky core had been expected. Juno also delivered spectacular pictures of **storms** at the poles. In December 2023 and February 2024, Juno flew past the volcanic moon **Io** at a height of about 1,500 kilometres.

gewusst: Juno carries three small Lego figures: Galileo Galilei, Jupiter and Juno.
With its solar wings, Juno is wider than a basketball court.

teile.einleitung: The largest planet in our solar system is Jupiter. It is a huge gas planet and heavier than all the other planets put together. In the night sky it often shines more brightly than any star.
wichtigste: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
It is about 11 times wider than the Earth; over 1,000 Earths would fit inside it.
Jupiter is heavier than all the other planets put together.
It is named after the chief Roman god.
Galileo Galilei discovered its four largest moons in 1610.
The second largest planet is Saturn.

abschnitte.text: Jupiter is about **11 times wider** than the Earth. **Over 1,000 Earths** would fit inside it. It is more than twice as heavy as all the other planets **put together**. Jupiter is a **gas planet** made of hydrogen and helium and has no solid ground. The second largest planet is **Saturn**. Jupiter spins very fast: a day there lasts not even ten hours.

Jupiter is named after the **chief Roman god**. The Greeks called this god Zeus. The name fits, because Jupiter is the king among the planets. On its surface you can see coloured bands of cloud. There is also the **Great Red Spot**, a storm that is bigger than the Earth.

In **1610**, **Galileo Galilei** pointed a telescope at Jupiter. He discovered four moons: **Io**, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. They are called the **Galilean moons**. On **Io** there are a particularly large number of active **volcanoes**. **Ganymede** is the largest moon in the solar system. Altogether, almost a hundred moons of Jupiter are known today.

Several space probes have visited Jupiter. NASA's **Juno** probe arrived at Jupiter in **2016**. It orbits the planet and explores its interior, its magnetic field and its auroras. The European probe **JUICE** has been on its way to Jupiter and its icy moons since 2023. With the naked eye you can often see Jupiter from Switzerland as a bright dot in the sky.

gewusst: Even with good binoculars you can make out the four Galilean moons as small points of light next to Jupiter.
Jupiter also has rings, but they are so dark and thin that they were only discovered in 1979 by the Voyager 1 probe.

teile.einleitung: On the Moon you feel much lighter than on Earth. You weigh only about a sixth there. But your body stays exactly the same; only the pull is weaker.
wichtigste: On the Moon you feel about a sixth as heavy as on Earth.
The Moon pulls less strongly because it is much smaller and lighter than the Earth.
A child of 30 kg would see about 5 kg on a scale on the Moon.
Your body stays the same; you do not get thinner.
You could jump about 6 times as high as on Earth.
A ball falls to the ground more slowly on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: Every celestial body pulls things towards it. This force is called **gravity** or the force of attraction. The bigger and heavier a celestial body is, the more strongly it pulls. The **Moon** is much smaller and lighter than the Earth. So its pull is only about **a sixth** as strong. That is why you feel much lighter there.

A bathroom scale measures how strongly you are pulled downwards. A child who weighs **30 kg** on Earth would see only about **5 kg** on the Moon. But the body has not changed. It still has the same number of bones and muscles and the same amount of water. So you do **not get thinner**. In physics, a distinction is therefore made between **mass**, which stays the same, and **weight**, the force that changes.

Between 1969 and 1972, twelve **astronauts** were on the Moon. Their spacesuits were heavy and stiff. Even so, they often moved forwards in **hops**, because in the weak pull this was easier than normal walking. Without a suit, a person on the Moon could jump about **6 times as high** as on Earth.

If you let go of a ball on the Moon, it falls to the ground **more slowly** than on Earth. This is because it is accelerated less strongly. On the Moon there is also no air to slow things down. That is why a hammer and a feather fall at exactly the same speed there. In 1971, an astronaut on the **Apollo 15** mission showed this in front of a running camera.

gewusst: On Jupiter you would feel more than twice as heavy as on Earth, if you could stand there.
The astronauts' footprints can probably still be seen on the Moon today, because there is no wind there to blow them away.

teile.einleitung: The surface of Mars is a red, cold and dusty desert. There are huge volcanoes, deep basins and polar caps of ice. Space probes and rovers have explored it closely over the last few decades.
wichtigste: The north of Mars is lower and smoother than the south.
The Martian crust consists mostly of **basalt**, a volcanic rock.
**Hellas Planitia** is a huge impact basin.
In the volcanic region of **Tharsis**, three mighty shield volcanoes stand in a row.
On average it is about minus 60 degrees on Mars.
The air pressure is less than 1 per cent of the air pressure on Earth.

abschnitte.text: Mars has two very different halves. The **north** is **lower and smoother**, with wide plains and few craters. The **south** lies higher and is covered with many craters. The crust consists mostly of **basalt**, a dark volcanic rock. The red colour comes from **iron oxide** in the dust, in other words from rust.

In the **Tharsis** region, three mighty **shield volcanoes** stand in a row. Very close by rises **Olympus Mons**, the highest known volcano in the whole solar system. It is about two and a half times as high as Mount Everest. Next to Tharsis, the enormous canyon system **Valles Marineris** stretches across a large part of the planet.

**Hellas Planitia** is a huge **impact basin** in the southern hemisphere. It formed when a large celestial body crashed into Mars a very long time ago. In the north lies the large plain of **Utopia Planitia**. The probe **Viking 2** landed there in **1976**. It took pictures and studied the ground, and on some mornings even frost could be seen.

On Mars it is on average **about minus 60 degrees**. The atmosphere is very thin: the air pressure is **less than 1 per cent** of the pressure on Earth. It consists mainly of carbon dioxide. At both poles there are **polar caps** of water ice. In the Martian winter, **frozen carbon dioxide**, in other words dry ice, also settles on them.
