On Mars, small whirlwinds swirl dust up into the air. They are called **dust devils**. They leave dark tracks on the surface. Sometimes large **dust storms** also form, which can cover the whole planet. This is a problem for rovers with solar panels, because dust can cover their panels.

gewusst: On Mars, dust devils have already blown rovers' solar panels clean and so given them more power.
A day on Mars lasts only about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The geocentric model puts the Earth at the centre of the universe. According to this idea, the Sun, Moon, planets and stars all circle the Earth. For almost 2,000 years, most scholars believed in it.
wichtigste: In the geocentric model, the Earth is at the centre of the universe.
The Greek word “ge” means earth.
The philosopher Aristotle held this view and shaped people's thinking for a long time.
People thought the celestial bodies were attached to transparent spherical shells.
The Moon was closest to the Earth, and the fixed stars formed the outermost shell.
The looping movement of the planets was hard to explain.

abschnitte.text: The term **geocentric** comes from Greek. “Ge” means **earth**, and “centre” means middle point. If you stand on the ground, you do not notice that the Earth is moving. The **Sun** seems to travel across the sky every day, and so do the Moon and the stars. So it seemed natural to think that the Earth rests firmly in the middle.

The Greek philosopher **Aristotle** lived in the 4th century BC. He held the geocentric view, and his teachings shaped thinking until the Middle Ages. In the 2nd century AD, the scholar **Ptolemy** from Alexandria described the model in great detail. With his tables, the positions of the planets could be calculated in advance. The Church also adopted this idea.

People imagined that the celestial bodies were attached to **transparent spherical shells**. These shells turned around the Earth. The closest was the **Moon**, followed by Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. The outermost shell carried the **fixed stars**. They are called that because their positions relative to each other do not change.

Some planets, such as Mars, sometimes move backwards and trace a **loop** in the sky. This **retrograde motion** did not fit with simple circles around the Earth. So Ptolemy invented extra small circles, the **epicycles**. This made the model very complicated. In the 16th century, **Nicolaus Copernicus** suggested putting the Sun in the middle and explained the loops much more simply.

gewusst: Even in ancient times, the Greek Aristarchus of Samos suspected that the Earth goes around the Sun, but he found hardly any followers.
We still say “the Sun rises” today, even though it is really the Earth that turns.

teile.einleitung: The Plough is one of the best-known star patterns in the northern sky. It consists of seven bright stars and helps you find the Pole Star.
wichtigste: The Plough consists of 7 bright stars.
It belongs to the larger constellation of the Great Bear.
4 stars form the box, and 3 stars form the curved handle.
In Switzerland you can see it all year round on every clear night.
You find it in the north.
If you extend the line of the back stars of the box, you reach the Pole Star.

abschnitte.text: The Plough consists of **7 bright stars**. **4 stars** form a rectangle, the **box**. The other **3 stars** form a curved arc, the **handle**. In German it is called the “Great Wagon”, because together they look like an old cart with a shaft. The Plough is actually not a constellation of its own. It is the brightest part of the larger constellation of the **Great Bear**.

abschnitte.titel: The way to the Pole Star
abschnitte.text: The Plough helps you find the **Pole Star**. You take the two back stars of the box, the side opposite the handle. You **extend** the line joining them upwards, about five times as far. That is where the Pole Star is. It points almost exactly **north**. In the past this helped sailors and walkers find their way.

In Switzerland, the Plough never sets. So you can see it **all year round** on every clear night. It is in the **northern sky**. During a night it **turns around the Pole Star**, because the Earth turns. In spring it is high overhead in the evening, and in autumn low above the horizon.

The middle star of the handle is called **Mizar**. Very close to it there is a fainter little star called **Alcor**. In German it is also called the “little rider”. If you can see the two separately, you have good eyes. In the past this was considered a simple eye test. With binoculars you can easily make them out.

gewusst: In North America the Plough is called the “Big Dipper”, which means a large ladle.
The stars of the Plough are at different distances from us. They only look like a pattern from the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's rotation is the spinning of the Earth on its own axis. In about 24 hours it turns all the way round once, and this creates day and night. Even though at the equator we travel along at over 1,600 kilometres per hour, we feel nothing of it.
wichtigste: The Earth spins once on its axis in about 24 hours.
It turns 15 degrees every hour.
It turns from west to east, which is why the Sun rises in the east.
The Earth's rotation creates day and night.
A place on the equator moves at about 1,670 km/h.
Measured against the distant stars, one rotation takes about 23 hours and 56 minutes.
In 1851, Léon Foucault made the Earth's rotation visible with a pendulum in Paris.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns around an imaginary line, the **Earth's axis**, which runs through the North and South Poles. One full turn of 360 degrees takes about 24 hours. If you divide 360 degrees by 24 hours, you get 15 degrees per hour. That is why neighbouring **time zones** usually differ by one hour.

The Earth turns from west to east. That is why the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west, although in reality it is we who are moving. The side that is facing the Sun has **day**, and the side facing away has night. The stars also seem to move across the sky at night, because the Earth is turning beneath them.

Measured against the distant stars, the Earth takes about 23 hours and 56 minutes for one rotation; this is called a **sidereal day**. It takes about 4 minutes longer until the Sun is back in the same place, because meanwhile the Earth has moved on along its orbit. This **solar day** of 24 hours is our normal day. Because the Moon slows the Earth down through the tides, the days are very slowly getting longer.

At the equator, a place covers about 40,000 kilometres in one rotation, which gives about 1,670 km/h. In Switzerland the distance is shorter, so here it is only about 1,100 km/h. At the poles you just turn on the spot. We do not feel the movement because it is very even and the air turns with us.

In 1851, the French physicist Léon Foucault hung a heavy ball on a 67 metre long rope in the **Panthéon** in Paris. Over the hours, the plane in which the pendulum swung slowly turned, although nobody touched it. In reality the Earth was turning beneath the pendulum. You can marvel at this **Foucault pendulum** in many museums today, for example in Swiss universities and science museums.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line through the North and South Poles, around which the Earth turns.
The time for one rotation of the Earth measured against the distant stars.
An area on Earth where the same time of day applies.
A long pendulum that makes the Earth's rotation visible.

gewusst: At the time of the last dinosaurs, a day was about half an hour shorter than today.
The Earth's rotation deflects winds, which is why large hurricanes in the northern hemisphere turn anticlockwise.
Because the Earth's rotation is not quite even, leap seconds have been added several times since 1972.

teile.einleitung: In space you cannot measure distances with a tape measure. That is why astronomers use many methods that build on each other like the rungs of a ladder: the cosmic distance ladder.
wichtigste: Each method of the ladder is calibrated with the one before.
In the solar system, radar signals give precise distances from their travel time.
Nearby stars are measured with parallax.
Standard candles such as Cepheids and supernovae reach much further.
Errors in the lower rungs are carried up the ladder.
For the most distant galaxies, redshift and a cosmological model are used.

abschnitte.text: No single method works for all distances. Methods for nearby objects are precise but do not reach far. That is why each method is **calibrated** with the one before, in other words set precisely using known values. This creates a chain from **rung to rung**. The disadvantage: each step takes on the uncertainties of the one before, so a small error at the bottom has an effect all the way to the top.

In the **solar system**, **radar signals** are sent to Venus and other bodies. The travel time of the signals gives precise distances and from them the **astronomical unit**, the average distance between the Earth and the Sun. For nearby stars, **parallax** is used: because the Earth circles the Sun, a nearby star seems to shift by a tiny amount over the course of the year. From this angle the distance is calculated.

In **main sequence fitting**, the stars of a cluster in the **colour-magnitude diagram** are compared with a known cluster. The shift in brightness needed gives the distance. With **spectroscopic parallax**, a star's true luminosity is worked out from its spectrum. Together with its apparent brightness, this gives the distance; despite the name, no angle is measured.

**Standard candles** are objects with a known luminosity, such as **Cepheids** or **type Ia supernovae**. For spiral galaxies, the **Tully-Fisher relation** is used: spiral galaxies that rotate faster are more luminous. The rotation is measured using the 21 centimetre line of hydrogen. For **elliptical galaxies**, the **Faber-Jackson relation** applies: the greater the spread of the stars' speeds, the more luminous the galaxy.

For the most distant objects, there are no more standard candles that can be measured directly. Their **redshift** is measured, in other words how much their light has been shifted to longer waves. Using a model of the expansion of the universe, this is converted into a distance. The accuracy of the whole ladder also affects the value of the **Hubble constant**.

gewusst: ESA's Gaia satellite has measured the parallaxes of over a billion stars.
A parsec is the distance at which the parallax is exactly one arcsecond, which is about 3.26 light years.

teile.einleitung: The cosmic background radiation is the oldest light in the universe. It comes from the time shortly after the Big Bang and today fills the whole sky as faint microwave radiation.
wichtigste: The background radiation has an almost perfect black body spectrum.
Today its peak lies in the microwave range.
When it was released, it was about 3,000 kelvin hot.
The temperature differences are only about 1 in 100,000.
Alpher and Herman predicted it in 1948.
John Mather and George Smoot received the Nobel Prize in 2006 for measurements with COBE.

abschnitte.text: In the young universe, everything was so hot that electrons and atomic nuclei were separate. The **photons**, the particles of light, kept bouncing off free electrons. Below about **3,000 kelvin**, electrons and nuclei joined to form neutral atoms. From then on, light could travel freely. This layer is called the **surface of last scattering**.

Since then the universe has expanded greatly, and the radiation has cooled down a great deal. Today it has a temperature of only a few kelvin, about 2.7 kelvin. Its peak is at wavelengths around one millimetre, in the **microwave range**. That is why it is also called the **cosmic microwave background**.

In 1948, **Ralph Alpher** and **Robert Herman** predicted leftover radiation of about 5 kelvin. They had calculated how the elements formed in the early universe. But their prediction was almost forgotten. The discovery of the radiation was strong evidence for the **Big Bang theory**. The **steady state theory** of a universe that always looks the same could hardly explain it and lost support.

In 1989, NASA's **COBE** satellite was launched. Its instrument FIRAS showed that the radiation has an almost perfect **black body spectrum**; the measured points lay exactly on the ideal curve. COBE also found tiny **temperature differences**. For this, **John Mather** and **George Smoot** received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2006. Later satellites such as WMAP and Planck measured the radiation even more precisely.

The temperature varies by only a few tens of millionths of a kelvin, about **1 in 100,000**. These **anisotropies** show tiny differences in density in the young universe, from which galaxies later grew. There is also a bigger difference, the **dipole anisotropy**. It comes from our own movement: because of the **Doppler effect**, the radiation seems a little warmer in the direction we are moving. The Sun is moving at about 370 kilometres per second relative to the background radiation.

gewusst: On old televisions, a small part of the noise on empty channels came from the background radiation.
The radiation was discovered more or less by chance in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1978.

teile.einleitung: In space there is icy cold and burning heat, often very close together. It depends on whether the Sun is shining on something or not. Because there is no air in space, the heat is not evened out.
wichtigste: In empty space far from stars it is about minus 270 degrees.
The lowest possible temperature is called **absolute zero**.
On the Moon it gets hotter than 100 degrees during the day and far below minus 100 degrees at night.
The Moon has no air to even out the heat.
An object in direct sunlight gets very hot in space.
The James Webb Telescope has a huge sunshield so that it stays cold.

abschnitte.text: Far away from all stars, space is very cold: about **minus 270 degrees**. It cannot get much colder. The lowest temperature there can be is called **absolute zero**. It is minus 273.15 degrees. There the smallest particles of matter would hardly move at all. So empty space is only just under three degrees warmer than this point.

abschnitte.titel: Heat and cold on the Moon
abschnitte.text: On the **Moon** the differences are huge. During the day, when the Sun shines, the ground gets **hotter than 100 degrees**. At night it cools down to **far below minus 100 degrees**. The reason: the Moon has **no air**. On Earth, the atmosphere acts like a blanket that stores heat and spreads it around. In deep craters at the Moon's poles, where the Sun never reaches, there is even water in the form of **ice**.

In space it makes a big difference whether the Sun is shining on an object. In direct sunlight it gets **very hot**, but in the shade it is ice cold. That is why space stations and satellites need good protection. Shiny foils reflect the sunlight, and special systems carry away extra heat. The astronauts' spacesuits also protect them from heat and cold.

The **James Webb** space telescope observes mainly **infrared light**, in other words heat radiation. If the telescope itself were warm, it would spoil its own pictures. That is why it has a huge **sunshield** made of several thin layers, about the size of a tennis court. It keeps out the light and heat of the Sun, Earth and Moon. This keeps the side with the mirrors far below minus 200 degrees.

The further a planet is from the Sun, the less heat it gets. Right out at **Neptune** it is **icy cold**, about minus 200 degrees high up in its atmosphere. From there the Sun only looks like a very bright star. The moons and dwarf planets in this region are also made largely of ice.

gewusst: Water on the Moon lies as ice in craters that no ray of sunlight has reached for billions of years.
The James Webb sunshield was unfolded in space like an umbrella.

teile.einleitung: A meteorite is a lump from space that has flown through the atmosphere and landed on the ground. Meteorites are often billions of years old and tell us a lot about how our solar system formed. Many have been found in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: A meteorite is a body from space that falls all the way to the ground.
The flash of light in the sky is called a meteor or shooting star.
As long as the lump is still flying in space, it is called a meteoroid.
The main types are stony meteorites, iron meteorites and stony-iron meteorites.
Iron meteorites consist mainly of iron and nickel.
Every year in August, the shooting stars of the Perseids are easy to see.
Many pieces of the Twannberg iron meteorite have been found in the canton of Bern.

abschnitte.text: Countless lumps of rock and metal fly around in space; they are called **meteoroids**. If one enters the Earth's atmosphere, it gets so hot from the friction of the air that it glows brightly. This trail of light is called a **meteor** or shooting star. Most lumps burn up completely. If a remnant reaches the ground, it is called a **meteorite**.

Many shooting stars come from dust that comets have lost along their orbits. When the Earth crosses such a trail of dust, you see a **meteor shower**. The best known is the **Perseids**, which are especially numerous every year around 12 August. On dark nights you can then sometimes see more than 50 shooting stars an hour. In December there is another strong shower, the Geminids.

Most meteorites are **stony meteorites**, which from the outside often look like ordinary stones. **Iron meteorites** consist mainly of iron and nickel and are very heavy. They come from the cores of broken minor planets. There are also rare stony-iron meteorites. Many meteorites have a dark, glassy fusion crust from their hot flight through the atmosphere.

In February 2013, a meteor about 20 metres across exploded over the Russian city of **Chelyabinsk**. The shock wave shattered many windows, and about 1,500 people were injured, mainly by splinters of glass. About 66 million years ago, a body about 10 kilometres across crashed into Mexico and contributed to the extinction of the dinosaurs. The **Barringer Crater** in Arizona was formed about 50,000 years ago by an iron meteorite. In Germany, the Nördlinger Ries is a well-known impact crater.

The best-known Swiss meteorite is the **Twannberg meteorite**, an iron meteorite from the area above Lake Biel in the canton of Bern. The first piece was found in 1984; since then collectors and researchers have discovered hundreds more pieces. You can marvel at meteorites in the Natural History Museum in Bern. The University of Bern is one of the world's important centres for meteorite research. If you think you have found a meteorite, you can have it checked by a museum.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lump that is still travelling in space.
The glowing trail in the sky when a lump burns up in the atmosphere.
Many shooting stars that seem to come from the same part of the sky.
The dark skin a meteorite gets during its hot flight through the air.

gewusst: Every day, many tonnes of cosmic dust fall onto the Earth, most of it tiny.
Some meteorites on Earth come from Mars or the Moon and were flung away from there by impacts.
Many meteorites are about 4.6 billion years old, which makes them older than any rock on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The main sequence is a band in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram on which most stars lie. A star stays there as long as it is fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. The Sun is also a main sequence star.
wichtigste: Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.
Stars spend about 90 per cent of their lives on the main sequence.
A balance between pressure and gravity keeps them stable.
Luminosity rises roughly with mass to the power of 3.5.
A star like the Sun stays on the main sequence for about 10 billion years.
Radiation pressure limits the mass of the largest stars.

abschnitte.text: If you plot stars by temperature and luminosity in a **Hertzsprung-Russell diagram**, most of them lie on a sloping band. This band is called the **main sequence**. At the top left are hot, bright and heavy stars, at the bottom right cool, faint and light ones. Where a star lies on the main sequence depends mainly on its **mass**. Stars spend about **90 per cent** of their lives here.

abschnitte.titel: The way onto the main sequence
abschnitte.text: Young stars form from clouds of gas and at first are still contracting. Young, Sun-like stars in this phase are called **T Tauri stars**. When it gets hot enough in the core, **hydrogen burning** begins. The position of the stars at this moment is called the **zero age main sequence**, **ZAMS** for short. The word “burning” does not mean fire but the fusing of atomic nuclei.

**Gravity** tries to squeeze the star together. The **pressure** of the hot gas inside pushes against it. As long as the two balance each other, the star stays stable for a long time. Heavy stars shine much more strongly. Roughly: luminosity grows with **mass to the power of 3.5**. So a star with 2 solar masses shines about **11 times** as brightly as the Sun. Stars much more massive than the Sun have a **convective core**, in which the gas is constantly churned around.

A star like the **Sun** stays on the main sequence for about **10 billion years**. Heavy stars use up their hydrogen much faster and live only a few million years. Small **red dwarfs**, on the other hand, can shine for trillions of years. At the top end, **radiation pressure** limits the mass, because too much light drives the gas outwards. At the bottom end, the limit is about 8 per cent of the Sun's mass; below that, hydrogen burning does not ignite.

gewusst: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and so has about half of its time on the main sequence behind it.
The most common stars in the Milky Way are small red dwarfs, which cannot be seen with the naked eye.

teile.einleitung: If you split sunlight into its colours, you see many fine dark lines in it. They are called Fraunhofer lines. From them, you can read what the Sun is made of and how fast it spins.
wichtigste: Fraunhofer lines are dark lines in the spectrum of sunlight.
In 1802, William Hyde Wollaston was the first to notice some of these lines.
From 1814, Joseph von Fraunhofer recorded about 570 lines.
They form because atoms in cooler layers of gas absorb certain wavelengths.
The yellow D double line at about 589 nm comes from sodium.
Lines A and B come from oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere.
Through the Doppler effect, the lines reveal the Sun's rotation.

abschnitte.text: If you send sunlight through a **prism**, a band of colours appears: the **spectrum**. The English chemist **William Hyde Wollaston** was the first to notice some dark lines in it in 1802. But he thought they were boundaries between the colours. From 1814, the Munich optician **Joseph von Fraunhofer** studied them closely with instruments he built himself. He mapped about **570 lines** and labelled the most noticeable ones with letters from **A to K**.

Light from deeper, hotter layers of the Sun passes through cooler **gas** further out. The **atoms** in this gas swallow very particular wavelengths. We say they **absorb** them. Which wavelengths these are depends on the energy jumps of the electrons. Every chemical **element** has its own pattern of lines, like a fingerprint.

The yellow **D double line** at 589.0 and 589.6 nanometres comes from **sodium**. You see the same colour in sodium vapour lamps or when table salt gets into a flame. The **C line** at 656.3 nm is produced by **hydrogen** when its electron moves from the third to the second shell. The strong **H and K lines** in the violet range come, despite their names, from **calcium ions**. They are the strongest lines in the visible solar spectrum.

Not all dark lines form on the Sun. Lines **A** and **B** in the red part of the spectrum only form when sunlight passes through the **Earth's atmosphere**. They come from **oxygen** in the air. Such lines, which form on Earth, are called **telluric**. The word comes from the Latin word for Earth.

The Sun spins. One edge is moving towards us, the other away from us. Because of the **Doppler effect**, the lines at one edge are slightly **shifted** towards blue and at the other slightly towards red. From this shift, the Sun's **rotation speed** can be calculated. Researchers use the same method to measure the movement of distant stars and galaxies.

gewusst: The element helium was first discovered in the light of the Sun and only found on Earth later.
The name helium comes from the Greek word “helios” for Sun.

teile.einleitung: The Messier catalogue is a famous list of nebulae, star clusters and galaxies. It was put together by the French astronomer Charles Messier in the 18th century. It is still very popular with amateur astronomers today.
wichtigste: The French astronomer **Charles Messier** put the catalogue together in the 18th century.
He did not want to confuse misty objects with **comets**.
The first version appeared in 1774 with 45 objects.
Today the catalogue contains **110** objects.
M 1 is the **Crab Nebula**, M 31 the **Andromeda Galaxy**, M 45 the **Pleiades**.
In the **Messier marathon**, people try to see all the objects in one night.

abschnitte.text: **Charles Messier** was a French astronomer who mainly searched for **comets**. In his small telescope, some objects in the sky looked like blurry patches. They looked like comets but did not move. So that he would **not confuse them with comets**, he wrote down their positions. This created a list of objects that comet hunters did not need to bother with.

The **first version** of the catalogue appeared in **1774**. It contained **45 objects**. In the following years, Messier added more, also with the help of other observers. Later, astronomers added a few more objects that Messier had observed but had not entered. Today the catalogue contains **110 objects**. Each has an M and a number, for example M 42.

The number **M 1** belongs to the **Crab Nebula** in Taurus. It is the remains of a star that exploded almost a thousand years ago. **M 31** is the **Andromeda Galaxy**, our large neighbouring galaxy. **M 45** is the **Pleiades**, a bright star cluster in Taurus that you can see with the naked eye. **M 13** in the constellation Hercules is a **globular cluster** with hundreds of thousands of tightly packed stars.

Almost all Messier objects are in the sky of the northern hemisphere. That is why they can be observed well from Switzerland too. In the **Messier marathon**, amateur astronomers try to find as many of the objects as possible in **a single night**. This only works **in March around the time of new moon**. Then none of the objects is too close to the Sun, and the Moon does not get in the way with its light.

gewusst: The Crab Nebula formed from a star explosion that was observed by people on Earth in 1054.
You can find many objects in the catalogue even with simple binoculars.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is a star and much bigger than anything else in our solar system. The Earth looks tiny next to it. Even so, compared with other stars, the Sun is only medium-sized.
wichtigste: About 109 Earths would fit side by side across the Sun.
About 1.3 million Earths would fit inside the Sun.
Almost all the matter in the solar system is in the Sun.
The Sun is made of hot gas, and its surface is about 5,500 degrees hot.
It is about 4.6 billion years old.
In many billions of years it will become a red giant.

abschnitte.text: The Sun has a diameter of about **1.4 million kilometres**. About **109 Earths** would fit side by side across it. If you wanted to fill it with Earths, you would need about **1.3 million** of them. **Almost all the matter** in the solar system is in the Sun, more than 99 per cent. All the planets, moons and comets together are almost nothing by comparison.

The Sun has no solid surface. It is made of **hot gas**, mainly **hydrogen** and **helium**. Its visible surface is about **5,500 degrees** hot. Inside it is much hotter, about 15 million degrees. There, hydrogen particles fuse into helium. This creates the energy that we feel as light and warmth.

abschnitte.titel: The same size as the Moon?
abschnitte.text: In the sky, the Sun and Moon look **about the same size**. But the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon. At the same time it is also about 400 times further away, about **150 million kilometres**. That is why both look the same size. That is why the Moon can exactly cover the Sun during a total **solar eclipse**. Important: never look directly at the Sun, as this damages your eyes.

There are **much bigger stars** than the Sun. The red supergiant **Betelgeuse** in the constellation Orion is hundreds of times wider. The Sun is about **4.6 billion years** old and roughly in the middle of its life. In many billions of years, the hydrogen in its core will run out. Then it will swell up into a **red giant**. In the end, a small, hot **white dwarf** will be left.

gewusst: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth. So we always see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago.
If you shrank the Sun to the size of a football, the Earth would only be as big as a pinhead.

teile.einleitung: The Event Horizon Telescope is not a single telescope but a network of radio telescopes all around the world. Together they work like a telescope almost the size of the Earth. With it, the first images of black holes were made.
wichtigste: The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes around the world.
It works with very long baseline interferometry, VLBI for short.
In 2017, observations were made at a wavelength of 1.3 millimetres.
The first image showed the black hole M87* with about 6.5 billion solar masses.
In May 2022, the image of Sagittarius A* in our Milky Way followed.
The dark area in the middle is the black hole's shadow.
The data were taken to the computing centres on hard drives.

abschnitte.titel: A telescope as big as the Earth
abschnitte.text: Seen from the Earth, a black hole is tiny in the sky. To see it, you need an extremely high **resolution**. That is why radio telescopes around the world observe the same target at the same time. The times are recorded precisely with **atomic clocks**. Later the data are combined by computer. This technique is called **very long baseline interferometry**, **VLBI** for short. A particularly important part of the network is **ALMA** in Chile, a group of many antennas on the Chajnantor plateau.

In 2017, the network observed at a wavelength of **1.3 millimetres**, which corresponds to 230 gigahertz. Short radio waves give a better resolution. In addition, they pass through the gas near the black hole. The resolution can be roughly estimated: wavelength divided by the size of the telescope. With 1.3 millimetres and 12,700 kilometres, this gives about **20 microarcseconds**. That is unimaginably fine.

Each station produced hundreds of **terabytes** of data per night. Together it was several petabytes. That was far too much to send over the internet. So the **hard drives** were shipped. They were analysed in Bonn and at MIT Haystack in the USA.

In 2019, the team showed the first image of a black hole. It lies at the centre of the galaxy **M87** and is called **M87***. You can see a bright ring of gas and a dark area in the middle. This is the black hole's **shadow**. It forms because light near the black hole is strongly bent. From the size of the ring, a mass of about **6.5 billion solar masses** was worked out.

On **12 May 2022**, the image of **Sagittarius A*** followed, the black hole at the centre of our Milky Way. The data came from the same measuring campaign in 2017. Sagittarius A* was harder to image. It is over a thousand times lighter than M87*, and the gas circles it in **minutes** instead of days. That is why the image kept changing during a night of observation.

gewusst: The amount of data was so large that aeroplanes carrying hard drives were faster than the internet.
The shadow of a black hole is about two and a half times as big as its event horizon.

teile.einleitung: New moon is the phase of the Moon in which you can hardly see the Moon. It is then roughly between the Earth and the Sun. With the new moon, a new cycle of the phases of the Moon begins.
wichtigste: At new moon, the lit side of the Moon faces away from the Earth.
The Moon is then roughly between the Earth and the Sun.
It rises and sets at about the same time as the Sun and so is in the sky during the day.
A solar eclipse can only happen at new moon.
A few days later, you see a thin crescent moon in the evening.
Nights at new moon are especially dark and good for watching the stars.

abschnitte.text: The Sun always lights up exactly one **half** of the Moon. Depending on where the Moon is in its orbit, we see more or less of this bright side. At **new moon**, the bright half faces exactly away from the Earth. The side facing us is dark. That is why we can hardly see the Moon.

abschnitte.titel: In the sky during the day
abschnitte.text: At new moon, the Moon is on the same side of the Earth as the Sun. So, seen from us, it is close to the Sun in the sky. It rises and sets at about the same time as the Sun. So the new moon is in the sky **during the day**, but you cannot see it in the bright sunlight.

After new moon, a little more of the Moon is lit every day. After one or two days, shortly after **sunset**, you can see a thin **crescent** low in the west. After that the Moon grows through half moon to full moon. It takes about **29.5 days** from one new moon to the next. In calendars, the new moon is drawn as a **filled-in dark circle** and the full moon as an empty circle.

For the Moon to cover the Sun, it has to be exactly between the Earth and the Sun. This is only possible at **new moon**. Even so, there is not a **solar eclipse** every month. This is because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted against the Earth's orbit. So most of the time the Moon passes a little above or below the Sun.

Without moonlight, the night sky is especially **dark**. Then you can see faint stars and the band of the **Milky Way** much better. That is why people who want to watch shooting stars or nebulae like to choose a night around new moon. It works best far from bright towns, for example in the mountains.

gewusst: In some calendars, such as the Islamic calendar, a new month begins when the first thin crescent can be seen after new moon.
The word “month” has the same origin as the word “moon”.

teile.einleitung: On the coasts of the seas, the water rises and falls every day. This movement is called the tides. When the water goes out it is called low tide or ebb, and when it rises it is called high tide or flood.
wichtigste: Ebb is when the seawater on the coast goes out.
Flood is when the seawater on the coast rises.
It takes about 12 hours from one high tide to the next.
At full moon and new moon, the difference between low and high tide is particularly large.
On the mudflats the tide can come back quickly, so people only walk there with a guide.
In Swiss lakes you do not notice any tides; they are too small.

abschnitte.text: If you go on holiday by the sea, you can see it: the water comes and goes. When it goes out, it is **ebb tide**. When it rises, it is **flood tide**. The highest level is called **high water**, the lowest **low water**. It takes about **12 hours** and 25 minutes from one high water to the next. That is why the times shift a little every day.

abschnitte.titel: The Moon and the Sun pull
abschnitte.text: The tides are caused mainly by the pull of the **Moon**. It pulls on the water of the seas and makes it swell into bulges of water. The **Sun** pulls too, but more weakly. At **full moon** and **new moon**, the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line. Then both pull together, and the difference between low and high tide is particularly large. This is called a **spring tide**.

On the North Sea there is the **Wadden Sea**. At low tide, a huge area of seabed dries out there, the **mudflats**. This is where the **lugworm**, for example, lives. It lives in the sand and leaves little heaps of sand behind. A **mudflat walk** is exciting but dangerous without a guide. The tide can come back quickly, and tidal creeks, which are channels of water, fill up fast.

Switzerland is far from the sea. In our lakes, such as **Lake Geneva** or **Lake Constance**, you do not notice any tides. The lakes are much **too small** for that. The Moon's pull works here too, but the difference is tiny. Only in large seas do bulges of water form that you can clearly see on the coast.

gewusst: The Wadden Sea on the North Sea is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site.
The solid land also rises and falls a little with the tides, but so little that we do not feel it.

teile.einleitung: The Moon is the Earth's natural companion and, after the Sun, the brightest object in our sky. It does not shine by itself but is lit up by the Sun. It is the only celestial body that humans have so far set foot on.
wichtigste: The Moon goes around the Earth once in about a month.
Its light is reflected sunlight.
It is on average about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth.
There is no air to breathe on the Moon.
When the Moon can be seen as a whole round disc, it is called a full moon.
In 1969, Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.
An experiment from Switzerland was part of the first Moon landing.

abschnitte.text: The Moon has a diameter of about 3,500 kilometres, which is about a quarter of the Earth's diameter. It is on average about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth. It takes about a month to go once around the Earth, which is where the word “**month**” comes from. Because it turns exactly once on its axis as it does so, we always see the same side from the Earth. The far side has only been known since space probes photographed it in 1959.

abschnitte.titel: Where does its light come from?
abschnitte.text: The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects **sunlight** like a big mirror made of rock. Depending on how much of its lit half we can see, the **phases of the Moon** come about. At full moon we see the whole lit disc, at new moon almost nothing. In fact the Moon's surface is quite dark, about as dark as worn tarmac. It only looks bright because the night sky around it is black.

There is no air and no liquid water on the Moon. That is why there is no weather and no sound there. The surface is covered with thousands of **craters** caused by impacts. The dark patches you can see with the naked eye are called **maria**, meaning seas, but they are solidified areas of lava. During the day it gets hotter than 100 degrees, and at night the temperature drops to far below minus 100 degrees.

The Moon probably formed about 4.5 billion years ago, when a body the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris. Its gravity causes **low and high tide** on the coasts of the seas on Earth. The Moon also keeps the tilt of the Earth's axis steady and so makes for a calmer climate. It moves about 3.8 centimetres further away from the Earth every year.

On 21 July 1969, on the Apollo 11 mission, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon. Buzz Aldrin followed shortly afterwards. The two also set up a **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern, the only non-American experiment on this mission. By 1972, twelve astronauts in total had landed on the Moon. Today the USA is planning to bring people to the Moon again with the Artemis programme.

begriffe.erklaerung: The changing shape of the Moon, depending on how much of its lit side we can see.
A round hollow formed by an impact.
A dark plain of solidified lava on the Moon; the plural is maria.
The regular rising and falling of sea level, low and high tide.

gewusst: The astronauts' footprints can probably still be seen today, because no wind blows on the Moon.
On the Moon you weigh only about a sixth as much as on Earth.
By firing laser beams at mirrors that astronauts set up on the Moon, its distance can be measured to within a few centimetres.

teile.einleitung: Mars rovers are driving robots that explore the surface of Mars. They photograph the landscape, study rock and look for traces of water. Since 1997, new rovers have kept arriving on the Red Planet.
wichtigste: The first rover on Mars was **Sojourner** in 1997.
**Opportunity** worked for almost 15 years instead of about 90 days.
**Curiosity** landed on Mars in 2012.
Curiosity and Perseverance each have **6 wheels** and a **radioisotope battery**.
By 2024, the helicopter **Ingenuity** had made 72 flights in total.
The Chinese rover **Zhurong** landed on Mars in 2021.

abschnitte.text: In **1997**, **Sojourner** became the first rover to drive around on Mars. It was only the size of a toy car and stayed close to its landing station. In 2004 came the twin rovers **Spirit** and **Opportunity**. A mission of **about 90 days** was planned. But Opportunity kept going for **almost 15 years**, until a huge dust storm in 2018 darkened its solar panels.

In **2012** the rover **Curiosity** landed, followed by **Perseverance** in 2021. Both are about the size of a small car and have **6 wheels**. They do not get their energy from solar panels but from a **radioisotope battery**. It produces electricity from the heat of decaying radioactive material. This lets the rovers work even in dust and in winter.

**Perseverance** is looking for traces of past life in an old lake basin. To do this, it drills rock samples and puts them into **small tubes**. These tubes are to **come to Earth later**, so that experts can study them closely in laboratories. How and when this will happen is still being planned. Much more precise measurements can be made on Earth than with a rover.

Perseverance brought a small helicopter with it: **Ingenuity**. It was the first aircraft to fly under its own power on another planet. Because of the very thin air, its rotors had to spin extremely fast. Only a few test flights were planned. But by the end of its mission in 2024, Ingenuity had made **72 flights**.

In **2021**, the Chinese rover **Zhurong** landed on Mars. That made China the second country after the USA to operate a rover successfully on Mars. Zhurong drove on the large northern plain of Utopia Planitia. It is named after a fire god from Chinese legend and ran on solar power.

gewusst: Radio signals to Mars take several minutes, so rovers drive many stretches on their own.
Ingenuity carried a small piece of fabric from the wing of the Wright brothers' first powered aeroplane.

teile.einleitung: Binoculars, in Switzerland often called a “Feldstecher” in German, consist of two small telescopes side by side. You look through them with both eyes. They are good for birds and mountains, but also very good for the night sky.
wichtigste: Binoculars have a separate small telescope for each eye.
With 10x50, 10 means the magnification and 50 the diameter of the objective lenses in millimetres.
The exit pupil is the objective diameter divided by the magnification.
Prisms turn the image the right way up and make binoculars shorter.
With strong magnification, a tripod helps against shaking.
With binoculars you can see the four large moons of Jupiter.
7x50 and 10x50 are considered good beginner binoculars for the night sky.

abschnitte.text: Every pair of binoculars has two numbers on it, for example **10x50**. The first number is the **magnification**. A bird 100 metres away looks as big as if it were only 10 metres away. The second number is the **objective diameter**, the width of the front lenses in millimetres. The bigger this number, the more light the binoculars collect.

If you hold binoculars at a distance in front of you, you can see a bright circle in the eyepiece. This is the **exit pupil**. You work it out like this: objective diameter divided by magnification. For 10x50, that is 50 mm divided by 10, so **5 millimetres**. In the dark, the pupil of our eye opens to about 7 millimetres. A suitable exit pupil makes for a bright image.

An objective lens on its own would give an image that is upside down. That is why **prisms** are built into binoculars. These are cut pieces of glass that redirect the light. They turn the image **the right way up** and fold the light path. This keeps the binoculars short and handy.

The amount of light collected depends on the **area** of the lens. A 50 mm lens collects about **50 times** more light than our eye with a 7 mm pupil. That is why star clusters and nebulae look much brighter. Binoculars such as **7x50** or **10x50** also show a large **field of view**, so objects are easy to find. With Jupiter, you can make out the four large **Galilean moons** as small dots in a line.

Every small movement of your hand is made bigger by the magnification. From about 10 times magnification, the image therefore shakes noticeably. With stronger binoculars, a **tripod** helps. You can also lean against a wall or rest your elbows. Important: never look at the **Sun** through binoculars, as this can seriously injure your eyes.

gewusst: With good binoculars you can already see many craters on the Moon.
In Switzerland, binoculars are usually called a “Feldstecher” rather than a “Fernglas” in German.

teile.einleitung: The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of the planet Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Galileo Galilei discovered them in 1610 with his telescope. Their discovery changed the way people saw the world.
wichtigste: The four Galilean moons are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
From the inside out, the order is Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto.
The names were suggested by the astronomer Simon Marius.
Galileo himself called them the Medicean Stars.
Their discovery showed that not everything circles the Earth.
Even with good binoculars you can see them as points of light.
Since 2023, the ESA probe JUICE has been on its way to Jupiter's icy moons.

abschnitte.text: Galileo Galilei discovered the four moons in **1610**. He dedicated them to the powerful **Medici** family in Florence and called them the **Medicean Stars**. But this name did not catch on. The German astronomer **Simon Marius** observed the moons at almost the same time. He suggested the names **Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto**. These names come from **Greek mythology** and stand for figures connected with Zeus, the father of the gods. To the Romans, Zeus was **Jupiter**.

abschnitte.titel: A new view of the world
abschnitte.text: At the time, many people believed that all celestial bodies circled the **Earth**. But Jupiter's moons could be seen circling **another planet**. That showed that not everything circles the Earth. So the discovery supported the view of the world with the **Sun at the centre**. This made Galileo an important defender of that idea.

**Io** orbits closest to Jupiter. It is made almost entirely of rock and an iron core and, at about 3.5 grams per cubic centimetre, is the **densest** of the four. There are many active volcanoes on Io. **Europa** has an icy crust, beneath which an ocean is suspected. **Ganymede** is the largest moon in the whole solar system. **Callisto** orbits furthest out and is covered with a great many craters.

The orbital periods of Io, Europa and Ganymede fit together exactly. While **Ganymede** goes once around Jupiter, **Europa** manages two laps and **Io** four. So they are roughly in the ratio **1 to 2 to 4**. Such a matching of orbits is called **resonance**. It means that the moons keep pulling on each other slightly and kneading each other.

The four moons are fairly bright. With **binoculars** held steady, you can see them on clear nights as small points of light next to Jupiter. Their positions change from night to night. The European probe **JUICE** was launched in April 2023 to explore Jupiter's icy moons. The **University of Bern** also helped with one of its instruments.

gewusst: Ganymede is even bigger than the planet Mercury.
Io is the body with the most active volcanoes in the solar system.

teile.einleitung: The geostationary orbit is a special orbit high above the equator. A satellite there circles exactly as fast as the Earth turns, and so it seems to stand still in the sky.
wichtigste: Geostationary satellites are all located above the equator.
They orbit the Earth at a height of about 36,000 kilometres.
One orbit takes a sidereal day, just under 24 hours.
They move from west to east, the same way the Earth turns.
Seen from the Earth they stand still, so satellite dishes do not need to be turned to follow them.
Near the poles, geostationary satellites cannot be received.

abschnitte.text: The further a satellite is from the Earth, the more slowly it orbits. At a height of about **35,800 kilometres** above the **equator**, one orbit takes exactly one **sidereal day**. That is 23 hours and 56 minutes, one whole turn of the Earth. The satellite flies **from west to east**, in the same direction as the Earth. That is why, seen from below, it always seems to be at the same point in the sky.

Many **television satellites** are in this orbit. You only need to set up a **satellite dish** correctly once and never turn it again. In **Switzerland**, the dishes usually point **south**, tilted a little to the east or west. That is where the equator is in the sky as seen from here. That is why you see many dishes on rooftops and balconies all facing the same way.

abschnitte.titel: Keeping an eye on the weather
abschnitte.text: **Weather satellites** also use the geostationary orbit. The European **Meteosat** satellites constantly watch Europe and Africa. Every few minutes they deliver new pictures of the clouds. The experts at **MeteoSwiss** also use them to make their weather forecasts. Switzerland is a member of **EUMETSAT**, the organisation that operates these satellites.

In 1945, the British writer **Arthur C. Clarke** made the idea of putting communications satellites into this orbit widely known. Three such satellites could reach almost the whole Earth. Just under twenty years later, the idea became reality. But in the far north and south, near the **poles**, the orbit lies below the horizon. There these satellites cannot be received.

gewusst: In honour of the writer, the geostationary orbit is sometimes also called the “Clarke orbit”.
A radio signal takes about a quarter of a second to travel to a geostationary satellite and back. That is why there are sometimes small delays in live broadcasts.

teile.einleitung: Moon rock means stones and dust from the Moon. Some of them were brought to Earth by astronauts and space probes; others fell to us by themselves as meteorites. Researchers learn a lot from them about the history of the Moon and the Earth.
wichtigste: The six Apollo landings brought back about 382 kilograms of Moon rock in total.
Most Moon rock is light grey to dark grey.
The dark lunar seas consist of basalt, a solidified lava rock.
Moon dust is very fine and sharp-edged, and to the astronauts it smelt like burnt gunpowder.
In 2020, the Chinese probe Chang'e 5 brought samples to Earth without people.
There are no fossils in Moon rock, because there was never life on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: Between 1969 and 1972, six **Apollo** missions landed on the Moon. The astronauts collected stones, cores from the ground and dust, about **382 kilograms** in total. Later, uncrewed probes also fetched samples: the Soviet **Luna** probes in the 1970s and the Chinese probe **Chang'e 5** in 2020. The samples are carefully stored in special laboratories and lent to researchers all over the world.

abschnitte.titel: What kinds of rock there are
abschnitte.text: The dark plains, the **lunar seas**, consist of **basalt**. This is a dark, hard rock made of solidified lava, which is also found at volcanoes on Earth. The bright **highlands** consist mainly of a light-coloured rock called **anorthosite**. There are also **breccias**, rocks made of fragments that were baked together in impacts. Almost everything is grey, in many shades.

On the Moon there is no water and no wind that could grind the dust grains round. That is why the grains are very **sharp-edged**. They clung to the suits and scratched the tools. When the astronauts took off their helmets back in the lunar module, they could smell the dust. Many said it smelt like **burnt gunpowder**.

When a large lump crashes into the Moon, stones can be flung away so hard that they fly into space. Some of them land on the Earth as **meteorites** after a long journey. Such **lunar meteorites** have been found, for example, in deserts and in Antarctica. Their composition shows that they really come from the Moon.

Switzerland was also part of the first Moon landing in 1969: the **University of Bern** had developed a **solar wind sail**. The astronauts set up this foil on the Moon. It caught particles coming from the Sun and was then brought back to Earth and studied in Bern.

gewusst: The Bern solar wind sail was set up on Apollo 11 even before the American flag.
Because there is no water on the Moon, Moon rock is much drier than almost any rock on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Halley's Comet is the most famous comet of all. It comes close to the Sun and the Earth about every 76 years and can then be seen with the naked eye.
wichtigste: Halley's Comet comes close to the Earth about every 76 years.
It is named after the scientist Edmond Halley.
It was last close to the Sun in 1986, and it is expected again in 2061.
In 1986, the European space probe Giotto flew past it.
Its nucleus is about 15 kilometres long.
Its dust causes shooting stars every year.

abschnitte.text: A **comet** is a lump of ice, dust and rock. When it comes close to the Sun, some of the ice evaporates. Then a glowing **tail** forms. Halley's Comet returns about **every 76 years**. It was last close to the Sun in **1986**. It is next expected in **2061**.

The English astronomer **Edmond Halley** studied old reports of comets. He realised that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were probably the same body. He predicted that the comet would return around 1758. Halley died before then, but the comet really did come. That is why it bears his name.

The comet was observed thousands of years ago. It can be seen on the famous **Bayeux Tapestry** in France. This long embroidered cloth tells the story of the conquest of England in 1066, when the comet was in the sky. In the past, many people thought comets were signs of coming misfortune. Today we know that they are completely natural celestial bodies.

In 1986, the European space probe **Giotto** flew close past the comet. It took the first close-up pictures of a comet's nucleus. The **nucleus** is about **15 kilometres** long, shaped like a potato and very dark. The comet loses dust every time it visits. When the Earth flies through this dust, the grains burn up in the air and we see **shooting stars**, for example in May and October.

gewusst: The Giotto probe is named after the Italian painter Giotto. Around 1305 he painted a comet as the Star of Bethlehem.
If you saw the comet as a child in 1986, with a bit of luck you can see it a second time in 2061.

teile.einleitung: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram sorts stars by their temperature and their luminosity. It is one of the most important tools in astronomy, because it shows at a glance what stage of its life a star is in.
wichtigste: The diagram is named after Ejnar Hertzsprung from Denmark and Henry Norris Russell from the USA.
Temperature is plotted horizontally, increasing towards the left.
Luminosity is plotted vertically.
Most stars lie on the main sequence; main sequence stars have the luminosity class V.
White dwarfs lie at the bottom left, red supergiants at the top right.
The age of a star cluster can be read from the turn-off point of the main sequence.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 20th century, two astronomers compared many stars independently of each other. One was **Ejnar Hertzsprung** from **Denmark**, the other **Henry Norris Russell** from the USA. Both noticed: if you plot temperature against luminosity, the stars are not scattered at random. They gather in particular groups. Since then the diagram has borne both their names.

On the **vertical axis** is the **luminosity**; bright stars are at the top. On the **horizontal axis** is the **surface temperature**. It usually **increases towards the left**, so hot blue stars are on the left. Often the spectral class is plotted instead of the temperature. In the **colour-magnitude diagram**, the **colour index** is used, such as B-V. This can be measured directly by comparing the brightness through different colour filters.

Most stars lie on the **main sequence**, a sloping band from top left to bottom right. In the **MK system** they have the luminosity class **V**; the Sun is a star of class G2V. At the **top right** are cool but huge and bright stars such as the **red supergiants**. At the **bottom left** lie the **white dwarfs**, hot but small and faint. A star with the same temperature as the Sun but 100 times the luminosity has **10 times the radius**, because luminosity grows with the square of the radius.

All the stars in a **star cluster** are about the same age. The heavy stars leave the main sequence first because they use up their hydrogen faster. That is why the main sequence bends off at a certain point. The lower this **turn-off point** lies, the **older** the cluster is. In old **globular clusters** there is also the **horizontal branch**. There are stars there that are fusing helium in their cores.

gewusst: The Sun lies fairly in the middle of the main sequence, so it is a completely average star.
Over the course of its life, a star moves through the diagram. The Sun will one day move up to the top right among the giants and finally end up at the bottom left as a white dwarf.

teile.einleitung: Gamma ray bursts are short, unimaginably bright outbursts of gamma rays from distant space. They are among the most powerful explosions known, and they were discovered by chance by military satellites.
wichtigste: Gamma ray bursts are short outbursts of very energetic gamma rays.
From 1967, the American Vela satellites recorded the first gamma ray bursts.
Short gamma ray bursts last less than about 2 seconds, long ones last longer.
Long gamma ray bursts usually form when a very massive star collapses.
Short gamma ray bursts form when two neutron stars merge; this was confirmed in 2017.
The radiation is focused in narrow jets.

abschnitte.text: In the 1960s, the USA sent the **Vela satellites** into space. They were meant to detect secret nuclear weapons tests. From 1967, they recorded short flashes of **gamma rays** that did not come from the Earth. The researchers only published the discovery in 1973. Gamma rays are light with a great deal of energy that our eyes cannot see. Because the Earth's atmosphere absorbs them, gamma ray bursts can only be observed with satellites.

For a long time, nobody knew whether gamma ray bursts were near or far. In the 1990s, the instrument **BATSE** on the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory counted about 2,700 bursts. They came **evenly from all directions** of the sky. This argued against them coming from our Milky Way. In 1997, the Italian and Dutch satellite **BeppoSAX** found the X-ray afterglow of a gamma ray burst for the first time. This made it possible to pin down the position and show that the sources are extremely far away.

Gamma ray bursts are divided by how long they last. The dividing line is about **2 seconds**. Most **long gamma ray bursts** form when the core of a very massive star collapses into a black hole. They happen together with special supernovae. **Short gamma ray bursts** form when two **neutron stars** merge. In August 2017, a short burst was observed at the same time as **gravitational waves**, which was the proof.

The radiation of a gamma ray burst comes out in narrow **jets** that travel almost as fast as light. You only see a burst if a jet is pointing roughly towards the Earth. If you calculate as if the source were shining in all directions, you estimate the energy far too high. Even so, gamma ray bursts release enormous energy in a short time. NASA's **Swift** satellite was launched in 2004. It turns towards a new burst within minutes so that its telescopes can measure the afterglow.

gewusst: The gamma ray burst GRB 221009A from October 2022 was the brightest ever measured. It was nicknamed “BOAT”, which stands for “Brightest Of All Time”.
The Swift satellite is named after the bird, the swift, because it turns so nimbly.
The burst GRB 221009A was so strong that it even measurably disturbed the upper atmosphere of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Cosmic inflation is a theory about the very first moments after the Big Bang. According to it, the young universe expanded unimaginably fast for a tiny moment.
wichtigste: In 1981, Alan Guth published the first model of inflation.
According to the theory, inflation was driven by a field called the inflaton.
It took place about 10 to the power of minus 36 to 10 to the power of minus 32 seconds after the Big Bang.
Inflation explains why space today is almost flat.
Tiny quantum fluctuations later became the seeds of galaxies.
Proof of primordial gravitational waves is still missing.

abschnitte.text: In 1981, the physicist **Alan Guth** suggested that the young universe expanded exponentially. **Exponentially** means that the size multiplies again and again in equal periods of time. Inflation only lasted from about 10 to the power of minus 36 to 10 to the power of minus 32 seconds after the Big Bang. In this time, the universe grew by at least a factor of 10 to the power of 26. Later models were developed by **Andrei Linde** and other researchers, among others.

According to the theory, inflation was driven by a hypothetical field, the **inflaton**. Its high energy density acted like a repulsion and blew up space. When the field decayed, inflation ended. Its energy heated up the universe; this is called **reheating**. After that, things developed as the classic Big Bang theory describes.

Space today is almost **flat**, hardly curved at all. Inflation explains this as follows: if you blow up a balloon to a huge size, every small piece of its surface looks flat. Grand unified theories predict many **magnetic monopoles**, which have never been observed. Inflation thinned them out so much that hardly any were left in our visible universe.

According to quantum physics, energy is constantly fluctuating on the smallest scales. These **quantum fluctuations** were stretched to cosmic size by inflation. This created tiny differences in density. From them, galaxies and **galaxy clusters** later grew. Traces of this can be seen in the background radiation.

Inflation should have produced **primordial gravitational waves**. They would leave a swirling pattern in the polarisation of the background radiation, the **B-modes**. In 2014, the **BICEP2** experiment reported such a find. But joint analyses with data from the Planck satellite showed that the signal came mostly from **dust in the Milky Way**. A signal of inflation is still unconfirmed today.

gewusst: During inflation, space expanded faster than light; this does not contradict the theory of relativity, because space itself was expanding.
According to the theory, everything we see in the universe today was smaller than an atom before inflation.

teile.einleitung: A light year sounds like a measure of time, but it is a distance. It is the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Astronomers need this huge unit because the distances in space are so enormous.
wichtigste: A light year is a unit of length, not a unit of time.
A light year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres.
At about 300,000 kilometres per second, light is the fastest thing there is.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light years away.
The abbreviation for light year is ly.
If you look far into space, you are also looking into the past.

abschnitte.text: A **light year** is the distance light travels through empty space in one year. So it gives a **distance**, not a time. Because light is incredibly fast, this distance is huge: about 9.5 trillion kilometres. That is a number with twelve zeros. A car travelling at 100 km/h would need more than ten million years for one light year.

The **speed of light** in a vacuum is almost exactly 300,000 kilometres per second. In one second, light could go around the Earth about seven and a half times. In one minute it gets about 18 million kilometres. Light takes about 1.3 seconds to get from the Moon to the Earth. Nothing that has mass can become as fast as light.

abschnitte.titel: Light times in the solar system
abschnitte.text: For shorter distances, light seconds and **light minutes** are used. The Sun is about 8 light minutes away from us. So if the Sun suddenly went out, we would only notice about 8 minutes later. Light takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune. The space probe Voyager 1 is so far away that its radio signals take almost a whole day to reach the Earth.

The nearest star after the Sun is called **Proxima Centauri** and is about 4.2 light years away. The bright star Sirius is about 8.6 light years away. Our Milky Way has a diameter of over 100,000 light years. The Andromeda Galaxy, our large neighbouring galaxy, is about 2.5 million light years away. Even so, on dark nights it can be seen with the naked eye as a faint patch.

Because light takes time, we always see celestial bodies as they were in the past. We see the Moon as it looked just over a second ago. The light from the Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million years old, so it set off long before modern humans existed. Large telescopes such as the **James Webb Space Telescope** can see galaxies from the early days of the universe in this way. Besides the light year, professionals also use the unit **parsec**, which is about 3.26 light years.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.
The speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second.
The distance light travels in a minute, about 18 million kilometres.
Another unit of distance in astronomy, about 3.26 light years.
The star closest to our Sun.

gewusst: Some stars we see in the sky today might no longer exist, because their light has been travelling for so long.
Even a journey to Proxima Centauri would take tens of thousands of years with today's space probes.
Moonlight is actually sunlight that takes a good 8 minutes to reach the Moon and then just over a second more to reach the Earth.

teile.einleitung: A nebula in astronomy is a huge cloud of gas and dust in space. In German it has the same name as fog on Earth, but that is all they have in common. There are bright and dark nebulae, and some of them are among the most beautiful things in the sky.
wichtigste: Astronomical nebulae consist of gas and dust.
Emission nebulae often glow red, because excited hydrogen gives off red light.
Reflection nebulae look bluish, because their dust scatters mainly blue light.
Dark nebulae such as the Horsehead Nebula hide the light behind them.
Planetary nebulae are the cast-off outer layers of dying stars.
New stars form in dense nebulae.

abschnitte.text: **Emission nebulae** glow by themselves. Hot young stars nearby give off strong radiation and make the gas glow. **Hydrogen** gives off mainly **red light** in the process. That is why many of these nebulae look red in photos. A well-known example is the Orion Nebula. **New stars** also form in such dense clouds, when gas contracts under its own gravity.

**Reflection nebulae** do not glow by themselves. Their dust scatters the light of nearby stars, a bit like smoke in the beam of a spotlight. Blue light is scattered more strongly, which is why they look **bluish**. **Dark nebulae** are dense clouds of dust that hide the light behind them. The famous **Horsehead Nebula** in Orion is such a dark nebula: against a glowing background it shows up as a dark horse's head.

At the end of its life, a Sun-like star casts off its **outer layers**. This glowing shell is called a **planetary nebula**. It has nothing to do with planets: in telescopes they only used to look similar to small planetary discs. A beautiful example is the **Ring Nebula** M 57 in the constellation Lyra. In a small telescope it looks like a grey smoke ring.

In the 18th century, the French astronomer **Charles Messier** searched for comets. He was bothered by misty patches that could easily be mistaken for comets. So he wrote them down in a list. To this day, his objects have an **M** and a number, such as M 42 for the Orion Nebula or M 1 for the Crab Nebula, the remains of a star explosion.

In the past, everything that looked blurry in a telescope was called a nebula. That is why the Andromeda Galaxy was called the **Andromeda Nebula**. Only in the 1920s did **Edwin Hubble** show that this nebula is a separate **galaxy** far outside the Milky Way. Even so, the old name stayed in use for a long time.

gewusst: The Crab Nebula is the remains of a star explosion that was observed and written down by Chinese astronomers in 1054.
Many nebulae are so faint that their colours only become visible in photos with a long exposure.

teile.einleitung: Ganymede is the largest moon of the planet Jupiter and the largest moon in the whole solar system. It is even wider than the planet Mercury and is the only known moon with its own magnetic field.
wichtigste: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system; its diameter is about 5,270 kilometres.
It is wider than the planet Mercury but has less mass.
Ganymede goes around Jupiter in about 7.2 days, so in about a week.
It is made of roughly half rock and half water ice.
Ganymede is the only known moon with its own magnetic field.
Beneath its surface there is probably an ocean of salt water.

abschnitte.text: **Galileo Galilei** discovered Ganymede in 1610 together with three other large moons of Jupiter. Ganymede measures about 5,270 kilometres, the planet **Mercury** only about 4,880 kilometres. But because Ganymede contains a lot of ice, it is lighter than Mercury. It takes about 7.2 days to go once around Jupiter. It always shows the same side to Jupiter, just as our Moon does to the Earth.

Ganymede is made of about half **rock** and half **water ice**. At its centre it has a core of iron. The surface shows dark, old areas with many craters and brighter areas with long grooves. In 2015, researchers observed its auroras with the **Hubble Space Telescope**. They sway less than they would without an ocean. This points to a **saltwater ocean** deep beneath the ice.

abschnitte.titel: A magnetic field of its own
abschnitte.text: In 1996, the space probe **Galileo** found that Ganymede has its own **magnetic field**. This has not yet been shown for any other known moon. It is probably created in the liquid iron core. Because of the magnetic field, Ganymede also has auroras. But they do not glow visibly for our eyes; they glow in ultraviolet light.

On 7 June 2021, the NASA probe **Juno** flew past Ganymede at a distance of just over 1,000 kilometres. It took sharp pictures. The European probe **JUICE** was launched in 2023. Around 2034 it is to become the first probe to go into orbit around Ganymede. No probe has ever orbited a moon other than the Earth's Moon. Researchers from Switzerland also worked on JUICE.

gewusst: In Greek legend, Ganymede was a handsome prince from Troy. Zeus took him to Olympus, where he poured wine for the gods.
If Ganymede orbited the Sun instead of Jupiter, it would probably be called a planet because of its size.

teile.einleitung: Many people see a face in the dark patches of the full moon: the “Man in the Moon”. In other countries, people see completely different pictures in them. Behind the face is an exciting story about the Moon and about our brains.
wichtigste: The face of the “Man in the Moon” is made of **dark patches** on the Moon.
The Moon always shows us **the same side**, which is why the face always looks the same.
In China or Japan, many people see a **hare** in the patches.
The side you never see is called the **far side of the Moon**, but it also gets sunlight.
Our brains like to look for faces, even in clouds or plug sockets.
You see the whole face at **full moon**.

abschnitte.text: The face of the “Man in the Moon” is made of **dark patches** on the Moon's surface. They are large, flat plains of solidified lava. In the past they were thought to be seas, which is why they are still called **maria**, the Latin word for seas. The bright areas between them are more mountainous and full of craters. You can see the whole face at **full moon**, when the Sun lights up the whole side facing us.

The Moon turns once on its axis in exactly the same time it takes to go around the Earth. That is why it always shows us **the same side**. So the Man in the Moon always looks the same. The other side, which you never see from the Earth, is called the **far side of the Moon**. But it is **not always dark**: it gets sunlight too, for example when it is new moon for us.

Not everywhere do people see a man in the Moon. In **China** or **Japan**, many people see a **hare** in the patches. In old stories, the moon hare pounds something in a mortar. Other cultures see a woman, a toad or a man with a bundle of wood. The patches are the same everywhere; only the pictures in people's heads are different.

How the face looks also depends on where you are on Earth. People in **Australia**, in the southern hemisphere, see the Man in the Moon **upside down**. For them the picture is turned round compared with ours. That is because they are looking at the Moon, so to speak, from the other side of the globe.

Why do we see a face in the Moon at all? **Our brains like to look for faces**. It has always been important for people to recognise faces quickly. That is why we also spot them where there are none: in clouds, in tree bark or in a **plug socket** with two holes as eyes. Experts call this **pareidolia**.

gewusst: The Chinese Moon rover Yutu is named after the Jade Rabbit from the Chinese Moon legend.
The first photos of the far side of the Moon were taken in 1959 by a Soviet space probe.

teile.einleitung: The Falcon 9 is a rocket made by the American company SpaceX. It carries satellites, cargo and astronauts into space. What is special about it: its first stage lands again after launch and can fly again.
wichtigste: The Falcon 9 flew for the first time on 4 June 2010.
The number 9 stands for the nine Merlin engines of the first stage.
It burns rocket kerosene and liquid oxygen.
In December 2015, a first stage landed after an orbital launch for the first time.
Grid fins steer the stage on its way back through the atmosphere.
In March 2017, a used first stage flew into orbit again for the first time.
With the Demo-2 mission in May 2020, astronauts flew on the Falcon 9 for the first time.

abschnitte.text: The Falcon 9 has two stages. The first stage is powered by **nine Merlin engines**, hence the number 9 in the name. The name “Falcon” is a reminder of the spaceship Millennium Falcon from Star Wars. The second stage has only **one** engine, the Merlin Vacuum. It has a large nozzle for working in the vacuum of space. The fuels are the kerosene **RP-1** and **liquid oxygen**.

The Falcon 9 flew for the first time on **4 June 2010** from Cape Canaveral in Florida. The smaller Falcon 1 had already launched for the first time in 2006. Since then, the Falcon 9 has become one of the most frequently launched rockets in the world. It carries satellites into space and supply flights to the International Space Station ISS.

In the past, rocket stages were thrown away after a flight. In **December 2015**, a Falcon 9 first stage returned after an orbital launch for the first time and landed **upright** on the launch site. As it falls through the atmosphere, four **grid fins** steer the stage precisely to the landing pad. If there is not enough fuel for the flight back, the stage lands on an uncrewed **drone ship** in the ocean. This first succeeded in April 2016.

In March 2017, SpaceX achieved something new on the **SES-10** mission. A first stage that had already flown in 2016 launched into orbit **again**. Afterwards it landed on a drone ship again. Reuse saves a lot of money. Today some first stages fly many times.

In May 2020, a Falcon 9 carried astronauts into space for the first time. On the **Demo-2** mission, Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken flew to the ISS in the **Crew Dragon** capsule. This was the first time since 2011 that astronauts had launched from the USA. Since then, crews have flown regularly on the Falcon 9.

gewusst: The larger Falcon Heavy is basically three Falcon 9 first stages joined together, with 27 engines.
The drone ships sail to the landing site without a crew on board.

teile.einleitung: The Hubble tension is a big unsolved puzzle in cosmology. Different measuring methods give different values for the rate at which the universe is expanding, and so far nobody knows for sure why.
wichtigste: The Planck data from 2018 give a Hubble constant of about 67 km/s per Mpc.
In 2022, measurements with Cepheids and supernovae gave about 73 km/s per Mpc.
Around 2022, the difference was given as about 5 sigma.
Measurements from the early universe are set against measurements from the late universe.
From 2023, the James Webb Telescope confirmed Hubble's Cepheid measurements.
One possible way out being discussed is “early dark energy”.

abschnitte.text: The **Hubble constant** describes how fast the universe is expanding today. It can be worked out in two fundamentally different ways. One way uses the **background radiation** from the early universe and calculates forwards to today with the **standard model**. The other way directly measures the distances and speeds of nearby galaxies. Both ways should give the same value, but they do not.

abschnitte.titel: The value from the early universe
abschnitte.text: ESA's **Planck** satellite measured the background radiation very precisely. The analysis from 2018 gives, in the standard model, H0 equal to 67.4 km/s per Mpc, with an uncertainty of only about 0.5. This value is projected from the conditions shortly after the Big Bang. So it is not a direct measurement of today's universe.

The group led by **Adam Riess** measures distances with a kind of ladder. **Cepheids**, pulsating stars, calibrate the brightness of **type Ia supernovae**. With these exploding stars, you can reach distant galaxies. In 2022 the group found about 73.0 km/s per Mpc. At about **5 sigma**, the difference is considered so clear that chance is practically ruled out.

The **James Webb Space Telescope** sees more sharply in the infrared and can separate Cepheids better from neighbouring stars. According to analyses by the Riess group, the distances match the Hubble data, so a simple measuring error became less likely. The group led by **Wendy Freedman** uses the tip of the **red giant branch** as a standard candle and finds values around 70. **Standard sirens**, gravitational waves from merging neutron stars, also give an independent value. The event GW170817 gave about 70, still with great uncertainty.

Perhaps there is an undiscovered error in one of the measurements after all. But many experts also think it is possible that the standard model needs to be extended. One idea often discussed is **early dark energy**, an extra form of energy shortly before the background radiation was released. It would change the analysis of the Planck data and give a larger Hubble constant. So far, no explanation has been generally accepted.

gewusst: In physics, a difference of 5 sigma is considered the threshold for a discovery.
The Hubble tension is one of the most discussed questions in astronomy today.
